faqs.question: What will I actually have in my hands after a term of online tuition?
faqs.answer: Five documents. A marked baseline paper from week one with every lost mark categorised as recall, method, command term or timing. A running error log showing which errors have stopped recurring. Annotated feedback on your child's own written work, given as comments and criterion references rather than replacement prose. A short note after each session recording what was covered and set. And a written mid-term review comparing the current position against the week-one paper. Ask for the baseline before you agree the hours, because a record cannot be reconstructed later and the comparison is what makes the term checkable.

faqs.question: Why does the first session produce a paper rather than teaching?
faqs.answer: Because a mark on its own cannot tell you what to buy. The same score comes from a student who knows the content and runs out of time, one who answers a different question than the one asked, and one with three blank topics, and those three need entirely different terms of work. Categorising the lost marks in week one tells you which situation you are in, in writing, before the hours are spent. It also creates the only thing a later paper can be honestly compared against. A term that skips the baseline never recovers the ability to measure itself.

faqs.question: How quickly should we expect the school report to change?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on what is being fixed, and the sequence is consistent. Command-term accuracy and answer structure usually show movement within two to five weeks, because they are habits rather than knowledge. Timing follows after three or four full papers under real conditions. Method discipline takes six to eight weeks. Content recall is slowest and needs a term or more of spaced retrieval. If your window is short, target the things that move in that window rather than the slowest category. Nobody can promise a grade, and anyone who does is making a claim they cannot support.

faqs.question: Where exactly does feedback on an internal assessment stop being legitimate?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the boundary is checkable. A tutor can explain the assessment criteria, model a technique on different material, ask questions about a draft, and say that a conclusion does not follow from the evidence presented. A tutor cannot supply sentences that end up in the submission, under any framing or label. If feedback arrives as replacement prose rather than questions and criterion references, the line has been crossed. One provider in the wider UAE results sells finished internal assessments at AED 3,750; buying that is a malpractice risk for the student rather than a shortcut.

faqs.question: My child is the only one at their school taking a particular Higher Level subject. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It matters quite a lot, and it is common in Abu Dhabi because Diploma cohorts here are small per school. A student alone in a Higher Level class has no peer to compare pace with, no study group, and sometimes a teacher covering the subject alongside others. The practical consequence is that misconceptions go unchallenged for longer. It is also the clearest case for reaching a specialist online rather than locally, because an in-home arrangement limits the pool to tutors willing to travel to your community at the time your child is free, which selects for geography rather than subject depth.

faqs.question: What does an inspection rating tell me about whether my child needs support?
faqs.answer: Less than parents assume. ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi and publishes inspection outcomes, and those outcomes describe a school rather than a subject. A strongly rated school can still have a thin Higher Level cohort in one subject, a mid-year teacher change, or a timetable that puts a demanding subject in the worst slot of the week. Reading a good rating as a reason not to need help, or a weaker one as cause for alarm, both skip the only reliable evidence: your child's own marked work in the specific subject.

faqs.question: How are session slots set around the Abu Dhabi school run?
faqs.answer: Around the time your child is genuinely home and free, which varies more by community than families expect. Khalifa City and Al Raha have the longest bus runs in the emirate, so students there are often home only after 16:00 and sessions sit at 17:30 or later. Island communities with short commutes can start at 16:30. Fixed weekly slots survive a term; flexible booking tends to drift and then collapse. Where a school internal deadline falls, the session sequence moves to fit the school's calendar rather than ours.

faqs.question: Does the tutor need a permit to teach my child, and can I check it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and yes. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Ask any tutor directly whether they hold it and to show it. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published.

faqs.question: Is my child's own school teacher allowed to tutor them privately for a fee?
faqs.answer: In Abu Dhabi the answer is no. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. This has been reported in the press rather than read from the current policy text, so verify the exact wording against ADEK's own publication. The underlying principle holds regardless: the person who sets and marks your child's school assessments should not also be paid privately to prepare them for it.

faqs.question: What do Abu Dhabi families actually pay per hour for IB support?
faqs.answer: Published market rates run roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour for budget or university-student tutors, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180 to 500 for an in-home visit with travel inside the rate, and AED 200 to 450 or more for an IB or A Level specialist. One premium provider publishes AED 650. Those come from provider pages and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, read in October 2026, and are the market rather than an IB Gram price list. Our figure follows the free trial and the baseline paper, because quoting before reading a script is guesswork.

faqs.question: How does a shared screen produce a better record than a tutor at the table?
faqs.answer: Three ways. A past paper annotated on screen is saved and reopened in the next session, where a page annotated in pencil usually goes into a folder and is never looked at again. A worked solution survives as a document rather than being wiped off a whiteboard. And the error log can be a live shared file that the student, tutor and parent are all reading the same version of, which is the mechanism by which an error gets crossed off rather than vaguely remembered. The record is the argument for online here, not the convenience.

faqs.question: My child works better with someone physically in the room. Is online still worth trying?
faqs.answer: Possibly, and the trial lesson is the right way to find out rather than a discussion. Some students, particularly younger ones and those who rely on the social pressure of a present adult, do work differently on a screen. What often changes the picture is the structure rather than the format: a camera on, a fixed slot, work set between sessions and marked before the next one. Say this at the trial so the tutor can run it accordingly. If it genuinely does not work, that is a real answer and better found in one free session than after a term.

faqs.question: What happens at the mid-term review if nothing has moved?
faqs.answer: You get told, in writing, with the comparison attached. The error log is set against the week-one baseline and the categories are counted again. If a category has not moved, the approach changes rather than the hours increasing, which sometimes means a different tutor and occasionally means a different kind of arrangement altogether. If the honest answer is that the gap is content rather than technique and a short block was the wrong purchase, saying so is more useful than selling another term. Ask at the outset how that conversation is handled.

faqs.question: Can one tutor support two IB subjects at once, or should we book separately?
faqs.answer: It depends on the pairing rather than on the tutor. Two subjects in the same group, such as Physics and Mathematics Analysis and Approaches, often share method and are efficient together because the error log overlaps. Two subjects with different assessment logic, such as a science and an English A course, generally do better with separate specialists, because the markbands and the skills being corrected have almost nothing in common. The practical test is whether the same error log would serve both. If it would not, you are really buying two arrangements and should price them as such.

faqs.question: Will you give us past papers, mark schemes and subject guides to work from?
faqs.answer: We will point you at them and work from them in session, but we will not send you bundles of them. IB subject guides, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the IB, and redistributing them is copyright infringement regardless of how widely it is done in this market. Current material is available through your child's school and the IB's own channels, which is also where the version that matches the current syllabus lives. A tutor handing over a folder of old papers as a selling point is offering something that is both unlawful to supply and frequently out of date.

abu-dhabi/ib-online-tuition.closingHeading: Ask for the baseline before you agree the hours
abu-dhabi/ib-online-tuition.closingBody: The useful test of IB online tuition in Abu Dhabi is not how impressive the first conversation sounds. It is whether you will be holding something readable after eight weeks: a marked baseline, an error log with items crossed off, draft feedback given as questions, and a written review against the first paper. Take the free trial lesson with the tutor who would actually teach, ask for the week-one paper to be marked and categorised before any hours are committed, and judge the arrangement on what it produces. Sessions run one-to-one over live video at Gulf Standard Time.

abu-dhabi/ib-online-tutor.tutorsIntro: Below are tutors currently working with Abu Dhabi students on Diploma and Middle Years courses. Read the course and the level before booking, because Higher Level and Standard Level versions of the same subject are different teaching briefs with different components attached.

intro.heading: The question is not whether online works. It is what is on the screen
paragraphs: Ten years ago the argument about online tutoring was about whether a child learns through a screen. That argument is over, and it was never the interesting one. What separates a good online Diploma hour from a wasted one is far more specific: whether the tutor can put the right thing in front of the student at the right moment, and whether the student can write on it. A physics tutor who cannot annotate a graph live, or a mathematics tutor who talks through a derivation the student never sees written, is doing a weaker job over video than they would do with a pencil and a kitchen table.

That is a solvable problem, and solving it is what distinguishes the specialists in this market. The equipment is unglamorous: a stylus, a shared canvas, a document camera or a phone propped over a page, a split screen with the question paper on one side and the mark scheme on the other. None of it is expensive. What is rare is a tutor who has thought about which configuration each Diploma component needs, because the components are genuinely different. A Language A individual oral rehearsal needs the extract on screen and the clock visible. A chemistry mechanism needs a canvas deep enough to draw six steps without scrolling.

So this page is organised by subject group rather than by benefit. For each of the six Diploma groups it sets out what the assessment actually demands, where Abu Dhabi students lose marks on it, what has to be visible during a live hour for that loss to be addressable, and what video genuinely cannot do. The honest limits are included because a provider who claims video does everything equally well is not someone who has taught a practical subject.

Delivery is stated plainly. Every session IB Gram arranges for a UAE family runs one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. In Abu Dhabi that constraint mostly works in a family's favour, because the emirate's Diploma cohorts are spread across many schools rather than concentrated in a few, and the number of people within a short drive who have actually taught a particular Higher Level course is often very small.

One framing note before the detail. Most marks lost in the Diploma are not lost to ignorance. They are lost to command terms, to timing, to a diagram without labels, to an evaluation written generically, to a student answering a question adjacent to the one asked. Those are all visible in written work and all fixable in a one-to-one hour, which is why a diagnostic matters more than a syllabus walk-through. A tutor who begins by asking what topic you want covered has skipped the only question worth asking first.

Nothing here promises a grade. No tutor can, and the providers who do are describing their marketing rather than their teaching. What a specialist can do over video is see precisely where a student's marks are going, teach the specific habit that stops it, and show you the before and after on marked work.

Online access to a second specialist in exactly that course is the practical answer to that, and it is a different answer from hiring whoever teaches the subject locally.

Online this is straightforward, because the task sheet, the criterion wording and the student's work can all be on screen at once.
programmes.countryNote: Middle Years work in Abu Dhabi is dominated by arrivals. A student joining MYP 4 from an American, Indian or British school part way through has no external benchmark, and the school's criterion scores take a term to become meaningful. Sessions in that first term are best spent building a benchmark rather than covering content nobody has yet established is missing.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The least discussed of the IB routes: at least two Diploma courses taken alongside a career-related study and a core of personal and professional skills, reflective project, service learning and language development. Where a school offers it, students still sit full Diploma courses, so the subject teaching is identical even though the overall certificate is not.
programmes.countryNote: Few Abu Dhabi schools run the Career-related Programme, which means families whose child is on it often find that nobody in the local tutoring market has heard of it. Sessions concentrate on the Diploma courses within it and on the reflective project, which is assessed and therefore subject to exactly the same honesty boundaries as an Extended Essay.

programmes.name: The step into DP1
programmes.ageRange: The eighteen months spanning MYP 5 and DP1
programmes.description: The crossing from criterion-referenced reporting to timed external papers catches out students who have never been wrong under a clock. Marks drop even where knowledge is sound, because the new skill being tested is producing a correct answer in a fixed time against a command term. It is a behaviour change, and behaviour changes respond quickly to one-to-one attention.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi has continuum schools where students move from the Middle Years into the Diploma in the same building, and schools that take a DP1 intake from British and American schools across the emirate. The second group usually arrives with better exam technique and weaker independent research habits, which decides what the first few online hours should address.

abu-dhabi/ib-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: Diploma courses Abu Dhabi families book most often, with the specific mark loss a live hour addresses in each. Confirm every weighting and criterion against the current subject guide your child's school is teaching; guides change between cohorts.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus and the Higher Level extension content are the areas where a generalist runs out. The session screen needs a canvas a student can write on while the tutor watches the working appear, because the error is almost always in a line of algebra rather than in the method chosen.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Technology is assumed throughout, so the calculator is part of the assessment. A session needs the student's own calculator visible on camera or emulated on screen, because a student who can do the mathematics but not drive the device loses marks that look like content failures.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Data-based questions concentrate marks around gradients, uncertainties and units. Online these are better taught than in a room, because the graph can be annotated, undone and redrawn in seconds while the student watches the consequence of each decision.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms need drawing space and arrows, and equilibrium needs algebra alongside a diagram. A shallow shared whiteboard forces scrolling mid-explanation, which is the most common reason an online chemistry hour feels thinner than it should.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Extended-response marks hang on command terms. The highest-value screen in a biology session is the student's own marked answer beside the mark scheme, because the gap between what they wrote and what was required is visible rather than described.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram marks are the cheapest in the Diploma and the most often discarded. A live canvas lets a tutor delete one axis label and ask what mark has just been lost, which teaches the habit faster than any amount of advice about being careful.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Application to stimulus material separates grades. The screen needs the case material and the answer side by side so a student can be shown that their paragraph would score identically if the company name were swapped, which is precisely why it is losing marks.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The individual oral is timed, rehearsed and marked against published criteria, which makes it the most improvable component in the Diploma. Video is better than a room here, because a rehearsal can be recorded and played back against the criteria immediately.

subjects.name: Spanish, French and Arabic B
subjects.description: Listening and the individual oral dominate the recoverable marks. Audio over a good connection is cleaner than audio across a room, and the oral can be rehearsed under the real time constraint with the stimulus visual on screen exactly as it will appear.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Paper 1 source work has a fixed shape and a fixed set of errors: describing a source rather than using it, skipping provenance, missing the comparison. All three are visible in the margin of a marked answer and drillable within a month.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: One of the hardest courses to staff locally in this emirate and one of the easiest to teach well over video, because code, output and error messages are all screen-native. Pseudocode in the papers is where marks are most often lost, not in programming itself.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: A transdisciplinary course that students often take as a second science and then underestimate. Marks concentrate in systems diagrams and in evaluating competing environmental value systems, both of which are drawing and structuring tasks rather than recall.

abu-dhabi/ib-online-tutor.regionsIntro: An online tutor is reachable from anywhere in the emirate, so geography stops deciding who teaches your child. What it still decides is when the hour can start and whether it survives a whole term. These are the Abu Dhabi patterns we plan sessions around.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment towers with short crossings to the island schools. The scheduling constraint is rarely travel and usually a second child doing homework in the same room, so a headset and a door matter more than a later slot.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Short bus runs from a dense cluster of nearby schools make a 16:00 start genuinely possible here. An early slot is worth protecting, because the hours that survive a full term are the ones that happen before the evening fills up.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Villa community with most children at schools a few minutes along the same corridor. Families here often run a weekend block for component work and keep weekday sessions for shorter, sharper technique drills.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Two bridge crossings a day and low-density housing. A single ninety-minute weekend block usually works better than two weekday hours, particularly for Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge work that needs uninterrupted thinking time.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Central and well served by long-established schools, with short home runs. Sessions can begin before the household eats, which protects them from being quietly dropped once evening commitments appear.

regions.name: Shakhbout City
regions.note: Large villas across the mainland with a wide spread of school choices, and often several children on different timetables. The scheduling question here is which child gets the hour, not which tutor lives nearby.

regions.name: Masdar City
regions.note: A small residential population with children bussed out to schools in the Khalifa City cluster, so the bus return time sets the earliest realistic start. Quiet study space is usually easier here than in the towers.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: Established central district close to several long-standing schools. Parents here are often home earlier, which makes a 17:00 slot viable and makes it easier for somebody to notice whether the hour actually happened.

schoolClusters.city: Island and central Abu Dhabi
schoolClusters.note: The older part of the emirate's private sector, with several schools that have run British or international programmes for decades. Diploma sets here are typically small, so a student who does not get on with the one teacher delivering their Higher Level course has limited options inside the building.
schools: American Community School of Abu Dhabi
Nord Anglia International School Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: The Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor
schoolClusters.note: Most of the emirate's newer Diploma capacity, clustered within a short drive. Mid-year moves between these schools are common and subject sequencing between any two of them is rarely identical, which is the most frequent cause of a sudden unexplained drop in marks.

abu-dhabi/ib-online-tutor.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named only as context for the Abu Dhabi education landscape that students we support attend. No affiliation, partnership or endorsement by any school, group or regulator is implied.
abu-dhabi/ib-online-tutor.modesIntro: Three ways Abu Dhabi families use an online Diploma tutor. They are not price tiers. They solve different problems, and buying the wrong one is the usual reason tuition disappoints.

modes.title: Weekly subject teaching
modes.description: A fixed hour each week on one named course at one named level, held with the same specialist over live video. This is the format for a content gap: a student who did not understand calculus in DP1 and now cannot do the Higher Level extension. It accumulates, which is its strength, and it is also the easiest format to drift in without a written plan.
bullets: Same tutor and same slot through a term
A shared canvas kept and reusable between sessions
Work set between sessions and marked before the next one
A review point with a stop option built in

modes.title: Technique intensives before a paper
modes.description: Short blocks aimed at exam behaviour rather than content: command terms, minutes per mark, reading a data question, structuring a seven-mark answer. These move marks fastest in students who already know the material, which is a surprisingly large share of the students families bring to us in DP2.
bullets: Timed papers under stated, repeatable conditions
Marked against the published scheme, not an impression
Error pattern named and drilled, then re-tested
Finite: a set number of hours with an end date

modes.title: Component blocks on internally assessed work
modes.description: A scoped block for one assessed component: the mathematics exploration, a scientific investigation, a Language A individual oral, a Theory of Knowledge exhibition. The student produces everything. The tutor teaches the method, questions what the student has drafted and gives criterion-level feedback, and the block ends at submission.
bullets: Attached to one component with a known school deadline
Feedback against the published criteria, in writing
A record of which draft received which comments
No rolling retainer afterwards

sections.heading: What has to be on screen, group by group
paragraphs: The useful way to judge an IB online tutor is to ask what their screen will look like during your child's session. For a Diploma course that is not a vague question. Each group has a dominant assessment behaviour, and each behaviour needs a specific thing visible. Get it wrong and the hour becomes a conversation about the subject rather than work on it.

Three configurations cover most of it. The first is the shared writable canvas, for anything where the student's own working is the diagnostic: mathematics, physics calculations, chemistry mechanisms, economics diagrams. The tutor must be able to watch the working appear line by line, because the error is almost always in a specific line rather than in the approach. The second is the split view, with the question paper on one side and the published criteria or mark scheme on the other, for anything written and externally marked. The third is audio-and-clock, for the orals and listening components, where the only things that matter are sound quality and the time constraint being real.

What fails without the right configuration is specific rather than general. A mathematics session run by talking produces a student who nods and cannot reproduce the step. A biology session without the mark scheme on screen produces advice to write more detail, which is the single least useful instruction in the Diploma. An oral rehearsal without a visible clock produces a student who runs long in the real thing, which costs marks on structure rather than on content.

This is worth asking about directly before booking anything, including from us. A specialist will answer in one sentence because they have a set-up they use every day. A generalist will say that they share their screen, which is not the same thing and is the most common answer in this market.

sections.heading: Handwritten mathematics over video, in practice
paragraphs: Mathematics is the subject families worry about most when considering an online tutor, and the worry is reasonable: mathematics is a handwriting activity. The resolution is equipment rather than compromise, and it is cheap. A student needs some way to write that the tutor can see in real time. A stylus on a tablet is ideal. A phone on a stand, angled over a sheet of paper, is almost as good and costs nothing. What does not work is a student writing on paper the tutor cannot see and reading out answers, because the whole diagnostic value is in the working, not the answer.

Once the working is visible, video has a genuine advantage over sitting side by side. The tutor can take the student's own line, copy it, and change one thing to show what happens. In Applications and Interpretation, where technology is assumed throughout, the calculator can be on screen at the same time as the question, and a student can be watched driving it. A surprising share of mathematics marks in this course are lost not to mathematics but to a student who cannot get the device to produce a regression or a distribution under time pressure, and that is invisible until somebody watches them try.

The Higher Level extension content is where the choice of tutor matters more than the choice of medium. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level includes material that a competent Standard Level teacher may never have taught. Proof by induction, the deeper calculus, the Higher Level toolkit in Applications: these are the areas where a generalist becomes visibly uncertain, and online that uncertainty is harder to hide than in a room, because the working is on screen and either it flows or it does not.

For the exploration, the medium is almost irrelevant and the conversation is everything. The twenty marks are split across five criteria, with the largest block on use of mathematics, which means the topic choice decides most of the ceiling before any writing happens. One well-spent hour interrogating a proposed topic is worth more than five spent tidying a draft, and that hour works identically over video.
bullets: A stylus, or a phone angled over paper, so the working is visible live
The student writes; the tutor watches the line where it breaks
The calculator on screen for Applications and Interpretation
Higher Level extension topics are a tutor-choice question, not a medium question

sections.heading: Group 4: what video does well, and the two things it does not
paragraphs: Science teaching online divides cleanly. Everything that is about handling data, reasoning about uncertainty, interpreting a graph or evaluating a method is at least as good over video as in a room, and often better, because the artefact can be manipulated. Everything that involves physically handling apparatus is not, and pretending otherwise is dishonest.

Start with what works. Data-based questions are where Group 4 marks concentrate and where cohorts leak them systematically. A student states an uncertainty and then does not carry it through to the final answer. A gradient is calculated from the wrong pair of points. Units vanish between lines. A graph is drawn with a line of best fit that ignores an obvious outlier without comment. Every one of those is visible on a shared screen, correctable in minutes, and testable on a fresh question a fortnight later. The internal investigation is similar: the criteria covering research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation are published, and evaluation is where whole cohorts lose marks because they list generic limitations instead of criticising the method they actually used.

Now the limits. First, no online session teaches apparatus skill. A student who has never set up a circuit or titrated will not acquire that from a screen, and the school laboratory is the only place that happens. Where a student has missed practical work, the honest statement is that we can teach the reasoning and the write-up and cannot replace the bench. Second, nobody outside the school can supply data. An investigation needs the student's own results, and a tutor who offers numbers is handing the student a malpractice finding rather than a favour.

The practical consequence for Abu Dhabi families is simple. If the problem is that your child is losing data-question marks, an online specialist is the right purchase and will show you movement on marked papers within weeks. If the problem is that your child has missed a term of laboratory sessions, talk to the school first, because that is a gap only the school can close.

sections.heading: The orals and the listening papers, where video beats a room
paragraphs: The components most improvable by an online tutor are the spoken ones, and almost nobody markets them. A Language A individual oral is a timed performance against four published criteria, prepared in advance, on extracts the student has worked with. Language B has an individual oral built around a stimulus. These are rehearsable in the way a music examination is rehearsable, and rehearsal is where marks live.

Video is better than a room for this, for three reasons. The recording is already digital, so a student can watch themselves immediately and mark their own attempt against the criteria, which is far more persuasive than being told. The clock is on screen and visible to both parties, so a student discovers in week one that they have been running two minutes long rather than discovering it in the real thing. And the stimulus can be displayed exactly as it will appear, rather than printed badly on a sheet at the kitchen table.

The listening papers reward the same treatment. Students lose marks on listening not because they cannot understand the audio but because they do not use the reading time, do not annotate while listening, or write an answer that does not match the question's form. Those are procedural habits. They are taught by doing a section under real timing, marking it, naming the specific lapse, and doing another. Clean audio over a headset is a better listening environment than most classrooms.

The one genuine caution is that the real individual oral will be conducted by the student's own teacher, in a room, under the school's arrangements. A rehearsal that happens only on screen can leave a student unused to the physical situation. The fix is cheap and we recommend it: once the content is secure, the last two rehearsals should be done standing up, away from the screen, with a phone recording and a parent holding the clock. The technique transfers. The nerves need the room.
bullets: Rehearsals recorded and marked by the student against the published criteria
A visible clock, so over-running is discovered in week one
Stimulus and extracts displayed exactly as they will appear
Final rehearsals moved off-screen deliberately, standing, with a parent timing

sections.heading: Where IB marks actually go missing, and how many hours each loss takes
paragraphs: Families usually describe the problem as a subject: he is struggling with chemistry. Marked work almost never agrees. The loss is normally one of a small number of recurring, nameable behaviours, and knowing which one changes both the number of hours needed and whether a tutor is the right purchase at all.

Command-term failure is the largest single category across Group 3 and Group 4. A student who knows the content writes a description where the question asked for an explanation, or explains where it asked for an evaluation, and loses the top band on every extended item. This is drillable within a month using the student's own previously marked answers, because they have already demonstrated that they know the material.

Timing failure is the second. A student who scores well on untimed work and badly under a clock does not have a content problem. They have never been taught minutes per mark, and they are writing a careful first answer at the cost of the last two questions. Three to five hours of timed work with a visible clock and a post-mortem each time usually resolves it, and the improvement is unusually easy to measure.

Then there are the smaller categories that are cheap to fix and large in aggregate: unlabelled diagrams in economics, missing units in physics, generic evaluation in a scientific investigation, no reference to the stimulus in a business answer. The remaining category is genuine content gap, which is the slowest and most expensive to close, and the one that deserves a weekly arrangement rather than an intensive. A diagnostic hour tells you which of these you are buying, which is why we would rather do that than start teaching topics in session one.

sections.heading: Connection, latency and the Abu Dhabi evening
paragraphs: The practical objection to online tutoring is rarely pedagogical. It is that the connection failed once and the family decided the format does not work. Worth separating the problems, because they have different causes and only one of them is actually about the internet.

The symptom that matters most is latency, not bandwidth. A session can run perfectly on a modest connection if the delay is short, and badly on a fast one if it is not, because teaching depends on interruption. A tutor needs to be able to stop a student mid-line. With half a second of delay that becomes impossible and the hour turns into alternating monologues. Video resolution, by contrast, barely matters: a shared canvas at low resolution is entirely usable, and turning the camera feed off is often the single most effective fix available.

Evening congestion in dense residential towers is real and predictable. Al Reem Island at 20:00 is a busier network than the same building at 16:30, which is one more argument for the earlier slot that this page keeps making for other reasons. A wired connection removes most of it. A headset removes most audio problems, because the worst audio in any online lesson is a laptop microphone in a tiled room with a television in the background.

The policy question is what happens when a session breaks anyway, and every provider should have a stated answer before you pay. Ours: if a session is lost to a connection failure on either side, it is rescheduled rather than charged, the shared canvas from the part that happened is saved, and work set is sent in writing so nothing depends on the student having heard it. Ask for that in writing. A provider without a policy has not had the conversation often enough.

sections.heading: Running a timed paper properly when the tutor is not in the room
paragraphs: Timed practice is the highest-value thing an online tutor does and the easiest thing to do badly. A paper done at home, over two evenings, with the mark scheme within reach, produces a score that means nothing and a false sense of security that lasts until the mock. If timed work is going to be the measurement, the conditions have to be real and they have to be written down.

The workable version is unglamorous. The paper is sent at an agreed time. The student has it for exactly the stated duration. The tutor is on the call, muted, with the camera on, doing their own work. There is no mark scheme in the room and no phone on the desk. At the end the student photographs or uploads the script immediately. Marking happens afterwards against the published scheme, and the marked script comes back before the next session with the losses categorised rather than just totalled.

Writing the conditions down matters more than it sounds, because the comparison is the point. Two papers four weeks apart only mean something if the duration, the content coverage and the marker are the same. Change any one and the second score is a different measurement. Families regularly conclude that tuition is not working on the basis of two papers that were not comparable, and occasionally conclude the opposite on the same basis.

The frequency question has a defensible answer: roughly one properly timed component a fortnight through DP2, more often in the final six weeks, and hardly at all in DP1 where the content is still arriving. Over-testing produces demoralisation and no new information, because the error pattern does not change week to week. Under-testing means nobody discovers until the mock that a student cannot finish the paper.
bullets: Conditions written down: duration, content covered, who marks it
Tutor present on the call, muted, camera on; no mark scheme within reach
Script uploaded at the bell, not after a break
Marked against the published scheme, with losses categorised not just totalled
About one timed component a fortnight in DP2; far fewer in DP1

sections.heading: Delivery, coverage and the permit nobody mentions
paragraphs: Sessions for Abu Dhabi families run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. We put that in writing before any payment, because two providers ranking for these searches route UAE parents to Indian telephone numbers without stating where the teaching happens, which is a trust failure rather than a logistical detail.

Coverage is the second thing most providers leave out. Higher Level courses with small cohorts across the whole emirate are genuinely hard to staff, and anybody claiming instant availability across every Diploma course is either guessing or about to put a generalist in front of a Higher Level student. Where no UAE-based specialist is free for the course and level required, we offer a specialist elsewhere, usually one of our India-based IB teachers, working on Gulf Standard Time so the family's evening does not change. Format and documentation are identical, and families are told in advance.

The regulatory position is worth knowing because almost nobody in this market explains it. Private tutoring in the UAE is permitted by permit: the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

One Abu Dhabi-specific point follows from that. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the holder's school. So the arrangement many families instinctively want, paying their child's own subject teacher for evening sessions, is the one to rule out. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it.

sections.heading: Choosing between two online tutors who both sound competent
paragraphs: Most families reach a shortlist of two and then choose on warmth, which is not a bad signal and is a poor primary one. Four questions separate them reliably, and all four can be asked in a message before a trial.

First: which course and level, exactly, and when did you last teach it? Not mathematics, but Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. The difference between a tutor who taught that course last year and one who taught Standard Level four years ago is the difference between fluency and reconstruction, and it shows up precisely in the Higher Level extension topics where your child needs help. Second: which guide is my child's school teaching, and what changed from the previous one? A specialist knows that guides change and asks which cohort your child is in. A generalist works from whatever they last used.

Third: what will be on your screen in the first session? A specialist answers concretely in one sentence, because they have a configuration they use daily. Fourth: what will I receive between sessions, and in what form? Marked work and a four-line note beats a long weekly message of reassurance, and a tutor who commits to the former in advance usually delivers it.

The trial lesson then settles it, if you use it as a diagnostic rather than a demonstration. A good first online hour spends its early part finding out where the marks are going and its later part proving one fix on the student's own work. A bad one is a tour of the syllabus. Ask your child one question afterwards: what will you do differently in the next piece of work? A specific answer is a good sign. A general one about understanding things better is not, however pleasant the hour was.
bullets: Name the exact course and level and ask when they last taught it
Ask which subject guide applies to your child's cohort
Ask what will be on the screen, and expect a concrete answer
Ask what arrives between sessions and in what form
After the trial, ask your child what they will do differently next time

process.title: Send the course, not the subject
process.description: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, examination session, school, and the specific difficulty. Add one photographed piece of marked work if you have it. That produces a specialist match rather than whoever teaches mathematics, which is the most common reason a first match goes wrong.

process.title: Use the trial hour as a diagnostic
process.description: The free session exists to find out where the marks are going, not to demonstrate teaching. Expect the tutor to look at written work, name a pattern and prove one fix. Ask for a short written view afterwards even if you book nothing further.

process.title: Set up the screen once, properly
process.description: A stylus or a phone on a stand for written subjects, a wired headset for languages, a wired connection if the building is congested in the evening. Twenty minutes of setup removes most of what families later describe as online tutoring not working.

process.title: Fix the slot early in the day
process.description: An hour that starts before the evening fills up survives a term; a 20:00 slot does not. We plan around school bus returns rather than around what looks tidy on a calendar, and in the towers an earlier slot also avoids evening network congestion.

process.title: Measure on timed components, then review
process.description: One properly timed component a fortnight in DP2, conditions written down, marked against the published scheme. At week six, compare against the baseline and decide to continue, change a variable, or stop. We will say when the answer is stop.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the course code, not the subject
whyPoints.description: Higher Level and Standard Level versions of the same course are different teaching jobs with different components and different extension content. We match on the course a student is entered for, and we say so when we cannot staff it inside the emirate.

whyPoints.title: A screen built for the component
whyPoints.description: A writable canvas for mathematics and sciences, split views for written papers against the criteria, clean audio and a visible clock for the orals. The configuration follows the assessment rather than the habit of sharing a slide deck.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what video cannot do
whyPoints.description: Apparatus skill is not teachable from a screen and we say so. Nobody supplies data for an investigation. Where the school laboratory is the gap, we tell families to talk to the school rather than selling them hours that cannot close it.

whyPoints.title: Online, one-to-one, stated before payment
whyPoints.description: Sessions run over live video on Gulf Standard Time. We do not send tutors to UAE homes. The trade is a specialist chosen for the syllabus rather than for the drive, which matters in an emirate where Diploma cohorts are small and spread out.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches method, questions a student's own draft and gives criterion-level feedback. They do not supply sentences, structure or data for assessed work. We decline the urgent requests as well, because the consequence falls on the student.

whyPoints.title: Sourced figures, no invented ones
whyPoints.description: AED figures on our pages are published market or competitor rates with the source named and the month stated. We publish no satisfaction percentages, no star ratings, and no IB examination dates that have not been confirmed at source.

faqs.question: What should be on an IB online tutor's screen during my child's session?
faqs.answer: It depends on the component, which is why the question is a good test of a tutor. Mathematics, physics calculations, chemistry mechanisms and economics diagrams need a shared writable canvas the student uses while the tutor watches the working appear. Written Group 3 and Group 4 answers need a split view with the student's marked work beside the published criteria. The orals and listening papers need clean audio and a visible clock. A specialist answers this in one sentence. A generalist says they share their screen, which is not the same thing.

faqs.question: How does a tutor see my child's handwritten mathematics working?
faqs.answer: Through a stylus on a tablet, or a phone on a stand angled over a sheet of paper, which costs nothing and works almost as well. What does not work is the student writing on paper nobody can see and reading out answers, because the whole diagnostic value sits in the working rather than the answer. Once the working is visible, video has an advantage over sitting side by side: the tutor can copy the student's own line, change one thing, and show the consequence immediately.

faqs.question: Does my child need a graphics tablet for online Diploma sessions?
faqs.answer: It helps for mathematics and the sciences and is not essential anywhere. A stylus and tablet give the cleanest result. A phone on a cheap stand over paper is the next best and is what most families use. For Group 3 subjects, languages and the core, a laptop and a wired headset are enough, because the work is typed or spoken rather than drawn. Spend on the headset before the tablet: poor audio damages more sessions than poor handwriting capture does.

faqs.question: Which Diploma components are genuinely harder to teach over video?
faqs.answer: Only the ones involving physical apparatus. A student who has never set up a circuit or run a titration will not learn that from a screen, and the school laboratory is the only place it happens. Everything else in Group 4 is at least as good online, often better, because graphs and calculations can be annotated, undone and redrawn. For Group 6 the artwork itself is made away from the session, but the assessed documentation and the critical commentary are screen-native and benefit from it.

faqs.question: Can a Language B listening paper be practised properly over video?
faqs.answer: Yes, and usually in a better acoustic environment than a classroom. Clean audio through a headset beats a speaker at the front of a room. Listening marks are mostly lost to procedure rather than comprehension: not using the reading time, not annotating while listening, writing an answer that does not match the question's form. Those habits are taught by doing a section under real timing, marking it, naming the exact lapse and doing another. The medium makes that cycle faster rather than slower.

faqs.question: How do we rehearse the individual oral if the real one happens in a room?
faqs.answer: Rehearse the content on screen, then deliberately move off it. Video is better for the early work: the attempt is already recorded, so a student can watch themselves and mark their own performance against the four published criteria, and a visible clock means over-running is discovered in week one rather than on the day. Once the content is secure, do the final two rehearsals standing up, away from the screen, with a phone recording and a parent holding the clock. Technique transfers; the physical situation needs practising separately.

faqs.question: Which connection problems actually ruin a session, and which do not?
faqs.answer: Latency ruins sessions; bandwidth mostly does not. Teaching depends on being able to interrupt a student mid-line, and half a second of delay turns an hour into alternating monologues. Blurry video is almost irrelevant, because the shared canvas is what matters, and turning the camera off often improves the lesson. Echo is a room problem solved by a basic headset. In towers, sessions degrade after 20:00 through evening congestion, which is one more reason to take an earlier slot.

faqs.question: What happens if the session drops out halfway through?
faqs.answer: Ask for the policy in writing before you pay, from us or anyone. Ours: a session lost to a connection failure on either side is rescheduled rather than charged, the shared canvas from the part that happened is saved so nothing is repeated from memory, and any work set is sent in writing so it does not depend on the student having heard it. A provider without a stated position on this has not had the conversation often enough to have formed one, which is itself informative.

faqs.question: How is a timed paper run properly when the tutor is not in the room?
faqs.answer: The paper is sent at an agreed time and the student has it for exactly the stated duration. The tutor stays on the call, muted, camera on, working on something else. No mark scheme within reach and no phone on the desk. The script is uploaded at the bell, not after a break. Marking happens afterwards against the published scheme, with losses categorised rather than totalled. Write the conditions down, because two papers only compare if duration, content and marker are the same.

faqs.question: How often should a DP2 student sit a properly timed component?
faqs.answer: Roughly one a fortnight through DP2, rising in the final six weeks, and very few in DP1 where content is still arriving. Over-testing produces demoralisation and no new information, because an error pattern does not change week to week. Under-testing means nobody discovers until the mock that the student cannot finish the paper. The value is not the score. It is the categorised list of losses afterwards, which is what the next two sessions are built from.

faqs.question: Which subject groups lose the most marks to command terms rather than content?
faqs.answer: Group 3 and Group 4, by a wide margin. A student who knows the material writes a description where the question asked for an explanation, or explains where it asked for an evaluation, and loses the top band on every extended item. It is the cheapest loss to fix, usually three to six hours using the student's own previously marked answers, precisely because the student has already demonstrated that the knowledge is there. A full content re-teach is the wrong purchase for this problem.

faqs.question: Does an online tutor know which subject guide my child's school is teaching?
faqs.answer: A specialist asks; a generalist assumes. Guides change between cohorts, and weightings, criteria and content can all move, so a tutor working from the version they last taught may be teaching the right subject to the wrong syllabus. Ask the question directly before booking, and expect the tutor to want the school's course outline. Nothing on any tutoring page, including this one, should be relied on over the guide your child's school is actually delivering.

faqs.question: Can one online session cover two Higher Level subjects?
faqs.answer: It can be done and it is usually a poor purchase. Two Higher Level subjects in one hour gives roughly twenty-five usable minutes each after settling and setting work, which is enough to review something and not enough to fix anything. Where a student genuinely needs both, the better structure is alternating weeks with work set in the off week, or two shorter sessions on different days. Combining them tends to reflect a budget decision, and it is worth naming that rather than pretending it is a teaching decision.

faqs.question: Is screen fatigue a real argument against online tuition for Diploma students?
faqs.answer: It is real and it is an argument about scheduling rather than about format. A student who has been on a laptop since 08:00 will not give you a good hour at 20:00, online or otherwise. The practical responses are an earlier slot, sixty minutes rather than ninety, the camera off when it adds nothing, and work on paper with the camera over it rather than everything typed. Families who fix the slot rather than the medium usually find the fatigue argument disappears.

faqs.question: Does ADEK or MoHRE issue a licence that makes a tutor an approved IB tutor?
faqs.answer: No such thing exists. ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi, not individual tutors. The relevant permit is federal: the MoHRE private tuition work permit under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, open to registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. It establishes that someone may lawfully tutor. It says nothing about whether they can teach Higher Level Chemistry, which is a separate question you have to test yourself.

abu-dhabi/ib-online-tutor.closingHeading: Ask what will be on the screen, then book the trial
abu-dhabi/ib-online-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB online tutor in Abu Dhabi, send the exact course and level, the examination session and one piece of marked work, and ask one question before anything else: what will be on your screen in the first session? The answer separates specialists from generalists faster than any credential list. Then use the free trial as a diagnostic rather than a demonstration, and afterwards ask your child what they will do differently in the next piece of work. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and we state the coverage position before any invoice.

abu-dhabi/ib-past-papers-practice.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach DP subjects at both levels and work on exam technique with the student's own completed papers. Each marks against the published assessment language your child's school uses and returns a written diagnosis after every session.

intro.heading: Doing papers is not practising; marking them honestly is
paragraphs: Almost every Abu Dhabi Diploma student does past papers. A much smaller number practise, in the sense that produces more marks. The difference is what happens in the twenty minutes after the paper is finished: whether it is marked against the scheme with real severity, whether the lost marks are categorised, and whether the same category shows up again next week. A student who completes twelve papers and marks none of them properly has spent twelve hours confirming what they already knew.

This page is about that second half, because the first half is freely available and the second half is where tutoring actually earns its fee. We work with the papers your child's school provides. We do not supply, host, email or reproduce IB past papers, mark schemes, subject guides or grade boundary tables, and any provider who offers to is distributing copyright material. The legitimate route is your child's teacher and the school's own licensed access, and a student who asks their teacher directly almost always gets what they need.

The second thing worth stating early is that past papers are a late-stage tool. A student working through a paper on content they have not yet been taught is not practising exam technique; they are discovering gaps in a slow and discouraging way. Papers earn their value once a topic is covered, and the sensible sequence is topic work first, topic-filtered questions second, whole papers under timed conditions third. Starting with whole papers in DP1 is one of the commonest wasted efforts we see.

Third, the marks lost in Diploma papers cluster into a small number of repeatable categories, and they are rarely content gaps. They are command term misreadings, answers that ignore the mark allocation, timing failures in the last third of a paper, working not shown, and data or source material not used where the question required it. Each of those is a technique fix rather than a revision topic, which is good news: technique moves faster than content.

We deliver this one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school evening. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. For paper work the shared screen is the right tool, because the student's own script, the mark scheme they are working from and the error log all need to be visible together. ADEK licenses and inspects the emirate's private schools, which set their own mock timetables, and those mocks are the fixed points we plan practice around. Fortnightly is the cadence that works for most families, because a student needs the intervening two weeks to sit a paper, mark it and rewrite the answers the last session identified.

abu-dhabi/ib-past-papers-practice.programmesIntro: Past paper work means different things at different stages of the IB continuum. Here is how it applies for a family in this emirate.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Written papers carry most of the grade in every DP subject, with internal assessment making up the rest. Each subject has its own paper structure, mark allocation and timing, and the command terms are shared across the programme. This is where past paper practice does the most work.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools generally run two sets of mocks, one late in DP1 or early in DP2 and one in the final term before the May session. Those mocks are the only timed full papers many students sit before the real thing, which makes the error log between them unusually valuable.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP assessment is criterion-based rather than paper-based, so there is no equivalent bank of past papers. What transfers to the DP is the command term vocabulary and the habit of reading what a task actually asks before answering it.
programmes.countryNote: Students arriving in DP1 from MYP in this emirate are often strong on extended writing and unused to tight mark allocations. The adjustment is technique rather than knowledge and takes a few weeks of question-level work.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: CP students taking DP courses sit the same papers in those subjects and benefit from the same practice discipline. The career-related study is assessed differently, so paper technique applies only to the DP components.
programmes.countryNote: CP cohorts are small in Abu Dhabi, which means fewer classmates sitting the same paper and less informal comparison. External marking of a practice script is correspondingly more useful.

abu-dhabi/ib-past-papers-practice.subjectsIntro: Paper technique is subject-specific below the level of command terms. These are the areas we work in and what practice has to target in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Method marks are the whole game. Students lose marks for correct answers with no working and for unjustified steps. Practice targets setting out, calculator and non-calculator discipline, and recognising which technique a question is testing from its phrasing.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Context questions where the modelling assumption has to be stated and interpreted. Marks go missing in interpretation sentences, where a student produces a number and never says what it means in the context the question set up.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Long-answer structure, units and significant figures, and the data-based questions where the answer must come from the graph or table provided rather than from memory. Practice focuses on extracting the required quantity before writing anything.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Calculation layout, state symbols, equation balancing and the explain questions where the mark depends on naming the correct interaction. Students who show every step of a mole calculation keep marks that students who go straight to an answer lose.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Terminology precision and command term discipline. An outline answer written as an explanation wastes time; an explain answer written as a list loses marks. Data-based questions reward reading the axes before reading the question again.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram marks, definition marks and evaluation marks, each with their own place in a structured answer. Paper technique here is largely about allocating time and words to match the mark allocation on each part.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case study and stimulus-based answers where the mark depends on applying theory to the organisation in the material rather than describing the theory. The commonest loss is a textbook-correct answer that never mentions the company in the question.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Source work and essay structure under time pressure. Practice targets the specific demands of each paper component and the discipline of answering the question asked rather than the question the student revised for.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided analysis and comparative essay technique, where marks follow from a line of argument rather than from feature-spotting. Timed practice is essential because the quality gap between a planned and unplanned response is visible immediately.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Extended response questions where the command term sets the structure and research studies have to be used as evidence rather than recounted. Practice focuses on building answers that evaluate rather than describe.

sections.heading: Where IB past papers legitimately come from
paragraphs: Start with the thing most pages in this market avoid. IB past papers, mark schemes, subject guides and grade boundary tables are the IB's copyright material. They are made available to schools through licensed access, and the proper route for a student is their own teacher or their school's internal resources. We do not supply them, host them, email them or reproduce any part of them, and a tutoring provider offering a drive full of papers is distributing material it has no right to distribute.

That is not a technicality for a family to shrug at. A student whose revision depends on an unofficial paper bank is also relying on material that may be incomplete, mislabelled or from a superseded syllabus, which is a real academic risk in subjects where the course has been revised. Papers obtained through the school are matched to the syllabus the student is actually sitting, which is the point.

What we tell students to do is specific. Ask the subject teacher for papers on the topics already covered, ask the coordinator what the school's practice is on releasing full papers before mocks, and use whatever platform the school provides. Teachers in Abu Dhabi are generally willing; the request fails when a student asks for everything at once rather than for the two topics they are currently revising.

Everything else on this page assumes the papers are in the student's hands by that route. Our work is on what happens next, and that work is entirely unaffected by who supplied the paper. A single well-marked question teaches more than a folder of unmarked ones, which is the argument against the paper bank even before copyright enters it.

sections.heading: Practice that moves marks, and practice that only fills time
paragraphs: There are five things a student can do with a past paper, and they are not equally useful. Reading through a paper and its mark scheme feels productive and changes almost nothing. Doing questions untimed with notes open builds content recall. Doing a timed paper cold tests performance. Marking your own script against the scheme produces diagnosis. Rewriting the lost-mark answers converts diagnosis into technique. Most students do the first two and stop.

The sequencing matters more than the volume. In DP1, while the syllabus is incomplete, question-level untimed work on taught topics is the right mode and whole papers are a waste. From the middle of DP2, timed whole papers become the main instrument, because by then the limiting factor is performance under time rather than knowledge. A student who inverts that order spends DP1 being discouraged and DP2 discovering timing problems too late.

The table below sets out the five modes with what each trains and when to use it. We put it on screen in a first session because families often arrive with a plan to do one paper a day, which sounds rigorous and is usually the least efficient possible use of the time available.

One more distinction worth drawing. A paper done to find out what you do not know is a diagnostic and should be done early. A paper done to prove you can perform is a rehearsal and should be done late and under proper conditions. Students who treat every paper as a rehearsal get demoralised in DP1; students who treat every paper as a diagnostic never practise performing.

sections.heading: Command terms are instructions, not synonyms
paragraphs: The IB publishes command terms and uses them consistently across subjects, and a large share of lost marks in Diploma papers comes from treating them as interchangeable. State and explain are different instructions with different mark values. Outline and describe demand different amounts. Evaluate and discuss both require judgement and reach it differently. A student who writes an excellent description in answer to an explain question has produced good prose and lost marks.

The pattern is easy to diagnose from a script. Answers that are too long for their mark allocation almost always indicate a command term read as a general invitation to write. Answers that are too short usually indicate a command term read as a lower-order one than it was. Both are corrected by the same exercise: before writing, underline the command term and the mark allocation, and decide the shape of the answer from those two things alone.

The table below covers the terms that cause the most trouble in practice. It is a working guide rather than the official list, which your child can find in their own subject guide through their school. We reference that document and do not reproduce it.

There is a Gulf-specific wrinkle worth naming. Many students in Abu Dhabi are working in English as an additional language, often to a very high standard, and command term errors in that group are frequently vocabulary-precision issues rather than comprehension failures. The fix is the same exercise done more explicitly, with the student writing their own one-line definition of each term in their own words.

sections.heading: The timing arithmetic a student should do once per paper
paragraphs: Timing failures cost real marks and they are entirely preventable with five minutes of arithmetic. Every paper has a total mark and a total time printed on it, and dividing one by the other gives minutes per mark. That single number tells a student whether a six-mark question deserves four minutes or ten, and it is the reference point for every pacing decision in the exam.

The common failure mode is not slowness but misallocation. A student spends twenty minutes on a question worth eight marks because it interested them, then has fourteen minutes for a section worth twenty. The marks lost at the end of the paper are almost always easier than the marks fought over at the start, which is why the arithmetic matters: the last section is where the cheapest marks in the paper usually sit.

The table below is a worked structure rather than a claim about any specific subject's paper, because paper lengths and totals differ by subject and level and are printed on the front of each paper. Have your child compute their own numbers from the papers they are actually sitting, write them on a card, and use them in every timed practice.

The second half of timing is the stall rule, decided in advance. When a question has consumed its allocation and is not working, the student marks it, leaves a line, and moves on. Students who have never agreed that rule with themselves lose entire final sections to a single question they could not abandon. Agreeing it is a one-minute conversation and it is worth more than most revision.

sections.heading: Marking your own script without lying to yourself
paragraphs: Self-marking is the highest-value skill in exam preparation and almost nobody is taught it. The default student behaviour is generous: they read the mark scheme, recognise the idea, remember that they knew it, and award the mark. The result is a script marked at ten points above its real value and a revision plan built on a fiction. Honest self-marking is a learnable discipline and it is the main thing our marking sessions actually teach.

The rule we give is that a mark is earned only if the words on the page would earn it from someone who has never met the student and will not infer anything. If the scheme requires a comparison and the script implies one, no mark. If the scheme requires a unit and the unit is absent, no mark. If the working is in the student's head, no method mark. Applying that rule hurts for about three papers and then becomes automatic.

We also mark independently and compare. The gap between the student's self-mark and ours is itself the diagnostic: a student who consistently over-marks by eight points on structured questions has a specific blind spot about what counts as an explanation, and that is more useful to know than the raw score. After a few sessions the gap narrows, and once it is small the student can self-diagnose without us, which is the point.

Three passes work better than one. First a cold mark with the scheme, severely. Second, a categorisation of each lost mark into a fault type. Third, a rewrite of the two answers with the most marks available, under time, to prove the fix took. That third pass is the one students skip and the one that converts the exercise into marks.
bullets: A mark is earned only by what is written, not by what was known

sections.heading: The error log: one page that does more than a shelf of papers
paragraphs: An error log is a single running document, one line per lost mark, with four columns: the paper and question, what the question asked for, what the student actually did, and the fault type. It takes two minutes per paper to maintain and it is the only artefact that makes practice cumulative. Without it, each paper is a fresh start and the same five mistakes recur for eighteen months.

The fault types matter more than the content. Across hundreds of Diploma scripts the categories repeat: command term misread, mark allocation ignored, working not shown, units or significant figures missing, source or data not used, question not actually answered, timing collapse in the final section, and content gap. Only the last of those is a revision problem. The rest are technique, and technique responds quickly.

What the log enables is targeted practice. A student whose log shows nine command term errors and two content gaps should spend the next fortnight on command terms, not on re-reading notes. A student whose log shows timing collapse in every paper's final section should practise final sections first, which almost nobody thinks to do. The log makes those decisions obvious, and without it students default to revising what they find comfortable.

It also gives a parent something real to look at. A log with twenty entries and a declining count of command term errors over six weeks is evidence of progress that a mark out of eighty cannot provide, because marks move slowly and noisily while fault frequencies move visibly. We ask students to bring the log to every session and we add to it together.
bullets: One line per lost mark: paper, what was asked, what was done, fault type
Eight recurring fault types, only one of which is a content gap

sections.heading: When to start, and what the mocks are for
paragraphs: Whole timed papers belong in the second half of DP2 and immediately before each mock. Before that, question-level work on taught topics does the same job with less waste and less discouragement. The exception is familiarisation: a student should read one paper of each type early, with the mark scheme, simply to know what the document looks like. That is an hour, once, not a programme.

The school's mocks are the fixed points. Abu Dhabi schools generally run a set late in DP1 or early in DP2 and a second set in the final term before the May session, and those are usually the only full papers a student sits under proper conditions before the real examinations. That makes the returned mock script the single most valuable document in the whole two years, and it is routinely glanced at and filed.

A post-mock session is therefore the one piece of tutoring we recommend to every Diploma family regardless of subject: an hour spent reading the returned script question by question, categorising the losses, and turning them into a revision order. The alternative, which is what usually happens, is a student who knows they got 58 and does not know which eight marks were the cheapest to recover.

Timing of practice through the year has to respect Ramadan, which compresses the school day across the emirate and moves the evening. Sessions move to post-iftar slots rather than pausing, and full timed papers are better scheduled either side of the month rather than inside it. Students sitting Cambridge or Pearson qualifications alongside the Diploma should note that UAE candidates sit the June and November series; the Cambridge February and March series is offered in India only.
