sections.heading: The PYP Exhibition, counted backwards from the showcase
paragraphs: The Exhibition is the final PYP year's long collaborative inquiry, presented to the school community. Each school sets its own brief and its own dates, so no two Abu Dhabi schools run it identically. What is consistent is where it goes wrong, and that is almost always at the start: the question is too wide, so the research sprawls, so the plan slips, so the last fortnight becomes a panic about the display board rather than the thinking.

The backwards count below is the structure that holds it together. It is written against a generic ten-week brief; your school's dates will differ and the school's brief always wins. Use it to ask your child one question each week, which is the whole of a parent's job here: not what have you found, but is your plan still right.

The academic-honesty boundary needs saying out loud on an Exhibition page, because this is where families get it wrong with good intentions. A tutor may ask questions, teach how to take notes, explain how to credit a source, review a draft the student has written and give feedback on it. A tutor may not write any part of it, dictate it, redraft it to completion, or build the presentation. The same rule runs all the way up the IB: the Exhibition, the Personal Project, the Internal Assessment and the Extended Essay are all the student's own work, and the habit of keeping that line clean is easier to build at age ten than at seventeen.

One practical note on the presentation. Rehearsing in front of a tutor over video has an accidental advantage: the child can be recorded and watch themselves back, which does more for delivery in one viewing than a term of being told to speak up. Two rehearsals with real questions, a week apart, is usually enough.

sections.heading: What primary tutoring costs in the Abu Dhabi market
paragraphs: Primary tutoring sits at the lower end of the UAE market, because it rarely needs a subject specialist. The published market bands give a usable picture. Budget online provision runs from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits around AED 150 to 300, with Unitors quoting IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits, travel included, run roughly AED 180 to 500, with Bestimate's 2026 rate table putting the band at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors asking AED 200 to 500.

Those are market figures published by the providers named, not IB Gram prices. For a primary child the relevant observation is that the premium bands exist for subject scarcity, and primary reading or Grade 4 maths is not scarce. A family paying specialist rates for early literacy is paying for something the market does not require. The things worth paying more for at primary age are consistency of tutor, short frequent sessions rather than long infrequent ones, and written evidence after each lesson.

The in-home premium deserves a specific note on a primary page. A home visit at primary level typically carries a minimum booking, often two hours, because the travel does not pay for itself on a 45-minute lesson. That is exactly the wrong shape for a nine-year-old: two hours after school is past the point of useful attention. The economics of in-home delivery push towards session lengths that primary children cannot sustain, which is a structural argument for online delivery rather than a marketing one.

Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session give a planning anchor: roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work. Monthly packages seen in the market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. IB Gram's own position is a free trial lesson first and a consultation that quotes against the actual subject and frequency, rather than a published rate card that would be wrong for most families.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the Primary Years Programme
paragraphs: Every private school in the UAE teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside whatever international curriculum it is licensed to deliver. The federal position is that a private school is not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the rule behind every emirate's mandatory-subject requirement, and it applies in Abu Dhabi as it does in Dubai.

In practice this means a PYP classroom runs two assessment cultures at once. The units of inquiry are assessed internally against the programme's own framework; the mandatory subjects are taught to a prescribed syllabus with its own expectations and, for Arabic, its own language of instruction rules. A parent who has only read about the PYP is sometimes surprised to find the first mark that worries them comes from a subject the PYP does not contain.

For a non-Arab child, Arabic as an additional language is where most primary tutoring requests land. The work is unglamorous and effective: script formation, high-frequency vocabulary, listening, and the short spoken responses primary assessments ask for. Frequency beats duration, as with reading, so two 30-minute sessions a week outperform one hour. Progress is visible quickly at this age, which is also why it is worth starting in Grade 2 or 3 rather than waiting for a report that says there is a problem.

One important boundary. For the mandatory UAE subjects, schools are required to teach the prescribed content, and using different or additional material without prior Ministry permission is not permitted. A tutor's job on these subjects is to teach the child the content the school is already delivering: vocabulary, script, comprehension and oral confidence. It is not to supply an alternative syllabus, and any tutoring offer that promises its own Arabic or Islamic Education curriculum is describing something a school could not use.

sections.heading: ADEK, inspection reports and reading the primary phase judgement
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi's private schools are overseen by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK is the single most useful source a primary parent in Abu Dhabi has and the one almost nobody uses. Of the competitor tutoring pages reviewed for this project, not one named it. Inspection reports are published per school, which means a family choosing between two PYP schools can read an independent judgement rather than a prospectus.

The detail that matters for a primary family is that inspection reports give phase-level judgements, not just a single overall rating. A school can be strong in secondary and weaker in its early years, or the reverse, and the overall band hides that. If you are choosing a school for a five-year-old, the primary phase judgement and the specific comments on teaching and assessment in the early years are worth more than the headline.

ADEK also sets professional-ethics expectations for school staff. Press reporting on the Abu Dhabi rules describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and notes that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That is press-reported rather than quoted from the current policy document, so verify it against ADEK's own published policy before relying on it. The practical consequence is simple and worth knowing: if your child's class teacher offers private lessons, that is a question to raise, not an opportunity to take.

None of this makes IB Gram an ADEK matter. IB Gram is not inspected, licensed or accredited by ADEK or by any UAE authority, holds no educational services permit, and operates no centre or office in the emirate. The regulators are named here because knowing what they govern is useful to a parent, not because any of them endorses this service.

sections.heading: From PYP to MYP: the gap that shows up in the first term of Year 7
paragraphs: The transition out of the Primary Years Programme is where the absence of marks finally becomes visible. A Grade 5 child who has been described as a developing communicator arrives in MYP Year 1, meets a task marked against four criteria out of 8 each, and gets a 3 on Criterion C for a piece of work that would have been praised the year before. Nothing has gone wrong with the child. The assessment has changed from a description of growth to a judgement against a descriptor.

Three skills carry most of the weight in that first term. Reading a command word and doing exactly what it asks, rather than writing everything known about the topic. Making notes from a source in the child's own words, with the source recorded. Structuring an answer so each paragraph does one job. All three are teachable in Grade 5, in the second half of the year, in about eight to ten sessions. All three are painful to teach in MYP Year 1 while the student is also being graded on them.

Families moving out of the PYP to a British curriculum school instead face a different gap, and the Abu Dhabi school market makes this the more common route. Year 7 in a British school assumes a child can take a test, revise for it, and work from a textbook. A child from an inquiry classroom may never have revised in their life, because there has been nothing to revise for. Revision is a skill, not a character trait, and the first six weeks of Year 7 is a poor time to discover it is missing.

The honest version of the recommendation: if your child is in the final PYP year and you are planning any transition, the highest-value tutoring is not subject content. It is note-making, command words, paragraph structure and how to prepare for a test. That is a short block, it is cheap at primary rates, and it removes most of what families later describe as the transition being hard.

process.title: Tell us the skill, not just the subject
process.description: The useful first message is specific: Grade 4, fractions, can do the procedure but cannot compare two fractions. Or Grade 2, reading, guesses from pictures. That is enough to match a tutor who has taught that exact thing rather than a generalist who covers primary.

process.title: A free trial lesson, with the diagnostic done in it
process.description: The trial is a real session, not a sales call. The tutor runs the twelve-minute reading screen or the twenty-item number-fact grid, teaches one thing, and sends you the result. You see the starting measurement before you decide anything. No card details are taken to book it.

process.title: A fixed weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time
process.description: Primary tutoring works on routine. One tutor, one slot, same day each week, set around your school run rather than around a tutor's driving time. Families in Al Reef and Khalifa City usually take a later slot; island families take an earlier one.

process.title: A session note every week and a measurement every eight
process.description: After each lesson you get what was taught, what the child got wrong and a five-minute daily practice. At week eight the week-one diagnostic is repeated identically, so the comparison is real. If the number has not moved, the plan changes rather than continuing.

process.title: A term summary you can take to the school
process.description: Each term you get two skills that moved, one that did not, and the evidence behind both. Bring it to the parent-teacher conference and ask whether the school's own assessment agrees. Where the two disagree is the most informative conversation available to a primary parent.

whyPoints.title: Subject match beats proximity
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means a family in Al Shamkha works with a tutor chosen for having taught early reading or Grade 5 fractions, rather than whoever is within a twenty-minute drive. At primary level the specialism that matters is the skill, and the pool for that skill is far larger than one emirate.

whyPoints.title: Session lengths that suit the age
whyPoints.description: Thirty minutes twice a week for an early reader, 45 minutes once a week from Grade 3. In-home delivery pushes towards two-hour minimums because travel has to be paid for; online delivery has no such pressure, so the lesson can be the length the child can actually sustain.

whyPoints.title: Evidence rather than reassurance
whyPoints.description: A running record, a diagnostic grid and an annotated writing sample after every third session. The claim being made is small and checkable: this specific skill moved this much in eight weeks. Nobody is predicting an MYP grade from a Grade 3 reading score.

whyPoints.title: A clear line on the student's own work
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach, review and give feedback. They do not write, redraft to completion or produce any part of an Exhibition, a Personal Project, an Internal Assessment or an Extended Essay. Building that habit at primary age is the cheapest academic-honesty insurance a family can buy.

whyPoints.title: Permit transparency
whyPoints.description: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and carries a code of conduct. We will tell you a tutor's permit position rather than leaving you to assume it.

whyPoints.title: Honest coverage limits
whyPoints.description: If no UAE-based tutor covers a niche primary need in the slot you want, we say so and offer the alternative, which may be a tutor based outside the UAE teaching in your time zone. Disclosing a coverage limit is more useful than quietly filling the slot with whoever is free.

faqs.question: Does my child need a tutor if the PYP has no exams?
faqs.answer: Not because of exams, no. The reason primary tutoring is worth considering is that the skills a PYP classroom assumes, decoding, fluency, number bonds, fraction sense and note-making, are either in place or not, and an inquiry classroom can mask a gap for a long time because the talk carries the child. A tutor's job at this age is to test those foundations, name which one is missing and teach it. If the diagnostic comes back clean, you have paid for one session and learned something useful. That is a reasonable outcome.

faqs.question: What does an IB PYP tutor actually teach in a 45-minute session?
faqs.answer: One skill. A typical session opens with a five-minute retrieval check on last week's work, spends about twenty-five minutes teaching the target skill with the child working rather than watching, then sets a five-to-ten-minute daily practice for the week. Nothing from the school's current unit of inquiry is pre-taught, because that hides the gap instead of closing it. You receive a note the same evening listing what was taught, what the child got wrong and the practice set. Every third session that note arrives with a marked piece of the child's writing attached.

faqs.question: How do I know my Grade 3 child is behind if the report card has no grades?
faqs.answer: Ask for two things the school already has: the portfolio, and which approaches-to-learning strand the teacher would prioritise next. Then get an independent measurement. A twelve-minute reading screen gives words correct per minute on an unseen passage plus an error type, and a twenty-item number-fact grid shows which facts are missing and how long recall takes. Those are numbers you can compare eight weeks later. The useful conversation with a school is not whether your child is doing well, which invites a reassuring answer, but whether the school's assessment agrees with an independent measurement.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my child prepare for the PYP Exhibition?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor can help narrow a vague interest into an answerable question, teach how to judge a source, show how to take notes in the child's own words, review a draft the student has written and give feedback on it, and run rehearsals with hard questions. A tutor cannot write any part of it, dictate it, redraft it to completion or build the presentation. The Exhibition is the student's own work, as the Personal Project, the Internal Assessment and the Extended Essay are later, and keeping that line clean at age ten is a habit that pays off at seventeen.

faqs.question: How long should an online lesson be for a seven-year-old?
faqs.answer: Thirty minutes, twice a week, rather than an hour once. Reading and number facts at that age respond to frequency because they are closer to motor habits than to understanding, so short and often beats long and rare. From Grade 3 upward, 45 minutes once a week works for most children, with a longer session only near something specific like an Exhibition presentation. An in-home visit usually carries a minimum booking of around two hours because the travel has to pay for itself, and two hours after a full school day is well past the point of useful attention for a primary child.

faqs.question: Will an online tutor hold a young child's attention?
faqs.answer: It depends almost entirely on how the session is run, not on the format. What works at primary age is a shared screen the child writes on rather than watches, short turns, frequent switching between talking and doing, and a session short enough to end while the child is still engaged. What fails is a tutor talking for twenty minutes. Practically, the setup matters: headphones, a fixed place the child sits each week, and a parent nearby for the first two sessions. Al Reem Island families in apartments usually find the quiet corner is the thing worth solving first.

faqs.question: My child moved from a British primary school to a PYP school in Abu Dhabi. What changes?
faqs.answer: The assessment culture, mainly. A British primary report gives you levels or percentages; PYP reporting is built on the learner profile, approaches to learning and a portfolio, and each school designs its own format within that. Children usually need a term to adjust to being asked what they think rather than what the answer is. The content gap is normally small; the habits gap is not. The two things worth checking early are whether the child can take notes from a source and whether they can explain a cause rather than retell an event, since both are assumed in an inquiry classroom.

faqs.question: Does the PYP cover Arabic and Islamic Education in Abu Dhabi schools?
faqs.answer: Those subjects run alongside the PYP rather than inside it. UAE private schools may choose their international curriculum, but they must still teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies and follow the Ministry's general regulations. So a PYP classroom in Abu Dhabi operates two assessment cultures at once: internal inquiry assessment, and prescribed mandatory-subject teaching with its own expectations. For non-Arab children, Arabic as an additional language is where most primary tutoring requests land, and it is often the first subject where a parent sees a mark they want to act on.

faqs.question: What does a PYP tutor send me after each lesson?
faqs.answer: A short note with three lines: what was taught, what the child got wrong, and the five-to-ten-minute daily practice for the week. Every third session it arrives with a piece of the child's writing marked for one teaching point rather than for every error, because marking everything teaches nothing. Fortnightly you also get a running record showing words correct per minute, error type and self-correction count. At week eight the week-one diagnostic is repeated identically so the comparison is genuine rather than impressionistic, and each term you get a summary of what moved and what did not.

faqs.question: When should we start tutoring before the move to MYP?
faqs.answer: The second half of the final PYP year is the right window, and the work is not subject content. Three skills carry most of the weight in the first term of MYP Year 1: reading a command word and doing exactly what it asks, making notes from a source in the child's own words with the source recorded, and structuring a paragraph so it does one job. Those take roughly eight to ten sessions at primary rates. Taught in Grade 5 they are cheap; taught in MYP Year 1 they are being learned while they are also being graded.

faqs.question: How much does primary tutoring cost per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published market bands put budget online provision at roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, while a qualified subject tutor online sits around AED 150 to 300. In-home one-to-one, travel included, runs roughly AED 180 to 500 on Bestimate's 2026 table and from independent home tutors. Those are the providers' own published figures, not IB Gram's. Primary work rarely needs the specialist bands above AED 300, which exist for subject scarcity rather than for early literacy or Grade 4 maths.

faqs.question: Do private tutors working with Abu Dhabi families need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service is listed as private tutor licensing with a two-working-day completion time, applied for through its app, website and e-services. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

faqs.question: Can the same tutor cover both maths and reading for my child?
faqs.answer: Often yes at primary level, and that is usually the better arrangement. Below MYP the specialism that matters is the skill rather than the subject, and a tutor who diagnoses reading well can generally run a number-fact grid too. What we would not do is stretch one tutor across both when the diagnostic shows two serious gaps, because 45 minutes split in half teaches neither properly. In that case the honest answer is two sessions, or one skill now and the other next term, and we will say which we think matters more.

faqs.question: Can lessons be scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school run and after-school clubs?
faqs.answer: That is the main scheduling constraint at primary age and it is the reason slots differ so much by community. Saadiyat and Al Bateen families, with short pick-ups, often take 3:30pm or 4pm. Khalifa City and Al Reef families, where a bus route can take forty minutes each way, generally need 5pm or a weekend morning. Because lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, there is no travel window to fit around, so the slot is set by your child's day. Families travelling in summer keep the same tutor and shift the time to their current zone.

faqs.question: Is it a problem that my child's class teacher also offers private lessons?
faqs.answer: It is at least a question worth asking. Press reporting on Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules describes a prohibition on school staff providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and notes that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That reporting is secondary, so check it against ADEK's current published policy rather than treating this answer as authoritative. The general principle is sound: the person assessing your child should not also be paid to prepare them.

abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-tutor.closingHeading: Start with a measurement, not a promise
abu-dhabi/ib-pyp-tutor.closingBody: The problem a PYP parent in Abu Dhabi has is not a shortage of encouragement. It is the absence of a number. So begin with one: a twelve-minute reading screen or a twenty-item number-fact grid, run inside a free trial lesson with no card details taken, and sent to you with the result written out. If the diagnostic is clean, you have spent one session and learned your child is fine. If it is not, you know exactly which skill is missing, how it will be taught, and what the same measurement should look like eight weeks later. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, timed to your school run rather than to a tutor's drive across the emirate.

abu-dhabi/ib-retake-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors work with Abu Dhabi students who are sitting a Diploma subject for a second time. They read the subject grade breakdown first, work out which component lost the points, and build the retake plan around that single component rather than restarting the whole course.

intro.heading: The cost of an IB retake in Abu Dhabi, before anything else
paragraphs: A retake is a budget decision before it is an academic one. Most Abu Dhabi families arrive at this page having already decided they want the grade; what they do not know is whether the plan costs two thousand dirhams or twenty. So start with the arithmetic. Published rates from UAE providers put qualified online subject tutoring at roughly AED 150-300 an hour, and IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialists at roughly AED 200-450 and above. TutorChase lists AED 270. Bestimate's Dubai rate table runs 200-450+ for specialist exam-year work. BartyED sits at AED 650 for a premium named tutor. Those are market figures, not an IB Gram price list.

Now multiply by hours rather than guessing. A single Higher Level subject being rebuilt for a November resit typically takes a weekly ninety-minute session from the summer through to the exam window, plus a tighter block of two sessions a week in the final six weeks. That is roughly thirty to thirty-six hours of teaching. At the mid band that is in the region of AED 6,000-9,000 for the subject; at specialist rates, more. Two subjects is not double, because paper technique transfers, but it is not far off either, and the honest version is that most families who retake two subjects spend more on tuition than they spent on the first year of DP support.

What changes the number in Abu Dhabi specifically is the shape of the market here rather than the headline rate. Abu Dhabi has fewer IB World Schools than Dubai and therefore a thinner pool of local subject specialists in the subjects people actually retake: Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, Chemistry Higher Level, Physics Higher Level, Economics Higher Level. An in-home tutor in Khalifa City who genuinely teaches Chemistry HL is a rare animal, and rarity is priced. Families who insist on a tutor driving to the villa are, in practice, choosing from a shortlist of two or three people and paying the travel premium on top: published in-home bands in the UAE run AED 180-500 an hour inclusive of travel, against AED 150-300 online.

The second thing that moves the number is how late you start. A retake planned in the week results arrive is a thirty-hour plan. A retake planned eight weeks before the November papers is a compressed forty-hour plan, because you are paying for intensity to replace time, and intensity costs more per unit of progress. The entry fee is separate again and is set by your school or the exam centre, not by us, and it has its own deadline that sits months ahead of the papers.

IB Gram delivers this as one-to-one online tuition to Abu Dhabi. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run in India only. For a resit that is an advantage rather than a compromise, because the constraint on a retake is subject specialism, not geography. A student in Al Reef gets the Economics HL teacher who has read two hundred Paper 3 scripts, rather than whichever generalist is within a twenty-minute drive of Al Reef.

abu-dhabi/ib-retake-tutor.programmesIntro: A retake conversation is almost always about the Diploma Programme, but the two programmes below it matter here too, because a sibling in MYP is usually the next student in the house and because the Career-related Programme has its own resit shape.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Each subject carries a grade from 1 to 7, with up to three bonus points from the TOK and Extended Essay matrix, for a maximum of 45. Subject grades are built from externally marked papers and an internally assessed component. A retake is organised by subject and by component, not by the whole Diploma, which is the single most useful fact on this page.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi's DP cohort sits in a relatively small number of schools licensed by ADEK concentrated on the island and in the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor. That concentration means retake students often know each other, and it also means school-side retake administration varies: some schools register former students as resit candidates without fuss, others ask you to go through an external centre. Confirm which applies before you plan the teaching.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Five years of inquiry-led study across eight subject groups, assessed against four criteria per subject on an eight-point scale, with the Personal Project in the final year. There is no external resit structure in MYP, because there is usually no external exam. What MYP students carry into DP is a criterion habit of mind and, often, a gap in algebraic fluency and in timed written work, both of which show up later as a Paper 1 problem.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi MYP cohorts are the feeder for the emirate's DP classes, and the subjects that generate retakes two years later are visible here: students who finish MYP with a 4 in mathematics and then choose Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level are the single most common retake profile we see in this emirate. Fixing it in Year 11 is cheaper than fixing it after results.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A smaller framework combining at least two DP courses with a career-related study, the Personal and Professional Skills course, service learning, a reflective project and a language development component. Students take the DP courses as individual certificates, which are graded 1 to 7 exactly as Diploma subjects are, so a CP student can resit a course in the same way a Diploma student can.
programmes.countryNote: CP provision in Abu Dhabi is thin compared with full Diploma provision, so CP students here often sit their DP courses alongside Diploma classmates and face identical paper formats. If a CP course grade is blocking a UAE or UK university condition, the resit route is the same, and so is the entry deadline.

programmes.name: Resit candidature
programmes.description: Not a programme, but the status your child holds for the second attempt. A resit candidate re-registers for named subjects for a later session, chooses whether to carry forward the existing internally assessed mark or submit new work where the subject allows it, and sits the external papers again. Grades from the two attempts do not average; the Diploma is reissued using the subject results that stand.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the practical question is who registers you. If your child has left the school, the school may still act as the registering centre, or may not. Ask the IB coordinator in writing, and ask early, because an entry deadline missed in the emirate is not something a tutor can fix with more hours.

abu-dhabi/ib-retake-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects Abu Dhabi families most often resit, with the component that usually caused the problem. A retake plan that does not name a component is a retake plan that will cost you the same money for the same grade.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The most resat subject in this emirate. At Higher Level, Paper 3 is the extended investigative paper and is where students who can do routine questions fall apart, because it asks them to follow an unfamiliar argument under time pressure. Marks also leak steadily from Paper 1, the no-calculator paper, through algebraic slips rather than conceptual gaps.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Technology-permitted throughout, which students mistake for easier. The losses are in modelling and interpretation: choosing the wrong model, then failing to comment on its limitations. Statistical tests are performed correctly and then described in language that earns no marks. A retake here is largely a writing and interpretation rebuild, not a calculation one.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics generate the most resit demand. Higher Level students lose marks on multi-step calculations where one unit error propagates, and on explanation questions where they describe what happens instead of why. The data booklet is underused: students who have not practised navigating it waste minutes they do not have.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The pattern in resits is a strong mechanics performance and a weak fields, induction and quantum performance, because those topics arrive late in the second year when coursework pressure peaks. Marks are lost in extended-response questions through missing reasoning steps rather than wrong answers, which is a trainable fault.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Volume is the problem rather than difficulty. Resit students usually know the content and cannot retrieve it precisely under timing, so answers drift into general description. Command-term discipline is the whole retake: distinguish, outline, explain and evaluate each carry a different mark structure, and answering the wrong one scores nothing.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Higher Level Paper 3 is the quantitative paper and is the most common single reason an Economics grade sits a point below expectation. Diagram labelling is the other recurring loss: a correct diagram with an unlabelled axis or a missing new-equilibrium point loses marks that cost nothing to secure.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tool application separates grades. Students name a framework and then do not use it on the stimulus, which earns description marks and no analysis marks. The Higher Level extension topics are often taught last and revised least. A resit plan here is a sequence of timed case responses with feedback on structure.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1, the guided textual analysis of an unseen text, is the resit driver. Students write about what the text says rather than how it works. The fix is mechanical: a repeatable approach to an unseen non-literary extract, practised against the assessment criteria until the structure is automatic.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Study recall is accurate and critical thinking is thin, which caps answers in the middle bands. Resit work concentrates on evaluating methodology and on the Higher Level extension content, where students commonly revise the approaches thoroughly and the extensions barely at all.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pseudocode under timed conditions is the recurring loss, alongside the Higher Level abstract data structures topic. Students who code fluently in a real language often cannot write the IB's pseudocode conventions accurately, and the paper marks the conventions. A short, targeted retake often moves this grade more than any other subject.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: Productive skills carry the grade and receptive practice dominates most students' revision, which is the wrong way round. Resit work is weighted towards timed writing in the required text types and towards the individual oral, with corrections at sentence level rather than general encouragement.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Case-study precision decides the top bands: named places, dated events, figures. Resit students usually have the concepts and a bank of vague examples. The Higher Level core extension is also frequently under-revised, and it carries its own paper, so the deficit is structural rather than incidental.

abu-dhabi/ib-retake-tutor.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi is not one catchment. Where you live changes which schools your child attended, what the evening looks like, and therefore when a resit session can realistically start. These are the parts of the emirate retake students actually come from.

regions.name: Abu Dhabi Island
regions.note: The oldest school stock and the densest. Apartment living means a quiet room for a two-hour online session is a genuine constraint, and families often shift sessions later to after the younger children are down.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Villa communities feeding several international schools licensed by ADEK. Retake students here are usually at home for the resit year rather than enrolled, which makes daytime sessions possible and makes mid-afternoon the cheapest time in the week to teach.

regions.name: Al Raha and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: A short commute to the island schools and a long one to anywhere else. A resit candidate no longer doing the school run gains back ninety minutes a day, and that recovered time is the main reason a compressed November plan works here.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Low-density, high-fee schooling with small DP cohorts, which means a retake student may be the only one in the emirate resitting that subject. There is no local study group to fall back on, so the tutoring has to carry more of the load.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Newer schools with younger DP cohorts and fewer years of results history. Families here often have less school-side experience of resit registration, so the administrative question needs asking earlier than elsewhere.

regions.name: Al Reef and Al Shamkha
regions.note: Mainland communities with long school commutes and a strong Indian and Arab resident mix. Arabic B and Mathematics resits cluster here, and post-Iftar session timing during Ramadan matters more than it does on the island.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Also under ADEK, ninety minutes inland, and almost entirely without local IB subject specialists at Higher Level. Online delivery is not a preference in Al Ain; it is the only way a student gets a Chemistry HL resit teacher at all.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Bateen
regions.note: Established central districts with a long-settled professional population and a high proportion of students carrying conditional offers to UK and UAE universities, which is the circumstance that makes a resit worth the money rather than a matter of pride.

schoolClusters.city: Abu Dhabi Island and Saadiyat
schoolClusters.note: The emirate's longest-established international provision. Resit candidates from these schools usually have a clear subject grade breakdown and an IB coordinator who has handled a November registration before, which makes the administrative side straightforward. Named here as context for the local schooling landscape only.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and the mainland
schoolClusters.note: Where most of the emirate's villa-community DP students sit. Cohorts are larger and subject choice at Higher Level is broader, but a specialist in a minority Higher Level subject is still hard to find locally. Listed as ecosystem context.

schoolClusters.city: Al Ain
schoolClusters.note: A separate catchment under the same regulator, with a smaller set of international schools and the thinnest local tutor pool in the emirate. Families here routinely plan resits without any in-person specialist option. Context only.

abu-dhabi/ib-retake-tutor.modesIntro: A resit runs to a fixed external deadline, so the format question is really a question about how many hours you can protect each week between results and the papers. These are the three shapes that work.

modes.title: Single-subject rebuild, weekly
modes.description: One ninety-minute session a week on one subject, from shortly after results through to the final weeks. This is the default and the cheapest route to a grade change, because it concentrates every hour on the component that actually lost the marks. It also leaves the student time to do the practice between sessions, which is where the grade is actually made.
bullets: One subject, one component focus, reviewed every fourth session
Written feedback on timed work completed between sessions
Scheduled on Gulf Standard Time, typically 16:00-21:00
Roughly 30-36 teaching hours for a Higher Level subject

modes.title: Two-subject parallel plan
modes.description: Two subjects taught in alternating sessions, usually one science and one mathematics, with paper technique treated as shared rather than duplicated. Cheaper per subject than two separate plans, but it demands more from the student, because the between-session practice doubles while the week does not get longer.
bullets: Alternating subject focus with a single shared timing discipline
One progress record covering both subjects
Suited to students not enrolled in school during the resit year
Honest caveat: two Higher Level resits in one short session is hard

modes.title: Final-stretch intensive
modes.description: Two sessions a week across the last six to eight weeks, built entirely around timed papers and the mark scheme. It is the right choice when a decision came late, and it is the most expensive per point of improvement, because intensity is being bought to replace time that no longer exists.
bullets: Full timed papers under exam conditions, marked and returned
Component-level diagnosis after each paper
No new content unless a specific gap blocks a whole topic
Costs more per grade point than starting in the summer

modes.title: Component clinic
modes.description: A short block of four to six sessions on one named component: Mathematics Higher Level Paper 3, Economics Higher Level Paper 3, an English Paper 1 unseen approach. Used when the rest of the subject grade was sound and one paper dragged the whole thing down, which is more common than parents expect.
bullets: Four to six sessions, one paper format only
Requires the subject grade breakdown to be worth doing
The lowest-cost intervention that can still move a grade
Not sufficient where two or more components underperformed

sections.heading: What an IB retake actually costs in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: An IB retake in Abu Dhabi costs the tuition hours plus the exam entry, and the tuition hours are the larger number. Using published UAE market rates as of October 2026, a single Higher Level subject rebuilt over a full resit cycle lands somewhere between roughly AED 4,500 at budget online rates and roughly AED 16,000 at premium specialist rates, for thirty to thirty-six hours of teaching. The entry is charged separately by your school or exam centre and is not a tutoring cost at all.

The table below is built from the cheapest option upwards, which is the opposite of how most tutoring sites present it, and the order matters. The budget band is real: EdFlik publishes from AED 45-65 an hour and Tutopiya from AED 33-52, both for online delivery with tutors who are often university students. For a Standard Level subject where the student mostly needs structure and accountability, that band can genuinely be enough. For a Higher Level resit where the losing component is Mathematics Paper 3, it is not, and paying it twice costs more than paying the specialist rate once.

What raises your own number in this emirate is subject rarity and timing, not postcode. A Biology Standard Level resit is cheap to staff anywhere. A Computer Science Higher Level resit in Al Ain in September is expensive to staff anywhere, because there are very few people who can teach it and the calendar gives them no slack. IB Gram does not publish an hourly price list on these pages; the free trial lesson and the consultation exist so that a quote is attached to a real plan rather than to a guess.

One figure to keep in view as context: KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year. Abu Dhabi fee regulation sits with ADEK and works differently, but the point holds for budgeting across the Gulf: school fees are the fixed cost in a family's education spend and tutoring is the variable one, which is exactly why a resit plan should be scoped to a named component rather than booked open-ended.

sections.heading: What you can resit, and what you are stuck with
paragraphs: A retake is organised by subject, and inside a subject it is organised by component. That is the fact that decides whether your money is well spent. A Diploma candidate re-registers for named subjects in a later session and sits the external papers again; the internally assessed component may in many subjects be carried forward from the first attempt rather than redone. You are not resitting the Diploma, you are resitting the parts of it that lost points.

This means the first piece of work is not teaching at all. It is reading the subject grade breakdown your school can obtain and identifying which component underperformed. A Chemistry Higher Level 5 can be a 5 because Paper 2 went badly, or because the internal assessment mark was low, or because Paper 1 timing collapsed. Those are three different plans with three different costs, and only one of them is worth thirty hours. Where the internal assessment mark was the weak part and the subject permits new work, the decision is more complex and needs the IB coordinator's input before any tuition is booked.

There are limits worth knowing before you build hopes on the outcome. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay feed the bonus points through a matrix, so a resit strategy that ignores them can leave a candidate one point short of a Diploma total for reasons unconnected to the subject being retaken. Your school's IB coordinator is the authority on what your child specifically may and may not re-register for, and on whether the existing internal assessment mark stands. We plan the teaching around their answer; we do not substitute for it.

The honest framing is this: a resit changes a subject grade, and a subject grade sometimes changes a university outcome. It does not rewrite two years. Families who get the best value from a retake tutor are the ones who arrive with the grade breakdown in hand, name the component, and ask for twenty hours on that component rather than a general course in the subject.
bullets: Re-register by named subject, not by Diploma
Identify the failing component before booking any hours
Ask the IB coordinator in writing whether the internal assessment mark carries forward
TOK and Extended Essay bonus points affect the Diploma total independently
Grades do not average across attempts; the result that stands is the one used

sections.heading: The November session counted backwards
paragraphs: Nobody in this search results page publishes a calendar, which is strange, because the calendar is the thing a resit family most needs. The IB assesses in two sessions each year, May and November. UAE schools sit the May session; the November session is the resit route most Abu Dhabi families use, because it is the first opportunity after results and it lands before most university deferral deadlines bite.

The table works backwards from the papers rather than forwards from today, because every deadline that matters is a subtraction. Note what it does not contain: specific dates. The IB's own site blocks automated checking, so no exam or results date in this project has been confirmed from the IB directly, and publishing one would be publishing a guess. Confirm every date with your school's IB coordinator or on ibo.org before you act on it. What is reliable is the order of events and the gaps between them, and that is what you plan against.

The gap that catches people is the first row. Re-registration closes months before the papers, and it closes while results are still being digested and university appeals are still open. A family that spends six weeks deciding whether to retake has, in several cases we have seen, decided correctly and then missed the entry. For Cambridge and Pearson qualifications the same structural point is documented and dated: Pearson's International GCSE November 2026 timetable ran to 19 November 2026 with results reaching students in January, and the November 2025 results landed on 22 January 2026. Entry closed long before any of that.

Build the teaching plan into the gaps the table shows. The weeks immediately after registration are for content repair, the middle block is for component-specific technique, and the final six weeks are for full timed papers and nothing else. A plan that is still teaching new content in the last fortnight has been mis-scoped, and that is a scoping failure rather than a student failure.

sections.heading: Online versus an in-home retake tutor in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Parents searching for a retake tutor in Abu Dhabi often mean someone who will come to the villa. It is worth answering that properly rather than deflecting it. In-home tutoring in the UAE is a real market with real prices: Bestimate's Dubai figures run AED 180-350 an hour, independent home tutors ask AED 200-500, and monthly in-home packages of four two-hour sessions are advertised around AED 1,599-1,799. That premium over online is mostly travel. A tutor crossing from the island to Khalifa City in the evening is paid for the journey whether anyone calls it that or not.

The trade-off that actually matters for a resit is not comfort, it is the size of the pool you choose from. Insisting on in-home narrows the shortlist to people who both teach the exact subject at the exact level and live within a sensible drive. For Biology Standard Level in Khalifa City that is a workable constraint. For Mathematics Analysis and Approaches Higher Level Paper 3, or Computer Science Higher Level, or Economics Higher Level Paper 3, it usually produces either nobody or somebody who teaches the subject one level below the one your child is resitting.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Lessons to Abu Dhabi families are delivered one-to-one over live video, and home tutoring is a service we provide only in India. We say that plainly because the alternative is wasting your time, and because for a resit the online route is genuinely the stronger one: the student gets the specialist, the session happens on time regardless of Mussafah traffic or weather, every worked solution is captured on a shared screen and can be reopened in October, and nobody loses a session because a tutor is stuck on the bridge.

One further practical point specific to a resit year. If your child has left school, the day has holes in it that did not exist before, and online delivery can use them. A 14:00 session on a Tuesday is possible for an online tutor in a different time zone and almost never possible for a local in-home tutor who is teaching in a school until 15:30. Cheaper hours and better hours are the same hours here.

sections.heading: Reading the results sheet before spending anything
paragraphs: The grade on the certificate is a summary. The useful document is the component breakdown, which your school can obtain and which shows how each paper and the internal assessment contributed. Until you have it, any retake plan is a guess, and a guessed plan is how families end up paying for thirty hours of general subject revision to fix a problem that lived in one paper.

Three patterns recur in Abu Dhabi resit candidates, and each points to a different and differently priced intervention. The first is a flat profile: every component a little below target, which usually means timing and exam-day execution rather than knowledge, and which responds to a block of full timed papers more than to content teaching. The second is a single collapsed component against sound performance elsewhere, which points to the component clinic and is the cheapest fix available. The third is a weak internal assessment mark with strong papers, which is the awkward case, because whether that can be changed at all depends on the subject and on what the coordinator says.

There is a fourth possibility that is not a tutoring problem. Where the breakdown looks inconsistent with everything the student produced across two years, an enquiry upon results is a cheaper and faster route than a resit, and it has its own short window immediately after results. We will say so when the breakdown suggests it. A tutoring business that never mentions the remark route is a tutoring business optimising for its own hours rather than your outcome.

Practically: ask the school for the breakdown the week results arrive, put it next to the student's own mock and internal assessment record, and look for the gap between the two. Where the mocks were consistently stronger than the final papers, you have an execution problem. Where the mocks predicted the result accurately, you have a content problem. Those cost different amounts and take different amounts of time, and knowing which you have is worth more than the first five hours of any tutor's time.
bullets: Request the component-level grade breakdown through the school, not just the grade
Flat under-performance across components points to timing, not content
One collapsed component points to a short clinic rather than a full rebuild
A weak internal assessment mark needs the coordinator's answer before planning
An enquiry upon results is sometimes cheaper and faster than retaking

sections.heading: ADEK, your old school, and who registers a resit candidate
paragraphs: Private schools in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which u.ae describes as supervising the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK is named by none of the competitor pages researched for this project, which is a strange gap given that it is the authority every Abu Dhabi school answers to. It regulates schools. It does not regulate tutoring rates and it does not approve tutors, and any page telling you otherwise is selling you something.

ADEK matters to a resit family for a different reason. Its professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from giving paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct making the same point. So the apparently obvious move, hiring your child's own subject teacher privately for the resit, is the one move to avoid. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it, but treat the direction of travel as settled.

On the registration question, the position in this emirate varies by school and nobody can answer it for you from a web page. Some Abu Dhabi schools will register a former student as a resit candidate for a later session as a matter of course. Others will not once the student has left, in which case you need an exam centre that accepts external candidates and you need it before the registration window closes. Ask in writing, ask the IB coordinator rather than the admissions office, and ask in the first fortnight after results.

Separately, on tutor legality: individuals providing private tuition in the UAE need the MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, the eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen, and tutoring without one exposes the individual to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you. IB Gram holds no ADEK, KHDA, MoE, IB or Cambridge approval, accreditation or partnership, and does not claim any.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not touch on a resit
paragraphs: If your child's internal assessment is in scope for the resit, the honesty boundary becomes the most important thing on this page. The IB's academic-honesty rules make the assessed work the student's own, and a breach is a malpractice finding against the student, not against the tutor. The consequences land on the person whose name is on the Diploma.

So here is the line, stated plainly. A tutor may teach the assessment criteria and what each one actually rewards. A tutor may discuss whether a proposed research question is answerable in the word count. A tutor may read a draft the student wrote and give feedback at the level of structure, argument and evidence. A tutor may teach referencing conventions and data-presentation technique. A tutor may mark practice work and explain where the marks went.

A tutor may not write any part of the work, supply text to be inserted, rewrite a paragraph into its final form, choose the research question outright, generate the data, or edit a draft to completion. There is a competitor in this market selling completed Internal Assessments at AED 3,750. That is not a cheaper version of tutoring; it is an expulsion risk sold at a price, and it is the single reason to be sceptical of any resit offer phrased around a guaranteed outcome.

The same boundary is why we publish no grade guarantee. A resit plan can change what a student knows, how fast they work and how accurately they answer a command term. It cannot promise a 7, and anyone promising one on a page like this is either misunderstanding the assessment or hoping you will not check. We also will not reproduce or supply IB, Cambridge or Pearson papers, mark schemes or syllabus documents as downloads. We cite them and link to the official source, which is both the lawful route and the one that keeps your child looking at the current version.
bullets: A tutor teaches criteria, reviews drafts and marks practice work
A tutor does not write, rewrite to completion, or supply text
Academic-honesty findings fall on the student, not the tutor
No grade or score guarantee is offered on any IB Gram page

sections.heading: The mandatory UAE subjects, and why a resit year does not excuse them
paragraphs: A detail that catches families whose child has left school for the resit year. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in UAE private schools alongside whatever international curriculum the school is licensed for; the federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, while adhering to the Ministry's general regulations. In Dubai, KHDA's published requirements were to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. ADEK applies the equivalent requirement in Abu Dhabi.

For a student still enrolled while resitting, that means the week is fuller than the resit plan assumes, and the resit sessions have to fit around mandatory-subject lessons that cannot be dropped. KHDA's guidance calculates mandatory-subject time on a forty-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and advises that no mandatory-subject lesson runs shorter than twenty-five minutes. Those are real hours in a real timetable, and a plan drawn up without them is a plan that collapses in week three.

The organisational rules are specific too, and worth knowing if Arabic is the subject being resat or supported. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Schools must ensure teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval.

One constraint applies to tutoring content directly: for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior MoE permission is strictly prohibited. So Arabic support in a resit year works from the school's own materials and the official programme, not from an alternative course a tutor prefers. That is a narrower brief than parents expect, and stating it is more useful than pretending the constraint does not exist.

sections.heading: MoE equivalency, and what the resit grade is actually for
paragraphs: Many Abu Dhabi resits are driven by a university condition rather than by the grade itself, so it is worth being precise about what the UAE Ministry of Education requires, and equally precise about what nobody can confirm. For the British track the requirements are published: students must show one accredited subject at Advanced Level at a grade no lower than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, and must pass five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE at a grade no lower than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic Education are not counted among those five.

That five-subject figure is worth stating because a currently ranking competitor publishes six, and a parent acting on six when the rule is five either sits an unnecessary exam or draws the wrong conclusion about their child's position. For the American track, English proficiency is met by an IELTS academic score of 5, a TOEFL iBT score of 61, or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, and mathematics requires at least 450 in SAT Math before applying.

For the IB there is no equivalency points threshold on this page, and that is deliberate. The source that documents the British and American tracks states no IB points figure, and publishing an unsourced one would be publishing a liability on a page a parent acts on. Check moe.gov.ae or the emirate's attestation authority directly, and treat any site quoting you an IB equivalency score without a government source as unreliable. Equivalency and attestation are processes you complete with the authority; IB Gram does not perform them, does not guarantee an outcome, and is not an intermediary in them.

The practical upshot for a resit decision is to find out what the grade is actually needed for before paying for it. A UK offer with a specific subject grade condition is a clear case. A general preference for a higher total is a weaker one. And no part of equivalency, admission or progression requires tutoring; anybody implying that it does is making a false-urgency claim about a regulatory process.

sections.heading: Ramadan, Gulf Standard Time and when a resit session actually happens
paragraphs: A resit cycle that runs from the summer through to November crosses the whole shape of the UAE year, and the scheduling realities are not decoration. Sessions run on Gulf Standard Time, and the usable evening window for a student still at school is roughly 16:00 to 21:00 after the commute home from an island or mainland school. For a student not enrolled during the resit year, the best hours are the daytime ones nobody else wants, and those are also the hours when a specialist in another time zone is most easily available.

Where Ramadan falls inside a resit cycle, timings shift rather than stop. School days shorten, the family rhythm reorganises around Iftar, and the productive study window for many students moves to after the evening meal. A plan that keeps insisting on a 17:00 session through Ramadan will lose sessions. One that moves to post-Iftar for the month keeps the continuity, and continuity is what a resit plan is actually built from.

The other calendar items worth building around are the school holidays and the family travel that tends to attach to them. Abu Dhabi families travel in the summer, which is exactly when a November resit plan needs its content-repair block. Online delivery survives that; an in-home arrangement does not, because the tutor is in Khalifa City and the student is not. Session continuity across travel is one of the quieter reasons the online route works better for resits specifically.

Practically, agree the week-by-week shape at the start and write down the weeks you already know will be lost. A thirty-six-hour plan with six weeks of travel in it is a thirty-hour plan, and discovering that in August is free while discovering it in October costs you the grade. Build the losses in, then protect what is left.
