abu-dhabi/ib-tok-essay-help.programmesIntro: Theory of Knowledge runs across both Diploma years and produces two assessed pieces. These are the stages at which an Abu Dhabi family might reasonably seek help, and what help is useful at each.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge in Diploma Year 1
programmes.description: Usually one timetabled lesson a week, the course's framework and concepts, and in most schools the exhibition. Because there is no homework in the conventional sense, this is the subject that loses every scheduling contest and the one students most often arrive in Year 2 having absorbed nothing structural from.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Diploma programmes vary considerably in how much Theory of Knowledge teaching time they give and in when the exhibition falls. Ask the coordinator where the exhibition sits in the school's year, because it is frequently a Year 1 deadline the family has not registered.

programmes.name: The exhibition
programmes.description: Three objects, each connected to one of the course's internal assessment prompts, with a written commentary of up to 950 words explaining how each object illustrates the prompt in a real-world context. Internally assessed and externally moderated, and a third of the Theory of Knowledge grade.
programmes.countryNote: The exhibition is the cheaper of the two components to get right because its structure is explicit: three objects, one prompt, a specified commentary length. Students lose marks by choosing objects that are abstract rather than specific, which is a selection problem rather than a writing one.

programmes.name: The essay on a prescribed title
programmes.description: One of six prescribed titles released by the IB for the session, answered in up to 1,600 words and assessed externally. Two thirds of the Theory of Knowledge grade. The title is chosen by the student, which makes selection the first and most consequential decision in the component.
programmes.countryNote: The school sets an internal deadline ahead of the IB's upload schedule, and in most Abu Dhabi schools it collides with Internal Assessment and Extended Essay deadlines. Ask the coordinator for all three dates together at the start of Diploma Year 2.

programmes.name: The bonus points and the failing condition
programmes.description: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together award up to three of the Diploma's forty-five points, and a grade E in either is a failing condition for the Diploma. That combination makes Theory of Knowledge simultaneously the most neglected and one of the highest-stakes components in the course.
programmes.countryNote: Confirm the current award rules and failing conditions with the school's IB coordinator rather than relying on any tutoring page, including this one. Award rules are revised and the coordinator holds the version that applies to the student's cohort.

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-essay-help.subjectsIntro: Theory of Knowledge has a defined vocabulary, and using it correctly is most of what separates a strong essay from a fluent one. These are the components of that vocabulary a plan works with.

subjects.name: Areas of knowledge
subjects.levels: History, the human sciences, the natural sciences, mathematics and the arts
subjects.description: The five domains in which knowledge claims are examined. An essay that names its area and describes how knowledge is actually produced in it is doing the subject; one that refers vaguely to science or to history in general is not.

subjects.name: The core theme: knowledge and the knower
subjects.description: The individual's relationship to knowledge, including the role of communities, perspective and identity. Useful for essays about bias and perspective, and the source of the most common error, which is sliding from how knowledge is justified into how the student personally feels.

subjects.name: The optional themes
subjects.levels: Knowledge and technology, language, politics, religion, indigenous societies
subjects.description: Schools select some of these for study, and the one a school chose shapes the examples a student has available. Worth establishing early, because an essay drawing on a theme the school never taught forces the student to build context they do not have.

subjects.name: Knowledge questions
subjects.levels: The form the prescribed titles take
subjects.description: Questions about knowledge rather than about the world: how a claim is justified, what counts as evidence in a domain, where the limits of a method lie. Recognising that a title is a knowledge question rather than a topic prompt is the single most important act in the component.

subjects.name: The twelve concepts
subjects.levels: Evidence, certainty, truth, interpretation, power and seven others
subjects.description: The course's working vocabulary, including justification, explanation, objectivity, perspective, culture, values and responsibility. Used precisely they give an essay its analytical spine; used loosely they become the vague abstraction that marks a weak essay immediately.

subjects.name: Claims and counterclaims
subjects.levels: The structural unit of the essay
subjects.description: A position supported by an example from a named area of knowledge, then a genuine challenge to it. The counterclaim has to be a real objection rather than a weaker version of the same point, which is the structural failure that caps otherwise competent essays.

subjects.name: Real-world examples
subjects.description: Specific, verifiable instances rather than invented hypotheticals. A named study, a named historical dispute, a named mathematical result, a named work of art. Invented examples cannot be interrogated and therefore cannot support an argument about how knowledge is justified.

subjects.name: The exhibition objects
subjects.levels: Three objects and a commentary of up to 950 words
subjects.description: Each object must be a specific thing with a real-world context, not a category or a concept. A particular photograph rather than photography, a particular document rather than legislation. Abstraction is the dominant failure in exhibition selection.

subjects.name: The internal assessment prompts
subjects.levels: The published prompts the exhibition answers
subjects.description: A fixed set of questions from which the student chooses one for their exhibition. The commentary has to answer the chosen prompt through the objects, which means the prompt is selected before the objects rather than fitted to objects a student already liked.

subjects.name: Essay structure within 1,600 words
subjects.levels: The practical constraint on everything above
subjects.description: An introduction that engages the title, two developed arguments with counterclaims, and a conclusion that reaches a position. No room for definitional preamble, no room for a fifth area of knowledge, and no room for a paragraph explaining what Theory of Knowledge is.

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-essay-help.regionsIntro: Delivery is online, so a student works with someone who has read the prescribed titles rather than with whoever is nearby. What the area changes is when a thinking session can realistically happen, because this subject needs attention rather than stamina.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: Long bus routes mean a student arriving home late with little attention left. Theory of Knowledge sessions work badly when a student is tired, because the work is argument rather than practice, so weekend mornings serve this subject better than weekday evenings.

regions.name: Al Reem Island and Al Maryah
regions.note: Short commutes make an after-school session genuinely workable, which suits a subject where a single paragraph can be interrogated properly in forty minutes while the student is still alert.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Cultural institutions within reach, which matters more here than for most subjects: the arts as an area of knowledge and the exhibition both reward specific, locally accessible objects and works a student has actually seen.

regions.name: Yas Island and Al Zeina
regions.note: Growing communities with substantial internal travel. Families here often schedule Theory of Knowledge work in the same slot as the Extended Essay, which is sensible because both are thinking work rather than practice.

regions.name: Al Bateen, Al Mushrif and the Corniche
regions.note: Established Diploma programmes where the exhibition is well scheduled and the optional themes are clearly taught. Students here usually arrive knowing which themes they studied, which makes example selection easier.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: A wide curricular mix with students who have transferred into the Diploma. A transferring student may have missed the first term of the course entirely, which means the framework and vocabulary need establishing before any title is chosen.

regions.note: Greater distances and, in Al Ain, a separate school ecosystem under the same emirate regulator. Online delivery matters most here, because a tutor who has read this session's prescribed titles is not a local resource in any emirate.

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-essay-help.modesIntro: Theory of Knowledge support is short and concentrated. Three shapes cover it, and none of them is a weekly commitment across a year.

The student chooses. The written outcome names the chosen title and the two areas of knowledge it will use.

modes.description: The student brings one paragraph; the session asks what area of knowledge the claim belongs to, what the example actually shows about how knowledge is produced there, and what an informed objection would be. The student rewrites. This is slow and it is how the subject is learned rather than described.

sections.heading: Choosing among the six prescribed titles
paragraphs: The IB releases six prescribed titles for each session and the student selects one. That selection is the most consequential decision in the component and it is routinely made in about four minutes, on the basis of which title sounds most interesting. A title a student finds interesting and has no examples for produces an essay of assertions. A title that sounds dull and for which the student has two strong real examples in two areas of knowledge produces a good essay.

So the selection should be a test rather than a preference. Three questions, applied to each of the six. Can I name two areas of knowledge this title can be examined in, and do I have a specific real example from each — a named study, a named historical dispute, a named mathematical result, a named work? Is there a genuine counterclaim available, something an informed person would actually argue against my position? And can this be answered in 1,600 words, or does answering it require defining three concepts first?

Most students find that two of the six pass all three tests and four do not, which is a far more useful position than having six options and no criteria. The exercise takes forty minutes and it is the one session in this component that reliably changes the grade, because everything downstream is constrained by the title and nothing downstream can fix a bad choice.

One further selection consideration specific to a school context. Schools teach some of the optional themes and not others, which determines which examples a student actually has at their disposal. A title that invites discussion of knowledge and technology is a different prospect for a student whose school taught that theme than for one whose school did not. Check which themes were studied before testing the titles, because it changes the answer to the first question.

sections.heading: Budgeting 1,600 words before writing any of them
paragraphs: At 1,600 words the essay is short, and almost every structural failure in a Theory of Knowledge essay is a budgeting failure. Students write until the words run out, which means the introduction and the first argument consume two thirds of the allowance and the counterclaim and conclusion are compressed into a paragraph each. The assessment instrument rewards a developed, balanced discussion that reaches a position, and a compressed second half cannot show one.

The budget that works allocates roughly a tenth to an introduction that engages the title directly rather than defining terms, about a third to the first argument with its example and its counterclaim, about a third to the second argument in a different or contrasting area of knowledge, and the remainder to a conclusion that states a position and acknowledges what would change it. The numbers are approximate; having them in advance is what matters.

Three paragraphs should not exist and routinely do. A paragraph defining knowledge, which the examiner does not need and the student cannot do well in 150 words. A paragraph surveying the history of a debate, which is background rather than argument. And a paragraph explaining what Theory of Knowledge is, which appears more often than it should and tells the reader the student is writing about the course rather than doing it.

The budget also disciplines example selection. One well-chosen real example per argument, described specifically enough to be interrogated, costs around a hundred words. Three examples per argument cost three hundred and show less, because none of them can be developed. Students believe more examples demonstrate more knowledge; the instrument rewards examples that are actually analysed, which at this length means one each.

sections.heading: Where Abu Dhabi TOK essays lose marks
paragraphs: The dominant loss is the slide from knowledge to opinion. A title asks how a claim is justified within an area of knowledge; the essay answers what the student thinks about the subject matter. This happens most often in essays drawing on the core theme, knowledge and the knower, because that theme invites reflection on perspective and a student's own perspective is the nearest available material. The repair is a question applied to every paragraph: is this about how knowledge is produced, or about what I believe?

The second is the decorative area of knowledge. An essay names five areas, says a sentence about each, and analyses none. The instrument rewards depth of analysis within areas rather than breadth of reference across them, so five mentions score below two developed treatments. This feels wrong to students who have been taught that Theory of Knowledge rewards range, and it is visible immediately in a marked essay.

The third is the hypothetical example. 'Imagine a scientist who...' cannot be interrogated, because nothing about an invented case is checkable and therefore nothing about it demonstrates how knowledge is actually justified in a domain. A named study, a named historical disagreement, a named mathematical proof or a named artwork can be examined, questioned and used. The substitution from hypothetical to real is a single instruction and it changes the analytical quality of a whole essay.

The fourth is the absent counterclaim. Students write a counterclaim paragraph that restates the original claim more weakly and then dismisses it, which is not a counterclaim but a straw figure. A real objection is one an informed person would actually press, and engaging with it is where the discussion becomes balanced. An essay with two arguments and no genuine objection to either reads as a position asserted twice.

sections.heading: The exhibition: a third of the grade, and the cheaper third
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge produces two assessed pieces, the exhibition and the essay, and the exhibition accounts for roughly a third of the grade. It is also the more tractable of the two, because its structure is explicit: a student chooses one of the published internal assessment prompts, selects three specific objects, and writes a commentary of up to 950 words explaining how each object illustrates the prompt in a real-world context.

The dominant failure is abstraction in object selection. An object has to be a specific thing with a real-world context — a particular photograph, a particular document, a particular instrument, a particular artefact — not a category or a concept. Students choose photography rather than a photograph, or legislation rather than a law, and the commentary then has nothing concrete to say about a real-world context because there is no real-world instance in front of it.

The second failure is sequence. Students pick three objects they find interesting and then look for a prompt the objects can be bent toward, which produces three forced connections. The prompt comes first. With the prompt chosen, the question becomes which specific objects genuinely illustrate it, and that is a much easier search than the reverse. One session usually settles both the prompt and the objects.

The third is the word budget, which is tighter than it looks. Up to 950 words across three objects is roughly 300 each, including the identification of the object, its real-world context, and the link to the prompt. There is no room for a general introduction to the prompt or for a conclusion drawing the three together, and students who write those find the third object compressed into two sentences. Budgeting before writing is the whole discipline, exactly as it is for the essay.

sections.heading: Why Theory of Knowledge gets neglected, and what that costs
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is the Diploma component most reliably postponed, and the reason is structural rather than a failure of character. It usually has one timetabled lesson a week, no content to revise, no past papers to drill and no weekly homework that will be marked. Every other subject has something due. In a competition for a Year 13 student's evening, Theory of Knowledge loses every time, and it loses quietly because nothing happens when it does.

What it costs is specific. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together award up to three of the Diploma's forty-five points, and those points count exactly as much as points earned in a subject. A student predicted 34 points with the core unaddressed is a student with three points available for work that is already on the timetable. Families who would pay for three more points in chemistry rarely think of the core as the same opportunity, and it is cheaper.

The more serious consequence is the failing condition. A grade E in Theory of Knowledge or in the Extended Essay is a failing condition for the Diploma, which means the component that receives the least attention is one of the ones that can remove the qualification. That asymmetry is worth stating plainly to a student who regards the subject as the one with no homework. Confirm the current award rules with the school's IB coordinator, because they are revised and the coordinator holds the version for the student's cohort.

The practical remedy is not more hours; it is scheduled hours. Three or four sessions placed deliberately — one on title selection, two on paragraph interrogation, one on the exhibition — address the component properly. Theory of Knowledge does not need a weekly commitment across a year. It needs to stop being the thing that gets moved when something else is due.
bullets: One lesson a week, no content to revise, nothing due: it loses every contest

sections.heading: The boundary, and why it is tighter here than it looks
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is the component where the line between helping and writing is easiest to cross without noticing, because the help a student most wants is an argument. A student stuck on a counterclaim will accept one if it is offered, and an offered counterclaim becomes the tutor's thinking in the student's essay. That is the specific risk in this subject and it is why the method here is interrogation rather than suggestion.

What a tutor may do: read the prescribed titles with the student and apply the selection tests, ask what area of knowledge a claim belongs to, ask what an example actually shows about how knowledge is justified, ask what an informed objection would be, say that a paragraph is opinion rather than analysis, name the word budget, and mark a draft against the published assessment requirements. Every one of those is a question or a judgement about the student's own work.

What a tutor may not do: supply a counterclaim, supply an example, write or rewrite a paragraph, choose the title, or draft any part of the exhibition commentary. The discipline is to let the student sit with a question until they answer it, which is slower and less comfortable than supplying the answer and is the only version that is theirs. A session in which the student does most of the talking is working correctly.

The consequence falls on the student. Work that is not their own produces a malpractice finding against them, and since a grade E in Theory of Knowledge is a failing condition, the exposure here is the Diploma rather than a mark. The market in this region sells written coursework: one UAE-facing site advertises completed Internal Assessments at AED 3,750, and the same market sells essays. Refuse it at any price, and ask any provider to state in writing what they will not do.

sections.heading: Abu Dhabi specifics: ADEK, deadlines and who may help
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi's private schools are regulated by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK is named by none of the competitor pages found in this research, which is a notable omission on pages written for families in this emirate, and it is the authority whose framework a school's academic and ethics policies sit within.

The deadline that binds a family is the school's. Abu Dhabi Diploma programmes set internal submission dates for the Theory of Knowledge essay and the exhibition ahead of the IB's upload schedule, and the essay deadline commonly collides with Internal Assessment and Extended Essay deadlines in the same weeks. Ask the IB coordinator in writing for all of those dates together at the start of Diploma Year 2, because the collision is predictable and a plan can be built around it.

One rule specific to this emirate affects how help is arranged. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That is press-reported rather than read from ADEK's current policy document, so verify it against the authority's own publication before relying on it.

Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated generally. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students, through MoHRE's own 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing' service with a stated two-working-day completion time. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published fine schedule.

sections.heading: What Theory of Knowledge support costs in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: This is the smallest purchase in the Diploma and among the best value per point. Three or four sessions do the work: one on title selection, two on paragraph interrogation, one on the exhibition. Published rates in this market, read in October 2026, put a qualified online subject tutor at AED 150-300 an hour, with Unitors listing IB tuition from AED 200 and TutorChase quoting AED 270 for specialist work. The Bestimate survey puts IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200-450 and above, and premium named listings reach AED 650.

Set that against the points. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together award up to three of the Diploma's forty-five points, and a grade E in either is a failing condition. Three or four sessions at the qualified band is a small outlay against a component that carries points and can remove the qualification. By comparison, the same number of hours spent on examination technique in a subject addresses a smaller share of a single grade with less certainty.

The thing not to buy is a weekly Theory of Knowledge commitment across a year. The component does not require it: it requires specific decisions made properly at specific points, and a provider proposing an open-ended monthly arrangement for this subject is proposing a shape that does not match the work. Ask for an hour count and a list of which sessions address which decision.

The in-home comparison runs as elsewhere in this market: the Bestimate survey puts qualified in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 an hour, with independent home tutors quoted at AED 200-500, against AED 150-300 for comparable work online. For this component online is also the correct format, because the method is a title on screen beside the student's own paragraph with comments in the margin and versions kept. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere in the UAE; home visits are an India-only service, and IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from the International Baccalaureate, ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education or MoHRE.

faqs.question: What does the IB TOK essay actually assess?
faqs.answer: An argument about how knowledge is produced and justified, built on one of six prescribed titles released for the session and written in up to 1,600 words. It is not an opinion piece, a philosophy essay or a general-knowledge display. A strong response takes a claim, anchors it in a named area of knowledge — history, the human sciences, the natural sciences, mathematics or the arts — tests it against a specific real example from that area, does the same with a genuine counterclaim, and reaches a position. Two areas handled properly score above five areas mentioned.

faqs.question: How should a student choose between the six prescribed titles?
faqs.answer: By testing all six rather than picking the most interesting. Three questions per title: can I name two areas of knowledge this can be examined in, and do I have a specific real example from each — a named study, dispute, result or work? Is there a genuine counterclaim available, something an informed person would actually press? And can this be answered in 1,600 words without defining three concepts first? Most students find two titles pass and four fail, which is far more useful than six options and no criteria. The exercise takes about forty minutes.

faqs.question: Why do fluent TOK essays score in the lower bands?
faqs.answer: Usually because they discuss the topic the title mentions rather than how knowledge in a named area is produced and justified. A title asking about certainty gets an essay about things the student is or is not certain of. This slide from knowledge to opinion is the dominant loss in the component and it is invisible to the student writing it, because the essay feels thoughtful and sincere. The repair is a single question applied paragraph by paragraph: is this about how knowledge is produced, or about what I believe?

faqs.question: How many areas of knowledge should a TOK essay use?
faqs.answer: Two, developed properly, in almost all cases. Students name five and write a sentence about each, believing that range is what the component rewards. It is not: depth of analysis within an area is what the assessment requirements ask for, so five mentions score below two genuine treatments. Choosing the two is part of the title selection test, because the two areas have to be ones in which the student actually has specific real examples. A contrast between the two areas usually produces a stronger essay than two areas that behave similarly.

faqs.question: Why do hypothetical examples weaken a TOK essay?
faqs.answer: Because nothing about an invented case can be interrogated. 'Imagine a scientist who discovers...' supplies no checkable detail, so it cannot demonstrate how knowledge is actually justified in the natural sciences — it only illustrates what the student already wanted to say. A named study, a named historical disagreement, a named mathematical result or a named work of art can be examined and questioned, which is what makes it evidence. Substituting one real example for a hypothetical is a single instruction that changes the analytical quality of an entire essay.

faqs.question: How should 1,600 words be divided in a TOK essay?
faqs.answer: Roughly 150 for an introduction that engages the title directly, about 500 for the first argument with one developed real example and a genuine counterclaim, about 500 for a second argument in a different or contrasting area of knowledge, around 250 for a conclusion that reaches a position and says what would change it, and about 200 spare. The figures are approximate; having them before writing is the point. Almost every structural failure in this component is a budgeting failure, with the first half consuming two thirds of the allowance.

faqs.question: Which paragraphs should a TOK essay not contain?
faqs.answer: Three, and they appear constantly. A paragraph defining knowledge, which the examiner does not need and which cannot be done well in 150 words. A paragraph surveying the history of a debate, which is background rather than argument. And a paragraph explaining what Theory of Knowledge is, which tells the reader the student is writing about the course rather than doing it. Deleting all three returns several hundred words to the arguments, which is usually where the compressed second half came from in the first place.

faqs.question: What makes a real counterclaim rather than a straw one?
faqs.answer: A counterclaim is an objection an informed person would actually press, one that threatens the argument rather than decorating it. Students write a weaker restatement of their own claim and then dismiss it, which produces a balanced-looking paragraph with no genuine opposition in it. The test is whether somebody who disagreed with the essay would recognise their own objection in it. If not, the counterclaim is a figure the student built in order to knock down, and the discussion has not actually become balanced.

faqs.question: What is the TOK exhibition and how is it different from the essay?
faqs.answer: It is the other assessed component, accounting for roughly a third of the Theory of Knowledge grade, and it is internally assessed with external moderation. A student chooses one of the published internal assessment prompts, selects three specific objects, and writes a commentary of up to 950 words explaining how each object illustrates the prompt in a real-world context. It is more tractable than the essay because the structure is explicit, and the dominant failure is abstraction: choosing photography rather than a photograph, or legislation rather than a specific law.

faqs.question: Does the exhibition prompt come before or after choosing the objects?
faqs.answer: Before, always. Students pick three objects they find interesting and then search for a prompt the objects can be bent toward, which produces three forced connections and a commentary that argues with itself. Choosing the prompt first turns the task into a much easier search: which specific objects genuinely illustrate this prompt in a real-world context. One session usually settles both, and most of it is spent rejecting abstract objects and having the student replace them with specific ones.

faqs.question: Why is Theory of Knowledge the most neglected part of the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Because nothing is ever due. It usually has one timetabled lesson a week, no content to revise, no past papers to drill and no weekly marked homework, so in any competition for a Year 13 evening it loses. The cost is concrete: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together award up to three of the Diploma's forty-five points, and those count exactly as much as points earned in a subject. Families who would pay for three more points in a science rarely see the core as the same opportunity, and it is cheaper.

faqs.question: What happens if a student gets a grade E in Theory of Knowledge?
faqs.answer: A grade E in Theory of Knowledge or in the Extended Essay is a failing condition for the Diploma, which means the component that receives the least attention is one of those that can remove the qualification. That asymmetry is worth stating to a student who regards Theory of Knowledge as the subject with no homework. Award rules are revised periodically, so confirm the current failing conditions with the school's IB coordinator rather than relying on any tutoring page, including this one.

faqs.question: Where exactly does TOK help have to stop?
faqs.answer: At supplying argument, which is precisely the help a stuck student most wants. A tutor may apply the title selection tests, ask what area of knowledge a claim belongs to, ask what an example shows about justification, ask what an informed objection would be, say that a paragraph is opinion rather than analysis, name the word budget, and mark a draft against the published requirements. A tutor may not supply a counterclaim, supply an example, write or rewrite a paragraph, choose the title or draft the exhibition commentary. A session where the student does most of the talking is working.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a TOK essay usually need?
faqs.answer: Three or four, placed deliberately rather than held weekly. One on title selection, which is the session that reliably changes the grade because everything downstream is constrained by the choice. Two on paragraph interrogation, where the student brings a paragraph and leaves with questions to answer in writing. One on the exhibition, mostly spent replacing abstract objects with specific ones. A provider proposing a weekly Theory of Knowledge commitment across a year is proposing a shape that does not match a component built on a handful of decisions.

faqs.question: Is online support suitable for a subject like Theory of Knowledge?
faqs.answer: It suits it well. The prescribed title sits on screen beside the student's own paragraph, comments go into the margin as questions rather than corrections, and every version is saved and dated so the development of an argument is visible rather than claimed. That version history also demonstrates the thinking was the student's, which matters in a component where supplying argument is the easy failure. The published cost difference runs one way too: AED 180-350 for qualified in-home work in this market against AED 150-300 online. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE.

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-essay-help.closingHeading: Test all six titles before writing one word
abu-dhabi/ib-tok-essay-help.closingBody: The session that changes a Theory of Knowledge grade is the first one, and it involves no writing. Read all six prescribed titles and test each against three questions: do you have specific real examples in two areas of knowledge, is there a genuine counterclaim available, and can it be answered in 1,600 words. Most students find two titles pass and four do not. Then budget the words before writing any. Send the titles, the themes your school taught and the internal deadline, take the free 30-minute trial lesson, and ask what the provider will not do.

Each has taken DP students through an exhibition commentary from object shortlist to final upload, and each works from the rubric wording your child's school uses.

intro.heading: What Abu Dhabi parents are actually asking when they search for TOK exhibition help
paragraphs: The TOK exhibition is the first of the two assessed tasks in Theory of Knowledge, and for most Abu Dhabi DP students it arrives in the first year of the Diploma, usually a term or two before anyone mentions the essay. The task is narrow and precisely specified. A student selects three objects, links all three to one of the thirty-five fixed internal assessment prompts, and writes a commentary of no more than 950 words explaining why each object belongs in an exhibition on that prompt. The whole thing is marked out of ten by the school and moderated by the IB.

That specification is why the task catches out strong students. A child who writes excellent History essays can lose four marks here because the commentary describes three interesting objects instead of arguing how each one answers a question about knowledge. The rubric does not reward the object. It rewards the link between the object, its real-world context, and the prompt. Parents searching for TOK exhibition help in Abu Dhabi are almost always reacting to a first draft that came back with a mark in the middle band and a comment nobody at home can decode.

Abu Dhabi adds its own pressure. ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, licenses and inspects the emirate's private schools, and the Diploma cohorts here are concentrated in a relatively small number of them: the island schools, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor, and the newer communities out towards Al Shamkha and Shakhbout City. TOK is frequently taught by a teacher whose main subject is something else, in a single weekly period, to a class of twenty. There is rarely time for individual object-by-object interrogation, which is exactly the part that moves a commentary from the satisfactory band to the good one.

Our answer to that is a short, specific block of one-to-one work delivered online over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For a task like this the online format is the better one anyway, because the work is screen work: the student shares the commentary document, the tutor marks the link sentence by sentence against the prompt, and the object images sit open in a second tab. Nothing about that improves by adding a forty-minute drive from Al Reem Island to Yas.

A typical engagement here is three to five sessions, not a year of weekly lessons. Session one interrogates the object shortlist and the prompt choice, because a weak prompt choice caps the mark before a word is written. Sessions two and three work through the commentary in three roughly equal 300-word blocks. A final session covers the justification of inclusion, the word count, and the image and citation requirements your child's school sets for upload.

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-exhibition-help.programmesIntro: TOK belongs to the Diploma Programme core, but the thinking it assesses is built earlier. Here is where each IB programme sits for an Abu Dhabi family and what it means for exhibition work specifically.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: TOK sits in the DP core alongside the Extended Essay and CAS. It runs across both years, is assessed through the exhibition and the essay, and is graded A to E. The exhibition is the first-year task: three objects, one IA prompt, 950 words, ten marks. The essay follows in the second year on one of six prescribed titles and is externally assessed.
programmes.countryNote: Most Abu Dhabi DP students meet the exhibition in the second or third term of DP1, which collides with the first round of subject internal assessments. Families here often ask for exhibition support as a short block rather than a running commitment, precisely because the Physics and Maths IAs are landing in the same weeks.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP does not include TOK, but it builds the two habits the exhibition rewards: justifying a claim with evidence and reflecting on the process of knowing. Interdisciplinary units and the Personal Project both ask a student to explain why a source counts as reliable, which is the same move the exhibition asks for in miniature.
programmes.countryNote: The IB continuum schools in Abu Dhabi, concentrated around Al Raha and Saadiyat, tend to produce DP1 students who are comfortable with reflection but unused to a hard word limit. The 950-word ceiling is often the first genuinely tight constraint they have written against.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP's inquiry cycle introduces the idea that a question can be about knowledge itself rather than about facts. The exhibition at the end of PYP is a different task from the TOK exhibition and should not be confused with it, though the shared name causes regular confusion in Abu Dhabi households with children in both programmes.
programmes.countryNote: Families with a Year 6 child and a DP1 child in the same Abu Dhabi school often receive two sets of exhibition emails in the same month. The PYP exhibition is a collaborative inquiry presentation; the TOK exhibition is an individually assessed written commentary worth one third of a DP core grade.

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-exhibition-help.subjectsIntro: An exhibition prompt sits inside a theme or an area of knowledge, and the choice shapes how hard the commentary is to argue. These are the territories your child can draw objects from, with the practical consequence of each.

subjects.name: Knowledge and the knower
subjects.description: The one theme every DP student studies. Prompts about bias, perspective and what counts as a good reason sit here. It is the most forgiving territory for an exhibition because almost any personal object has a knower attached, and the most dangerous, because commentaries drift into autobiography.

subjects.name: Knowledge and technology
subjects.description: The most commonly chosen optional theme in UAE schools. Objects are easy to find and hard to make specific: a phone, an app screenshot and a smart speaker is three versions of the same object. A strong commentary here names a particular artefact with a particular history.

subjects.name: Knowledge and language
subjects.description: Unusually strong in Abu Dhabi, where a student may study in English, hold family conversations in Arabic, Malayalam, Tagalog or Russian, and sit MoE-mandated Arabic alongside the Diploma. A translated document or a bilingual sign is a genuinely specific object with a real context.

subjects.name: Knowledge and politics
subjects.description: Rewarding and the one to handle with care. Prompts about whose knowledge gets heard work well with institutional objects such as a census form or a published statistical release. Keep the object and the argument squarely about knowledge claims rather than about contested political positions.

subjects.name: Knowledge and religion
subjects.description: Prompts here concern how religious knowledge is justified and transmitted, not whether a belief is true. The distinction is the whole task. A commentary that argues for or against a doctrine misses the prompt; one that examines how a text is interpreted and by whom hits it.

subjects.name: Knowledge and indigenous societies
subjects.description: The least chosen theme and often the highest scoring, because the objects are specific by nature: an oral map, a navigation technique, a plant used medicinally. The research load is heavier, so it suits a student who started the exhibition early in DP1.

subjects.name: Natural sciences
subjects.description: Instruments, datasets and retracted papers all make excellent objects. Students doing HL Chemistry or Biology already have a lab notebook, which is a real object with a real context and a defensible claim about how scientific knowledge is produced and checked.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The classic source of objects and the easiest place to lose marks, because a historical object invites narration. The commentary needs the object to do epistemic work: what does this particular artefact show about how historical knowledge is constructed, selected or lost?

subjects.name: Human sciences
subjects.description: Surveys, questionnaires and published indices are specific, dated and easy to contextualise. A student who has sat a school wellbeing survey has an object with a context they can describe first-hand, which is normally stronger than one found through a search.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Underused and genuinely distinctive. A proof, a graphing tool output or a flawed statistical chart raises questions about certainty and justification that few classmates will have written about, which helps when a moderator reads thirty commentaries from one school.

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-exhibition-help.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi is useful to an exhibition writer because it supplies specific, datable, local objects. These areas carry DP cohorts and each offers object material a moderator will not have seen on thirty other commentaries.

regions.name: Abu Dhabi island and the Corniche
regions.note: The older school stock and the densest DP cohorts. The Corniche's own signage, tide markers and public-information boards are specific local objects with documented installation histories, which makes contextualising them straightforward.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment living, a short hop to the island schools, and a planning history documented in public municipal material. Students here regularly use construction notices or land-use maps as objects for prompts about expert knowledge.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: The villa corridor that feeds several of the emirate's IB and British schools. Evening sessions here usually start at 5pm or later once the school run and activities clear, which is the single most common scheduling constraint we work around.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Museum and cultural-district objects sit on the doorstep, with published catalogue entries and acquisition dates. An object with a curator's label attached already has the real-world context the rubric asks for.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Mixed-community schooling and a lot of DP students who travel for sport. Recorded sessions and asynchronous commentary feedback matter more here than anywhere else in the emirate, because weekends disappear to fixtures.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Large family households and a wide spread of curricula. Students often juggle MoE-mandated Arabic and Islamic Education alongside DP subjects, which makes a 950-word task with a hard deadline easier to fit than an open-ended one.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Reef
regions.note: The newer mainland communities, where commutes are long and after-school time is short. A 45-minute online session at 7pm is often the only workable slot, and the exhibition is short enough to finish inside four of them.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Also under ADEK, with a smaller DP population and fewer local TOK specialists. Online delivery is the practical difference between a weekly specialist session and none, which is the honest case for the format in this part of the emirate.

schoolClusters.city: Abu Dhabi island and Al Bateen
schoolClusters.note: Established Diploma cohorts where TOK is usually taught in a single weekly period by a teacher with another main subject. Students we support here typically arrive with a marked first draft and a band comment they want decoded.
schools: American Community School of Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas
schoolClusters.note: The corridor with the heaviest concentration of IB continuum provision in the emirate. Exhibition deadlines here tend to cluster in the same fortnight, which is why specialist availability tightens sharply at that point in DP1.

schoolClusters.city: Saadiyat, Al Reem and the newer mainland communities
schoolClusters.note: A mix of IB and British provision, with families who moved emirate or country mid-programme. Transfer students often meet the exhibition having covered a different optional theme at their previous school.
schools: Nord Anglia International School Abu Dhabi

abu-dhabi/ib-tok-exhibition-help.modesIntro: The exhibition is a short task with a hard deadline, so support for it is better bought as a block than as an open-ended weekly arrangement. These are the three shapes that actually work.

modes.title: The four-session exhibition block
modes.description: The standard request. One session on prompt and object choice, two on the commentary in 300-word blocks, one on justification, word count and upload requirements. Booked to land two to three weeks before the school's internal deadline so there is room for the student to revise between sessions.

modes.description: For students who want the whole core handled: exhibition in the first year, prescribed-title essay in the second, and the thinking skills that sit under both. A weekly 60-minute slot on Gulf Standard Time, usually at 5pm or later once the Abu Dhabi school run clears.

sections.heading: What TOK exhibition help in Abu Dhabi actually covers
paragraphs: TOK exhibition help in Abu Dhabi means one-to-one coaching on a single assessed task: selecting three objects, pinning them to one of the thirty-five IA prompts, and producing a commentary of no more than 950 words that earns marks out of ten on a holistic rubric. It is coaching, questioning and marking. It is not drafting, and under IB academic honesty rules it cannot be.

In practice a session looks like this. The student shares their document. The tutor reads the first object paragraph aloud and asks one question: which words here connect this object to the prompt? Nine times out of ten the student cannot point at a sentence, because there is not one. That is the diagnosis, and it is the same diagnosis for most mid-band commentaries written anywhere in the emirate. The fix is the student rewriting that paragraph with the link made explicit, in their own words, between sessions.

The second thing the work covers is specificity. The rubric wants real objects in real contexts, and a surprising number of first drafts contain a category rather than an object. "Social media" is a category. "The screenshot of my own Instagram feed taken on 14 September 2026" is an object, with a date, an owner and a context. Students in Abu Dhabi have unusually good access to specific objects because the emirate documents itself well, from museum catalogue entries on Saadiyat to published municipal planning notices.

The third element is the administrative tail that loses marks for no intellectual reason at all: three images, the correct prompt reproduced without alteration, citations in whatever style the school requires, and a word count under the ceiling. We check all four, because a commentary moderated down for a missing image is the most avoidable loss in the DP core.
bullets: Prompt selection before writing, because a weak prompt caps the achievable mark
Object specificity: a named, dated, contextualised thing rather than a category
The link sentence in each object paragraph, written by the student and marked by the tutor
Word count, images, unaltered prompt wording and the school's citation requirement

sections.heading: The task as the rubric specifies it, component by component
paragraphs: Every number in the table below is a specification, not a guideline, and each one is somewhere a mark is quietly lost. The commentary ceiling is 950 words; the three objects are not two and not four; the IA prompt is used exactly as published and not reworded to suit the objects a student has already chosen. That last one is the most common structural error we see in Abu Dhabi drafts, and it is usually a sign the objects were picked first.

The exhibition is internally assessed by the school and externally moderated by the IB, which has a practical consequence parents rarely hear explained. The teacher's mark is a proposal. If the moderator disagrees with the school's standard across the sample, the whole cohort's marks can move. This is why a commentary that explicitly evidences the rubric language, rather than relying on a teacher who already knows what the student meant, is worth more than a charming one.

The exhibition is one third of the TOK grade and the prescribed-title essay is the other two thirds. Both are marked out of ten. TOK is then graded A to E, combined with the Extended Essay grade in a published matrix worth up to three points on the 45-point scale, and a grade E in either TOK or the Extended Essay is a failing condition for the Diploma. That is the real reason a ten-mark task matters more than its size suggests.

Read the band descriptors in your child's own copy of the TOK subject guide rather than any version reproduced online. We reference the guide and work from the school's wording; we do not supply IB documents, past prompts or mark schemes, because reproducing them is a copyright matter.

sections.heading: Choosing one of the thirty-five IA prompts without closing off your own argument
paragraphs: The prompt is chosen from a fixed published list and cannot be edited, which means the choice is a strategic decision made once and lived with. Some prompts are generous: they accept objects from several areas of knowledge and allow three genuinely different arguments. Others are narrow, and a student who picks one of those often finds that their second and third objects are restatements of the first. The mark suffers not because the writing is weak but because the exhibition has only one idea in it.

The question we ask in a first session is simple: for this prompt, can you name three objects that make three different claims? If the honest answer is no, the prompt is wrong for this student even if it is intellectually appealing. We then test two or three alternative prompts against the same object pool before anything is written. Twenty minutes spent here routinely saves a fortnight of rewriting.

A second consideration is cohort overlap. If a whole DP1 class in a Khalifa City school picks the most discussed prompt about technology and bias, thirty commentaries land on a moderator's desk with overlapping objects. Nothing in the rubric penalises that, but a distinctive prompt and an object nobody else could have chosen makes the rubric's demand for real-world context dramatically easier to satisfy.

Finally, match the prompt to the thinking the student already does well. A student strong in Natural Sciences who picks a prompt about certainty has a lab notebook, a retracted paper and an instrument calibration record available. A student strong in Language and Literature who picks the same prompt is working uphill. The prompt should sit where the student's evidence already lives.
bullets: Test the prompt against three objects making three different claims before writing
Avoid the prompt your whole class is using if your objects are also the class's objects
Choose a prompt that sits in an area of knowledge where you already have evidence
Never reword the prompt; the published wording is part of the task

sections.heading: Where the ten marks actually go, band by band
paragraphs: The exhibition rubric is holistic: a single judgement across five bands rather than separate criteria to be added up. That design trips parents who are used to the lettered criteria of a subject internal assessment, where a student can be strong on criterion B and weak on criterion D. Here the marker forms one overall impression of how well the commentary justifies the inclusion of three objects for the chosen prompt, and places it in a band.

In practice the bands are separated by a small number of observable features. A commentary in the lower bands describes the objects and asserts a connection. One in the middle bands explains the connection for some objects but not consistently, or links to the theme rather than to the prompt itself. One in the upper bands makes the link explicit for all three objects, grounds each in a specific real-world context, and shows why these three together form an exhibition on that prompt rather than three unrelated paragraphs.

The table below sets out what we look for when reading a draft cold. It is a diagnostic tool, not the official rubric, and it should be read alongside the band descriptors in your school's TOK subject guide. Its purpose is to let a student self-check before submission, which is also the point at which a mark is still movable.

One detail worth knowing: because the task is holistic, a single genuinely excellent object paragraph does not drag the mark up. Three consistent paragraphs do. Students who have spent four hours perfecting object one and twenty minutes on object three are in the most common mark-losing position in the whole task, and it is the easiest one to fix with time rather than talent.

table.caption: EXHIBITION DRAFT DIAGNOSTIC - WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE ON THE PAGE
rows: Objects described; the prompt appears once, at the top, and is not used again
Write one sentence per object that names the prompt and makes a claim
A connection is asserted for each object but never argued or evidenced
Replace each assertion with a because clause tied to the object's context

Give the weakest object a dated, located, specific real-world context

Consistent justification, specific contexts, and three objects answering the prompt from different angles

sections.heading: Objects an Abu Dhabi student can use that nobody else will have
paragraphs: The rubric's demand for a real-world context is where local knowledge becomes a mark advantage. An object a student has physically encountered, in a place they can describe, with a date they can name, is easier to contextualise than anything found through a search engine. Abu Dhabi is unusually well supplied here because the emirate documents itself: museum catalogue entries, published inspection reports, municipal planning notices, bilingual public signage, and the MoE-mandated subject timetables that sit alongside the Diploma in every private school.

A few examples of the kind of thing that works, offered as illustration rather than as a list to copy. A student in Saadiyat used a single museum label, with its acquisition date and attribution line, for a prompt about how knowledge is validated by institutions. A student in Khalifa City used her own Arabic as an additional language workbook, against a prompt about language and knowledge, and contextualised it with the fact that private schools in the emirate teach Arabic to Arab and non-Arab students in separate classes under different curriculum expectations. A student in Al Ain used a dated school inspection report published by the regulator for a prompt about who decides what counts as quality.

What makes those work is not cleverness, it is provenance. Each object has a where, a when and a who, and the student can write about the context from first-hand knowledge rather than from a summary. That is the difference between a commentary that sounds like a search result and one that sounds like a person who was there.

The practical instruction we give is to spend one evening collecting candidate objects before thinking about prompts at all. Photograph eight things. Note where each came from and when. Bring the list to the first session. A shortlist built from a student's actual week in Abu Dhabi beats a shortlist built from a list of popular TOK objects every time.
bullets: A dated museum or exhibition label, with its attribution line, from the Saadiyat cultural district
A bilingual public sign where the Arabic and English do not say quite the same thing
The student's own marked work, with the teacher's comments visible as part of the object
A published regulator document the student's school is actually assessed against

sections.heading: Exhibition, essay, and how the two combine into points
paragraphs: Parents often discover late in DP1 that TOK produces a letter grade, not a mark, and that the letter interacts with the Extended Essay grade in a published matrix worth up to three points on the 45-point total. Those three points decide university offers at the margin, and more importantly a grade E in either TOK or the Extended Essay is a failing condition for the Diploma regardless of how strong the six subject grades are. A ten-mark commentary written in a rush in DP1 is part of that calculation.

The two TOK tasks reward different skills, which is why some students who struggle with the exhibition are fine on the essay and vice versa. The exhibition is concrete, personal and bounded: three things, one prompt, 950 words, chosen by the student. The essay is abstract, comparative and externally assessed: one of six prescribed titles released by the IB, 1,600 words, usually argued across two areas of knowledge. A student who thinks in examples finds the exhibition easier. A student who thinks in arguments finds the essay easier.

Knowing which one your child is changes the sequencing. For an example-thinker, we bank a strong exhibition mark early in DP1 and spend the time saved on essay structure in DP2. For an argument-thinker, we spend more of the exhibition block on the justification move, because that is the one essay skill the exhibition genuinely tests, and the practice transfers.

The comparison table below is the one we put on screen in a first session with a DP1 family, because it usually answers three questions at once: what is the difference, which is worth more, and when does each one happen.

sections.heading: What TOK and core support costs in the Abu Dhabi market
paragraphs: Nobody in this part of the market publishes a number, so here is what the market charges, with the sources named. These are market rates we have read on other providers' pages and on a published Dubai rate survey, not our prices. IB Gram quotes after a free trial lesson, because a four-session exhibition block and a two-year weekly core commitment are different purchases and a single hourly figure would mislead you about both.

Start from the monthly number rather than the hourly one, because that is the number a household budget actually feels. A short exhibition block is four sessions inside a single month, so even at the specialist end of the market it is a one-month commitment rather than a standing cost. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table puts weekly one-hour tutoring at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. A core-only block sits at the bottom of that range by duration, not by rate.

On hourly rates, the published figures run as follows. EdFlik advertises online tutoring from AED 45 to 65 an hour and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, both at the budget online tier. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes AED 270. Bestimate's survey puts IB and IGCSE specialist rates at AED 200 to 450 and above, and in-home visits including travel at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors quoted from AED 200 to 500. BartyED publishes AED 650 for a named premium tutor. All of those are the providers' own published figures, read in October 2026.

The second thing to weigh is what you are buying hours of. TOK is a low-hours, high-leverage component: four well-spent hours on a 950-word commentary in DP1 can move one third of a core grade, and the core grade interacts with the Extended Essay for up to three points. Compare that with the same four hours spread across an HL subject, where it buys one topic. This is the one calculation we actively encourage families to run before booking anything, including with us.
