abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-s.programmesIntro: The Arabic question looks different at each stage of the continuum, because the mandatory provision and the IB language structure interact differently in each.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic literacy and the mandatory subjects run alongside an inquiry-led English-medium programme, and the balance between the two languages in these years shapes everything later. A child who reaches Year 6 with strong Standard Arabic reading has the Arabic A route genuinely available; one who does not may find it has quietly closed.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi primary schools vary considerably in how much Standard Arabic reading they build, as distinct from spoken fluency. For an Arabic-speaking family that distinction is the one to ask about, because household Arabic is often dialectal while the course is in Standard Arabic.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Language and literature is assessed against criteria A to D with published descriptors, and this is where an Arabic-speaking student first meets the difference between fluency and literary analysis. Students who speak Arabic confidently at home can score modestly here, which is confusing until the distinction is explained.
programmes.countryNote: The decision about whether a student is on an Arabic first-language or additional-language pathway is usually settled during these years, on school assessment. Ask what evidence it rests on and whether it is reviewed, because it determines which Diploma routes remain open.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Candidates take a studies-in-language-and-literature subject and a language-acquisition subject, and Arabic can occupy either depending on the student and the school's options. The combination also determines whether a bilingual diploma is available, which is a structural question rather than an achievement one.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Diploma candidates normally sit the May session. Internal deadlines for internal assessments and the core are set by each school and differ across the emirate, and Arabic-speaking candidates often carry mandatory subject assessments in the same weeks, which is worth mapping in September.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: CP candidates take DP courses alongside a career-related study, and language provision depends on the school's offer. For a student whose strength is in Arabic and whose intended route is regional, the CP is sometimes a better structural fit and is rarely raised unprompted.
programmes.countryNote: A small number of Abu Dhabi schools offer the CP. Recognition differs by destination, including inside the UAE, so ask the school's counselling team how its CP leavers have been treated by the institutions your family is considering.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-s.subjectsIntro: What each subject actually assesses for an Arabic-speaking candidate, and where the marks go. The Arabic courses and the English-medium subjects fail in completely different ways.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Assesses analysis of literary and non-literary texts, including unseen material, and comparison across works. Fluency is assumed rather than credited; marks go to sustained argument about how a text produces its effects. Confident speakers routinely lose marks for writing appreciation instead of analysis.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Literature
subjects.description: A narrower literary focus with more weight on works studied in depth and on sustained comparison. Marks are lost where a candidate narrates a text rather than arguing about it, and where the comparative task becomes two separate readings placed side by side.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: A language-acquisition course assessing listening, reading, writing and speaking against published criteria, with text types that have conventions worth learning deliberately. Native and near-native speakers are not normally placed here, and where a school's placement looks wrong it is worth questioning early.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Taught in UAE private schools alongside the licensed international curriculum, with separate provision for Arab and non-Arab students. For Arab students the published requirement is Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction, and the content follows the Ministry's material rather than any alternative syllabus.

subjects.name: UAE social studies and moral education
subjects.description: Required alongside any licensed curriculum, with Arabic as the primary language of instruction for Arab students in social studies. It is usually the least academically demanding of the mandatory subjects and the one most often left out of a revision plan, which then collides with it.

subjects.name: Chemistry, Physics and Biology in English
subjects.description: The difficulty for an Arabic-speaking candidate is rarely the science. It is the precision of the English the mark scheme credits: state, outline, explain, evaluate and discuss each require a particular kind of sentence, and a correct idea expressed loosely collects fewer marks than a narrower idea expressed exactly.

subjects.name: Mathematics in English
subjects.description: The most language-light subject in the Diploma and often where an Arabic-speaking candidate is strongest. The exceptions are the exploration, which is extended writing, and the word-heavy modelling and statistics questions where the reading is the difficulty rather than the mathematics.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Management in English
subjects.description: Language-heavy and evaluation-dependent, which makes these the subjects where academic English support pays best. Marks live in a supported judgement, and reaching one requires discourse markers and hedging that are learned rather than absorbed.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Both written in the language of the programme and both demanding a position argued across a long piece. For a candidate writing at length in a second academic language this is the heaviest writing load in the Diploma, and it carries both points and a failing condition.

subjects.name: English A or English B
subjects.description: Placement here interacts directly with the Arabic decision and with whether a bilingual diploma is available. It is often settled quickly and is hard to reverse, so the evidence behind the placement is worth asking about in writing during the first weeks.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-s.regionsIntro: Arabic-speaking households are spread across the whole emirate, and session timing depends on the school run and, in Ramadan, on the hour of the day. These notes are about that.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Karamah
regions.note: Established island communities with a long-settled Emirati and Arab population and manageable travel. Families here often want Arabic A support at a level the school itself handles well, and the gap is literary analysis rather than language.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: A central island community with strong school provision and short commutes, which allows earlier weekday sessions. For candidates carrying both Arabic A and three sciences in English, protecting one early weekday slot is the practical move.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: A large villa catchment with a long term-time school run, which pushes sessions to 5pm or later. During Ramadan the same households usually shift to post-Iftar timing, which works better here than elsewhere because the commute is already over.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: A substantial mainland catchment with a wide spread of school choices and long travel to the island. Specialist Arabic A support is not available locally in any meaningful sense, which makes live video the only route rather than the convenient one.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Newer communities with a growing school-age population and a long commute. Families here often have children across more than one school, which makes the week's scheduling the binding constraint rather than the syllabus.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Dense apartment living with short travel, suiting shorter and more frequent sessions. For academic English work in the sciences, where repetition matters more than session length, that is a real advantage.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: An hour inland with a large Emirati and Arab population and very few IB specialists on the ground. An Arabic A candidate in Al Ain has no local route to a tutor who marks literary commentary to the published criteria.

schoolClusters.city: Island and central Abu Dhabi
schoolClusters.note: Where the longest-established schools sit, with strong mandatory-subject provision and a high proportion of Arabic first-language students. The Arabic course here is usually taught well, and the demand is for depth in literary analysis rather than for language support.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor

sections.heading: What the mandatory subject rules actually require
paragraphs: The federal baseline is simple: private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Every emirate implements that through its own regulator, and KHDA has published the clearest public statement of the detail. It is worth reading even for an Abu Dhabi family, because it describes the structure that produces your child's timetable.

KHDA's guidance requires Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with those requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited due to the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction.

The language-of-instruction rules are specific. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Arabic is the primary language for social studies for Arab students. For non-Arabs, the school's licensed-curriculum language applies in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies. Schools are also required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate approval from the regulator to teach these subjects, which is a concrete and checkable thing for a parent to ask about.

Two further details govern what a tutor can legitimately do. Instructional time for these subjects is calculated based on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and it is advised that any mandatory subject lesson is at least 25 minutes. And for these subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is strictly prohibited. That last clause means support for Islamic Education or social studies has to work with the school's own material, not an alternative syllabus.

sections.heading: Arabic A or Arabic B: the route choice and what it closes
paragraphs: In the Diploma, a candidate takes a studies-in-language-and-literature subject and a language-acquisition subject, and Arabic can occupy either depending on the student and the school's option list. Arabic A, in its Language and Literature or Literature form, is a first-language course: it assumes fluency and assesses analysis. Arabic B is a language-acquisition course, assessing listening, reading, writing and speaking against published criteria. The two are not a graded pair; they are different courses for different purposes.

The route matters for three reasons. First, it determines what the student is actually assessed on, and therefore what any tutoring should address. Second, it determines whether a bilingual diploma is in reach, since that depends on the combination of subjects and languages taken rather than on performance; the specifics should be confirmed with your school's IB coordinator. Third, it affects how a candidate's profile reads to universities in the region and beyond, which is a question for admissions offices rather than for a tutoring page.

The common mistake is placement by convenience. A native speaker put into Arabic B because that is the class that runs is being assessed on a language they already hold, which looks comfortable and teaches them very little. A student whose household Arabic is dialectal and whose Standard Arabic reading is weak, placed into Arabic A because they are an Arabic speaker, is in a literature course they cannot yet access. Both situations are common and both are visible early.

The way to settle it is evidence rather than category: a piece of unseen Standard Arabic analysis attempted under timed conditions, marked against the published criteria. That shows whether the gap is language or literary technique, which are different problems. Ask the school what evidence its placement rests on and whether it is reviewed, in writing, during the first weeks rather than after a year.

sections.heading: Where Arabic A candidates actually lose marks
paragraphs: The first and largest loss is appreciation written in place of analysis. A candidate who is genuinely moved by a text and writes about its beauty, its importance and its themes is writing something valuable and largely uncredited. The criteria reward an account of how the text produces its effects: which choices the writer made, what those choices do to a reader, and how the evidence supports the claim. That is a different kind of sentence, and it is learnable in a term.

The second is the comparative task becoming two separate readings. A response that discusses one work thoroughly and then another work thoroughly, with a concluding paragraph noting similarities, sits below one that holds a single comparative line of argument throughout. This is a structural habit rather than a knowledge gap, and it is the single clearest band divider in the course.

The third is unseen analysis under time pressure. Native fluency does not supply a method for approaching a text never seen before, and candidates either produce a confident but unfocused response or spend too long reading and run out of time. A method, practised under the real duration, resolves most of it: what to notice first, what to do with it, and when to stop reading and start writing.

The fourth is the oral component, where candidates are often strongest in delivery and weakest in structure. A fluent speaker with no argument scores below a less fluent one with a clear line and evidence. Rehearsing, recording and reviewing against the criteria is uncomfortable and effective, and it is one of the few places where a student can hear the gap themselves rather than being told about it.

sections.heading: Studying six subjects in English when the home language is Arabic
paragraphs: This is the other half of the page and it is the half families are least likely to name correctly. A candidate who understands Chemistry at higher level and writes a correct but loosely worded extended answer is not short of Chemistry. They are short of the specific English the mark scheme credits, which is a narrow and teachable thing: command-term language, the distinction between stating and explaining, the hedged phrasing that evaluation marks require, and the discourse markers that signal an argument is being made rather than a list offered.

The diagnosis is straightforward once someone looks. Read a marked extended answer and ask whether the idea is right. If the idea is right and the marks are not there, the problem is expression; if the idea is absent, it is content. Families and schools frequently resolve this as a content problem because that is the familiar category, and then buy science teaching for a language issue, which is slow and expensive and does not work.

Where the problem is genuinely expression, the work belongs inside the subject rather than in a general English class. A student needs to see what a full-mark Chemistry evaluation sentence looks like and why, not to improve their English in the abstract. That is why this support is delivered by a subject tutor who can mark the paper, rather than by a language tutor, and it is usually shorter than families expect.

There is one subject where the pattern reverses. Mathematics is the most language-light course in the Diploma and often where an Arabic-speaking candidate is strongest, with two exceptions: the exploration, which is extended writing assessed partly on communication, and the word-heavy modelling and statistics questions where the reading is the difficulty. Both of those are language work inside a mathematics course, which is a specific thing to ask for.

sections.heading: Islamic Education and social studies: what support may and may not look like
paragraphs: These subjects sit outside the IB and are governed by the regulator, and the rules change what a tutor may do. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is strictly prohibited. That means a tutor cannot offer an alternative syllabus, a summarised set of notes drawn from elsewhere, or material from another system. Support here means working with the school's own material.

What that leaves is genuinely useful and quite narrow: helping a student read the set material accurately, building the vocabulary the assessments use, practising the forms of answer the school's assessments ask for, and organising revision against the school's own schedule. For a student whose Standard Arabic reading is weaker than their spoken Arabic, comprehension support with the school's material is often the highest-value help available.

The regulator's rules also give families something concrete to verify. Schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate approval from the regulator to teach these subjects, so a parent concerned about provision has a specific question to ask rather than a general complaint to make. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with lesson length variable provided the weekly total is met and an advised minimum of 25 minutes per lesson, which gives a basis for asking whether the timetabled time matches the requirement.

For Diploma candidates the practical issue is collision. Mandatory subject assessments do not pause for internal assessment deadlines or mock weeks, and an Arabic-speaking candidate carries more of this load than a non-Arab classmate. Mapping all of it onto one calendar in September, including the school's mandatory subject assessment dates, is a free exercise that prevents a term of avoidable pressure.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the school week and when study actually happens
paragraphs: Almost nothing written for this market acknowledges that the academic year in the UAE contains a month in which the entire daily rhythm changes, and for Arabic-speaking Muslim families that month reshapes study more than any other factor on this page. School hours shorten, energy distributes differently across the day, and the productive study window moves to the evening after Iftar. A revision plan written in October that assumes a 5pm session throughout the year is wrong for several weeks of it.

Handling it well is mostly a matter of planning rather than of effort. Sessions move to post-Iftar timing. Heavy new content is scheduled before or after rather than inside the month. Work that suits shorter, lighter sessions, such as vocabulary, command-term practice and marked short answers, fits the period better than two-hour timed papers. And the weeks immediately after are the natural place for the full timed rehearsals that were deferred.

The calendar interacts with the examination season too. Where the month falls relative to a school's mock window, internal assessment deadlines and the May session changes from year to year, which is precisely why no page should publish specific dates for it. The useful action is to ask the school in September how it intends to handle its own deadlines in relation to the month, because schools make that decision at different times and some make it late.

There is also a simple equity point in planning terms. A candidate carrying Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies alongside six Diploma subjects has less discretionary time than a classmate carrying the additional-language versions. Any honest plan starts by counting the real hours rather than the nominal ones, and that count is different for this student.

sections.heading: How lessons run, and the limits worth stating
paragraphs: Lessons are one-to-one over live video, with screen sharing, a shared whiteboard and the student's own marked work open. For Arabic A the session typically works through a marked commentary line by line; for the English-medium subjects it works through a marked extended answer and the phrasing that cost marks. Gulf Standard Time lessons are scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school week and move to post-Iftar timing during Ramadan without changing the plan.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India. For this page the argument is specialist availability rather than cost, although the cost argument exists: in-home one-to-one in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 by independent home tutors, against AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor online and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an IB specialist, per Bestimate's rate table with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200. A tutor who marks Arabic literary commentary to the published criteria is scarce, and a twenty-minute radius is not where you find one.

Private schools in Abu Dhabi are overseen by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai's regulator is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, whose published mandatory-subject guidance is quoted throughout this page, Sharjah's is the Sharjah Private Education Authority, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from any of them, or from the IB or any examination board, and no page of ours should imply one.

Three limits. Individual private tutors in the UAE need the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, and you may reasonably ask whether a tutor holds it. ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. And where no specialist is free for Arabic A or for a higher level subject at the hours you need, we say so and offer a different slot, a later start or a referral rather than filling the hour.

faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic fluently but their Arabic A marks are low. Why?
faqs.answer: Because Arabic A assumes fluency rather than crediting it. The criteria reward analysis: an account of how a text produces its effects, which choices the writer made, and evidence supporting the claim. A candidate who writes about a text's beauty, importance or themes is writing something valuable and largely uncredited. That is a different kind of sentence, it is learnable in a term, and it is the single largest source of lost marks in the course for confident speakers.

faqs.question: Should a native Arabic speaker take Arabic A or Arabic B?
faqs.answer: Normally Arabic A, and a native speaker placed in Arabic B for timetable reasons is being assessed on a language they already hold. The honest exception is a student whose household Arabic is dialectal and whose Standard Arabic reading is weak, who may not yet be able to access a literature course. Settle it on evidence rather than on category: one piece of unseen Standard Arabic analysis under timed conditions, marked against the criteria, shows whether the gap is language or literary technique.

faqs.question: Does my child have to take Islamic Education and social studies as well as the IB?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must follow the Ministry's general regulations, so they run alongside any licensed international curriculum. KHDA's published guidance requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited due to different curriculum expectations and language of instruction.

faqs.question: Can a tutor teach the Islamic Education syllabus?
faqs.answer: Only using the school's own material, and that is a rule rather than a preference. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is strictly prohibited. What support can legitimately cover is reading the set material accurately, the vocabulary the assessments use, the forms of answer the school asks for, and revision organised against the school's schedule. For a student whose Standard Arabic reading is weaker than their speech, that comprehension help is often the most valuable available.

faqs.question: Which language is Islamic Education taught in?
faqs.answer: It depends on the group. The published requirement is Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with Arabic also the primary language for social studies for Arab students. For non-Arabs, the school's licensed-curriculum language applies in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies. Schools are also required to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate approval from the regulator for those subjects, which is a specific thing a parent can ask about.

faqs.question: My child knows the science but loses marks in English. What should we buy?
faqs.answer: Subject-specific academic English, delivered inside the subject by a tutor who marks the paper, not general English support. The diagnosis is simple: read a marked extended answer and ask whether the idea is right. If the idea is right and the marks are missing, the problem is expression, which means command-term language, the difference between stating and explaining, and the hedged phrasing evaluation marks require. That is narrower and faster than science teaching, and it is usually what the family actually needs.

faqs.question: Is a bilingual diploma worth aiming for?
faqs.answer: It can be, and it is a structural question rather than an achievement one: whether it is available depends on the combination of subjects and languages a candidate takes rather than on how well they perform. Because the specifics are set by the IB and the combination is set by your school's option list, confirm both with your IB coordinator before assuming it is in reach. For a student whose Arabic is genuinely strong it is often available with little additional work, which is a reason to ask early.

faqs.question: How do we handle study during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: By planning for it rather than pushing through it. School hours shorten, the productive study window moves to the evening after Iftar, and sessions move with it. Work that suits shorter lighter sessions fits the period well: vocabulary, command-term practice, marked short answers. Heavy new content and two-hour timed papers are better scheduled before or after. Ask your school in September how it intends to handle its own deadlines in relation to the month, because schools decide that at different times.

faqs.question: Where do Arabic A candidates lose the most marks in the written papers?
faqs.answer: Four places, in order. Appreciation written where analysis was required, which is the largest. Comparative tasks answered as two separate readings with a concluding paragraph on similarities, rather than one comparative argument throughout. Unseen analysis approached without a method, producing confident but unfocused responses or running out of time. And oral components delivered fluently but without a structured argument. All four are structural habits, which means all four respond to marked practice within a term.

faqs.question: Does my child's Arabic help or hurt their Diploma workload?
faqs.answer: Both, honestly. Strong Arabic makes Arabic A a realistic strength and brings a bilingual diploma within reach, which is an advantage. At the same time an Arabic first-language student carries Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education in Standard Arabic and social studies in Arabic alongside six Diploma subjects, which is more timetabled load than a non-Arab classmate carries. Any plan that counts nominal free hours rather than real ones will fail in the fourth week, and this student has fewer.

faqs.question: Can you find an Arabic literature specialist in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: We look for one who can mark Arabic literary commentary against the published criteria, which is a scarce specialism in any city rather than a regional shortage. Delivery is online precisely because that search cannot be restricted to a driving radius: an in-home arrangement limits the choice to whoever can reach your address, which is the wrong filter for this subject. Where no specialist is free at the hours you need, we say so and offer a different slot, a later start or a referral.

faqs.question: Is Mathematics easier for an Arabic-speaking candidate?
faqs.answer: Usually, because it is the most language-light course in the Diploma, and it is frequently where these candidates are strongest. Two exceptions matter. The mathematical exploration is extended writing assessed partly on communication, so it carries the same language demand as any written component. And the word-heavy modelling and statistics questions can be a reading problem rather than a mathematics problem. Both are language work inside a mathematics course, which is a specific thing to ask a tutor for.

faqs.question: What should we ask the school in the first weeks of the year?
faqs.answer: Five things, all answerable in one email. Which Arabic stream your child is in and what evidence that rests on. Which stream they are in for Islamic Education and social studies, and in which language. The weekly timetabled time for each mandatory subject. The internal deadlines for internal assessment and the core. And how the school intends to handle those deadlines in relation to Ramadan. Those five answers prevent most of the avoidable pressure in an Arabic-speaking candidate's year.

faqs.question: How much does this kind of support cost in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Market rates in the emirate run AED 150 to AED 300 an hour for a qualified subject tutor online, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200, and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an IB specialist, per Bestimate's Dubai rate table, with TutorChase at AED 270. In-home one-to-one is quoted at AED 180 to AED 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 by independent home tutors, the difference being the journey. Those are market figures rather than an IB Gram price list; our route is a free trial lesson and a consultation.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-s.closingHeading: Separate the Arabic from the English, then ask the school five questions
abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-s.closingBody: The useful first step costs nothing: read one marked Arabic commentary and one marked extended answer from an English-medium subject side by side. That tells you whether you are buying literary technique or academic English, which are different purchases at different rates. Then send the school one email asking which Arabic and Islamic Education streams your child is in, on what evidence, how much weekly time each mandatory subject gets, and what the internal deadlines are. Book a free trial lesson with the specialist the marked work points to, and expect a plan that counts the real hours in the week.

intro.heading: Strong students, unfamiliar marking, and a bill that depends on which
paragraphs: Indian families are one of the largest school communities in the UAE. In Dubai, Indian curricula accounted for 26% of the emirate's private-school enrolment in 2024-25, in a sector serving 387,441 students across 227 private schools and offering 17 different curricula. Abu Dhabi's distribution differs, but the practical reality is the same: a great many households here are choosing between an Indian-curriculum school and an international one, and many have children in both at once.

When a child moves from CBSE or ICSE into an IB programme, the first marked work is usually disappointing and almost always misread. The content is not the problem. Indian board teaching is thorough and often ahead of the equivalent IB year in procedural mathematics and factual coverage. What is new is the marking: criterion descriptors rather than totals of correct answers, command terms that each mean something specific, independent investigations with no CBSE equivalent, and extended written reasoning where the previous system wanted the answer.

That distinction decides the bill. Learning to read a criterion descriptor and write to it is a handful of sessions. Learning to design and write a Diploma internal assessment is a defined piece of teaching measured in weeks. Closing a genuine content gap, which does exist in a few places, is the expensive case. Market monthly estimates in the emirate run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work, per Bestimate's Dubai rate table, so across two children and three subjects the diagnosis matters more than the hourly rate.

There is a second cost conversation specific to Indian households here, and it is about siblings. Families frequently have two or three children in school simultaneously and are quoted per child, per subject, per hour, which compounds quickly. The honest arithmetic is that a shared tutor across two children in the same subject saves something real, a shared session does not, and the largest available saving is not buying support for the child who turns out not to need it. This page sets that out rather than quoting a package.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service we offer only in India, and families who used home tuition before moving should know the service here is different. The in-home market in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 500 an hour because the journey is priced into every lesson, and for a household running two or three children's schedules, removing travel from the equation is worth more than the rate difference alone. It also widens the choice of tutor from whoever lives nearby to whoever can actually mark the subject to the published criteria.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-indian-students.programmesIntro: An Indian-curriculum family in Abu Dhabi is usually comparing systems rather than schools. These are the IB programmes available here, described against what a CBSE or ICSE family already knows.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, with no graded examinations and continuous reporting against the programme's framework. Parents used to term tests and ranked results often read a PYP report as containing no information at all. The adjustment is cultural rather than academic, and children usually complete it faster than their parents do.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi PYP schools will translate a report into plain terms if asked: which skills are secure, which are emerging, what would change the picture. Asking that question in term one removes most of the pressure to buy tutoring at primary level, where it is rarely the right purchase for a child from an Indian board.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Each subject is assessed against criteria A to D with published descriptors, which is the first real break from Indian board marking. A student who scored consistently in CBSE tests can drop a band here while knowing more than their classmates, purely because the descriptor asks for something the answer did not do.
programmes.countryNote: Some Abu Dhabi schools run MYP to Year 11 and others switch to IGCSE at Year 10. For an Indian family planning a possible return, that distinction matters, because an IGCSE certificate and an MYP record are read differently by schools and by recognition processes.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at two levels plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and creativity, activity and service. For a CBSE or ICSE student the unfamiliar parts are the internal assessments in every subject, the core components, and the expectation of sustained independent work rather than preparation for a terminal paper.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Diploma candidates normally sit the May session. For families weighing the Diploma against staying in an Indian board, the honest comparison is not difficulty but shape: the Diploma spreads assessment across two years and rewards independent work, while Indian boards concentrate it in a final examination.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: DP courses alongside a career-related study and a reflective project, offered by a small number of schools in the emirate. Recognition differs by destination and is worth checking explicitly, particularly for families who may apply to universities in India as well as elsewhere.
programmes.countryNote: Because the CP is less familiar to Indian households, it is often not raised at all. If the course load of a full Diploma is the concern rather than ability, it is worth asking prospective schools whether they offer it and how their leavers have fared.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-indian-students.subjectsIntro: Where an Indian-curriculum student stands in each IB subject area, described as a direction of travel rather than as a deficit. Most arrive ahead somewhere and behind somewhere else in the same subject.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The most favourable transfer in the Diploma. CBSE and ICSE algebra and calculus arrive ahead of where the course needs them, and the work sits in the exploration, in unstructured problems with no scaffolding, and in writing out method rather than producing answers.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Content feels easy and the marks do not follow, because the course rewards interpretation. A test chosen correctly and concluded without reference to significance and context scores below a response that does both, and that is the one thing Indian board mathematics rarely asks for.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Theory overlap is high and the internal assessment is entirely new: an independent investigation assessed against published criteria, including evaluation of limitations with their impact. This single component accounts for most of the genuine work an Indian-curriculum student faces in the subject.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Numerical fluency arrives strong. The marks go on extended written reasoning and on data questions where uncertainty has to be propagated and discussed. A correct answer with no reasoning line is the recurring pattern in early work and a fast repair.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The subject where a recall-trained student loses most, because the command terms are decisive. Accurate, detailed answers written to the wrong command term earn the knowledge mark and nothing above it, which feels arbitrary until the pattern is explained once.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Management
subjects.description: Frequently chosen by Indian families and frequently underestimated. The marks live in evaluation and in application to the stimulus material, not in definitions, and a thorough balanced summary scores below a supported judgement.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Placement between English A and English B is one of the most consequential decisions of the first fortnight and is often made quickly. English A assumes a different relationship with literature and with unseen analysis than most Indian board English courses have built.

subjects.name: Hindi as a language option
subjects.levels: Language A or Language B, where offered
subjects.description: Available in the IB structure as a literature or language-acquisition option, including school-supported self-taught routes at standard level in some cases. Whether it is actually offered depends on the school's options list and staffing, which has to be confirmed rather than assumed.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Taught in UAE private schools alongside the licensed international curriculum, and new to most arriving students. For a child joining in the upper years with no Arabic, the school's placement decision and its expectations should be established in writing early.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Both unfamiliar, both carrying points, and a grade E in either is a failing condition for the diploma. The Extended Essay in particular rewards a narrow answerable research question, which is a skill no Indian board course has had reason to teach.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-indian-students.regionsIntro: Indian households in Abu Dhabi are spread widely across the emirate, and the commute shapes the week far more than the syllabus does. These notes are about where sessions can realistically sit.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: One of the largest Indian communities in the emirate, with a wide fee spread and long travel to the island schools. For a household running two or three school schedules, removing tutor travel from the week is the single biggest practical gain.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Growing mainland communities with villa housing and a long term-time school run. Weekday sessions realistically begin at 5pm or later, which usually means one weekday slot per child plus a weekend block.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: A substantial Indian and British-curriculum population with a school run that can take forty minutes each way. Families with children in two different schools here have two different runs, which is the constraint that actually determines scheduling.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment living with short commutes, which makes shorter and more frequent sessions realistic. For criterion-referenced work, where the gains come from repetition rather than duration, that is a genuine advantage.

regions.name: Baniyas and Al Wathba
regions.note: Further from the island with fewer international-curriculum schools nearby, so families travel or choose locally and supplement. This is where live video is the only route to an IB subject specialist at Diploma level.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Nahyan
regions.note: Older island communities with mixed school provision and manageable travel. Households here often have one child in an Indian-curriculum school and one in an IB school, which is a scheduling and budgeting problem as much as an academic one.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: An hour inland under the same emirate authority, with a long-established Indian community and a thin local pool of IB specialists. A Diploma candidate here wanting internal assessment feedback has no local route to a subject specialist.

schoolClusters.city: Mainland Abu Dhabi
schoolClusters.note: Where most Indian households are concentrated and where both Indian-curriculum and international schools sit close together. Families frequently split children between the two, which makes the comparison in this page a live decision rather than a theoretical one.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor
schoolClusters.note: The largest IB and British-curriculum cluster in the emirate, and where a child moving out of an Indian board usually lands. Programme routes differ: some schools run MYP to Year 11, others switch to IGCSE at Year 10.

schoolClusters.city: Island, Saadiyat and Al Ain
schoolClusters.note: Smaller IB cohorts with longer waiting lists in the capital, and a separate long-established community in Al Ain with fewer international options. A student here may be one of very few in their year who moved from an Indian board.

modes.description: Short and bounded. The work is understanding how the new system marks: criterion descriptors in MYP, command terms and internal assessment format in the Diploma. For most students arriving from an Indian board below the second Diploma year this is the whole requirement, and buying more is usually waste.

sections.heading: Two systems, one household: what Indian families in Abu Dhabi are actually choosing between
paragraphs: Most Indian families here are not choosing between schools so much as between systems, and the decision is usually made under time pressure with incomplete information. An Indian-curriculum school keeps a familiar syllabus, a familiar assessment rhythm and a straightforward path back to India. An IB school offers a different kind of education with wider international recognition and a different workload shape. Both are legitimate and the right answer depends on where the family expects to be in five years, which is rarely knowable.

What can be established is the consequence of each choice rather than its merit. A child in an Indian board follows a syllabus that continues if the family returns, sits a terminal examination, and meets the February/March Cambridge series only if they are in India, since that series is offered to India only. A child in the IB meets criterion-referenced marking from the start, builds a portfolio of internal assessments, and takes a qualification whose recognition in India is determined by the receiving institution and the recognised equivalence authority rather than by the school.

The household version of this question is harder, because many families end up with children in both systems. That is a reasonable outcome of mid-cycle moves and school availability, and it produces a particular pattern of tutoring need: an older child managing Diploma internal assessments while a younger one follows a familiar syllabus, each requiring different support at different rates. Quoting a single family package across both is how a budget becomes unpredictable.

The practical advice is to decide the system question deliberately rather than by default, and to ask each prospective school three things in writing: which programme route it runs through Year 11, which subjects and levels it can actually timetable, and what its approved fee schedule is including extras. Those answers make the comparison concrete.

sections.heading: Language options: Hindi, Arabic and the IB structure
paragraphs: The IB language requirements catch Indian families out more than any other part of the programme, because the structure is unfamiliar and the choices are made early. Broadly, a Diploma candidate takes a studies-in-language-and-literature subject and a language-acquisition subject, and the available options are set by the school's own staffing rather than by the IB. That is why two schools in the same emirate can offer quite different language lists.

Hindi has a place in that structure, as a literature option or as a language-acquisition option, and in some cases through a school-supported self-taught route at standard level. Whether any of those is actually available in a given Abu Dhabi school is a staffing question with a definite answer, and it should be asked before enrolment rather than discovered at option-choice time. Families who assume availability and find none have lost a choice they cared about.

Arabic sits in two different places at once, and the distinction matters. As a UAE-mandated subject it is taught alongside the licensed international curriculum in private schools, with separate provision for Arab and non-Arab students and specified languages of instruction. As an IB subject it may also be available as a language-acquisition option. A child may therefore be studying Arabic in two senses, which is worth clarifying with the school because the expectations differ.

For a family planning a possible return to India, the language choice carries weight beyond the Diploma, since continuity in a home language is easier to maintain through a formal course than to rebuild later. That is a family decision rather than an academic one, and it is worth making explicitly rather than by timetable accident.

sections.heading: What IB support costs per child in Abu Dhabi, and the sibling arithmetic
paragraphs: Published market rates in the emirate are these. Budget online tuition runs AED 33 to AED 65 an hour, with Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to AED 65. A qualified subject tutor online sits between AED 150 and AED 300, with Unitors publishing IB tuition from AED 200. IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialists run AED 200 to AED 450 and above, per Bestimate's Dubai rate table, with TutorChase at AED 270, and BartyED publishes AED 650 for a premium named tutor. These are market figures, not an IB Gram price list.

Converted to the month, which is how a household budget works, Bestimate's estimates for weekly one-hour sessions are AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work. Observed packages are AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. The gap between those two packages is the travel, not the teaching.

Now the sibling arithmetic, which this market never publishes. A shared tutor across two children in the same subject saves preparation and coordination and is usually worth asking for. A shared session across two children at different stages saves money and costs both of them teaching time, which is a false economy. And by far the largest saving available is not buying support for the child who, on marked evidence, does not need it, which in Indian-curriculum households is more often the case than families expect because content is rarely the issue.

IB Gram publishes no rate card on this page, because the honest figure depends on the programme, the subject count, whether internal assessment work is in scope and how many children are involved. The route is a free trial lesson, on the condition that it is a single lesson, then a consultation. A family with two or three children should expect that conversation to end with fewer subjects than it started with.

sections.heading: The exam calendar change nobody flags on arrival
paragraphs: Families who have managed examinations in India arrive with a calendar in their heads, and one part of it does not travel. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series, and the additional February/March series is offered to India only. A candidate entered through a centre in Abu Dhabi therefore cannot sit it. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE follows the same pattern here, available in May/June and November each year.

That matters most for a family in a British-curriculum school or weighing one, and it matters practically rather than theoretically: a household that plans a revision block around a February window has lost a term. It also matters for a child who moved mid-cycle and was expecting to sit a February series in their old school's calendar. The replacement route is the June series, with November available for resits and for sequencing.

For IB families the calendar question is different and the honest answer is more cautious. Abu Dhabi Diploma candidates normally sit the May session, but this page publishes no IB exam or results dates, because the IB's own site could not be verified by automated checking for this project and a wrong date is the one error a family acts on. Internal deadlines for internal assessments and the Extended Essay are set by each school, differ across the emirate, and should be obtained from the coordinator in writing.

One Cambridge administrative point is worth repeating for families in British-curriculum schools: every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Ask the centre which zone it is in before building a revision calendar.

sections.heading: Where Indian-curriculum students lose IB marks
paragraphs: The first and largest loss is command terms, and it is the one students find most unfair. Describe, explain, outline, suggest, evaluate and justify each have a mark-scheme meaning, and a long, accurate, well-informed answer written to the wrong one collects the knowledge mark and stops. A student trained to write everything they know about a topic is actively penalised by this, which feels arbitrary until someone explains the system once, after which it largely resolves.

The second is data handling in the sciences. The IB asks candidates to propagate uncertainty, to discuss its effect on a conclusion, to name limitations with their impact, and to justify which point in a dataset is anomalous. Indian board science teaching covers the content thoroughly and asks for these behaviours rarely, so a student with excellent theory produces thin answers on the questions that carry the method marks.

The third is the absence of scaffolding. Indian board questions are frequently structured; IB extended questions and Mathematics problems often are not, and the candidate has to decide what the question is asking before doing anything. Strong students lose marks here not through inability but through waiting for a structure that never arrives, and the repair is practice in framing rather than in technique.

The fourth is writing length against mark allocation. A student who writes a page for a three-mark question has spent time they needed at the end of the paper, which shows up as unattempted final questions. This is the single easiest loss to fix and the one most often mistaken for a content gap. Reading a marked script shows it immediately: look for where the writing thins out.

sections.heading: Internal assessment: the component with no CBSE or ICSE equivalent
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject carries an internal assessment, and for a student from an Indian board it is the genuinely new thing. A science investigation designed and conducted by the student, a mathematics exploration on a question they chose, a history essay on a topic they framed: each assessed against published criteria, each written over weeks, each worth a fixed share of the subject grade. Nothing in CBSE or ICSE practice prepares a student for designing their own assessed work.

The criteria are where the marks are, and they are specific in ways that reward reading them. Evaluation criteria typically ask for limitations with their impact on the conclusion, not a list of limitations. Communication criteria ask for defined variables, consistent notation and appropriate structure. Personal engagement, where it applies, asks for evidence of independent thinking rather than a statement of interest. Students who read the descriptors in full score better than students who are told about them.

The boundary on help here is firm and worth stating because this is exactly where this market misbehaves. A tutor may teach the skills the task requires, explain each criterion and its descriptor, discuss the student's own draft, point out an unclear method or an unsupported conclusion, and model the technique on a different example. A tutor must not write, complete or produce any part of the work. One site in this market sells completed internal assessments at a fixed price; the consequence of using such a service falls on the student as a malpractice finding.

Feedback is therefore given against criterion letters and logged with dates. That keeps the work the student's own and gives them a record if authorship is ever questioned, which is a real protection for a student whose family is new to the system and who may be the only person in the household who has ever written one.

sections.heading: Staying or returning: what the qualification has to do
paragraphs: Many Indian families in Abu Dhabi hold both possibilities open, and the qualification question is better approached as a recognition question than as a quality one. For study or work recognition inside the UAE, a school-leaving certificate goes through the Ministry of Education's equivalency process, which is run by the authority and is separate from any university's admissions decision. On the British track the published rule counts five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among the five, plus one subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade.

No IB points figure for UAE equivalency is published on this page, because none has been read on the Ministry's own pages or on an emirate attestation authority's page for this project. Figures circulate online; one ranking competitor already publishes the wrong IGCSE subject count, and inheriting that kind of error is worse than saying nothing. Verify your own case through the official channel.

For universities in India, recognition of an international qualification is determined by the receiving institution and by the recognised equivalence authority rather than by a school or a tutoring service. The practical action is the same in both directions: ask the specific institution, in writing, what it requires and what it accepts, well before an application cycle. Families who ask in the final year sometimes find a requirement that needed planning two years earlier.

Nothing here should be read as implying that tutoring is required for equivalency, admission or school progression. Those are institutional and regulatory processes with published criteria, and academic support affects a grade rather than a process.

sections.heading: How lessons run, and the limits we state
paragraphs: Lessons are one-to-one over live video, with screen sharing, a shared whiteboard and the student's own marked work open during the session. Gulf Standard Time lessons are scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school week, and for households with children in two different schools the sessions are set around the two school runs rather than around a single one. During Ramadan sessions move to post-Iftar timing. Where a family travels to India during holidays, sessions can continue against the student's local time.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India, which is worth stating directly to families who used home tuition before moving: the service they knew is not the service here. The in-home market in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 by independent home tutors, with the difference against online rates being the journey. For a household coordinating several children, that journey is also an hour of somebody's evening.

Private schools in Abu Dhabi are overseen by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate; Dubai's regulator is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority and Sharjah's is the Sharjah Private Education Authority. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from any regulator or board. Individual private tutors in the UAE need the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, and asking whether a tutor holds it is reasonable.

Two limits. Where marked evidence shows a child does not need paid support, we say so, which for Indian-curriculum students is a common outcome because the content is usually sound. And where no specialist is free for a subject at the hours you need, we offer a different slot, a later start or a referral rather than filling the hour with somebody who cannot mark to the criteria.

process.title: Ask whether the mark is content or marking
process.description: One question per subject to the teacher, and it costs nothing. For a student from CBSE or ICSE the answer is usually marking rather than content, which changes the purchase from a term of teaching to a few sessions on criteria and command terms.

process.title: One marked piece per subject in question
process.description: A single session per subject in which a piece of the student's own work is marked against the published criteria and read back with them. That separates a command-term habit from a genuine content gap, and across two children it usually reduces the subject list.

process.title: Free trial lesson with the subject specialist
process.description: One free trial lesson, on the condition that it is a single lesson, with the person who would teach the subject. For a family new to the IB this is also the moment to confirm the tutor knows the programme, the level and the school's internal deadlines.

process.title: Settle the language and level placements
process.description: Confirm in writing whether the child is placed in English A or English B, whether Hindi is available as an option and at what level, and what is expected in the mandatory Arabic and Islamic studies streams. These decisions are made early and are hard to reverse later.

process.title: Teach internal assessment as its own job
process.description: The component with no Indian board equivalent gets its own sessions, built around the criteria read in full, with feedback on the student's own draft logged with dates. We do not write, complete or produce any part of the work.

process.title: Review per child, monthly
process.description: Each child's plan is reviewed monthly against marked evidence, and the expectation is that it shrinks. Where a child no longer needs support we say so rather than continuing. For a household with several children that review is where the budget is actually controlled.

whyPoints.title: Written for CBSE and ICSE specifically
whyPoints.description: The gaps a student brings from an Indian board are particular: command terms, data discussion, unscaffolded questions, length against mark allocation. Naming those is more useful than a general page about new arrivals, and it shortens the diagnosis to a single marked piece.

whyPoints.title: Sibling arithmetic set out honestly
whyPoints.description: A shared tutor across two children in the same subject saves something real; a shared session short-changes both; and the largest saving is not buying support for the child who does not need it. No page in this market publishes that last line, because it is the one that reduces a bill.

whyPoints.title: The calendar difference flagged plainly
whyPoints.description: The Cambridge February/March series is offered to India only, and UAE candidates sit June and November. Families arriving with an Indian examination calendar in mind need that said in the first few lines, not discovered after a term of planning.

whyPoints.title: Language options treated as a real decision
whyPoints.description: English A against English B, Hindi where a school offers it, and Arabic in its two separate senses. These placements are made in the first weeks and are hard to reverse, and they are rarely explained to a family that is new to the structure.

whyPoints.title: Internal assessment taught, never written
whyPoints.description: The one genuinely new component gets its own teaching, with criteria read in full and feedback given on the student's own draft and logged with dates. One site in this market sells completed internal assessments; the malpractice consequence falls on the student.

whyPoints.title: No regulator claims and no statistics
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry, the IB or any board, and says so. There are no attainment or satisfaction figures here, because no dataset supports one and an unsourced number helps nobody.

faqs.question: My child was a strong CBSE student but IB marks are low. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly the marking rather than the content. Indian board teaching is thorough and often ahead of the equivalent IB year in procedural mathematics and factual coverage. What is new is criterion-referenced assessment and command terms: describe, explain, outline, suggest, evaluate and justify each have a specific meaning, and a long accurate answer written to the wrong one earns the knowledge mark and nothing above it. A few sessions on the marking system usually resolves far more than a term of content teaching.

faqs.question: Is Hindi available as an IB subject in Abu Dhabi schools?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it depends entirely on the individual school's staffing rather than on the IB. Hindi can sit in the IB structure as a literature option or as a language-acquisition option, and in some cases through a school-supported self-taught route at standard level. Because availability varies, ask prospective schools directly whether it runs, at which levels, and whether group size affects whether it runs in a given year. Families who assume availability sometimes lose a choice they cared about.

faqs.question: Can my child sit the February March exam series from Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series, and the additional February/March series is offered to India only, so a candidate entered through a centre in Abu Dhabi cannot sit it. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE is available in May/June and November here. If you have planned a revision block around a February window because that was your calendar in India, the replacement is the June series with November available for resits.

faqs.question: What is the IB internal assessment and why does my child find it so hard?
faqs.answer: Every Diploma subject carries one: an investigation, exploration or essay the student designs and writes themselves, assessed against published criteria and worth a fixed share of the subject grade. Nothing in CBSE or ICSE practice prepares a student for designing their own assessed work, which is why it is the genuinely new thing rather than the hardest thing. Reading the criterion descriptors in full is the single most effective step, because the marks are described there precisely.

faqs.question: How much should an Indian family in Abu Dhabi budget per child?
faqs.answer: Bestimate's Dubai rate table gives monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions of AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work. Hourly, qualified subject tutors online run AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200 and TutorChase AED 270. Those are market figures, not an IB Gram price list. Budget per child and per subject, then cut the subjects marked evidence does not support.

faqs.question: Can one tutor teach two of my children to reduce the cost?
faqs.answer: Across two children in the same subject, yes, and the saving in preparation and coordination is real if modest. In the same session, no: two children at different stages doing unrelated work short-change each other, and the hour is worth less to both than two shorter individual sessions. The largest saving available is different and nobody sells it, which is not buying support for the child who, on marked evidence, does not need it.

faqs.question: Should we keep our children in an Indian-curriculum school instead?
faqs.answer: It is a legitimate choice rather than a compromise, and the honest comparison is about shape and recognition rather than quality. An Indian board keeps a familiar syllabus and a straightforward path if the family returns. The IB spreads assessment across two years, rewards independent work, and has its own recognition pathway both in the UAE and in India, determined by institutions rather than by schools. Ask prospective schools what they can timetable and what their approved fee schedule is, in writing, then decide deliberately.

faqs.question: Will an IB diploma be recognised if we return to India?
faqs.answer: Recognition of an international qualification by an Indian university is determined by the receiving institution and by the recognised equivalence authority, not by a school or a tutoring service. The practical action is to ask the specific institutions your family would consider, in writing, what they require and accept, and to do it well before an application cycle rather than in the final year. Nothing about tutoring changes a recognition decision, and no provider should present itself as a route through one.

faqs.question: Does my child have to study Arabic even in an IB school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must follow the Ministry's general regulations, so those subjects run alongside any licensed international curriculum. KHDA's published guidance for Dubai requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in several of these subjects and prohibits combined classes. Ask your school which stream your child joins, in which language, and what is expected of a student new to the country.

faqs.question: My child writes long detailed answers and still loses marks. Why?
faqs.answer: Two causes, and a marked script shows which. The first is command-term mismatch: a detailed description where an explanation was asked for earns knowledge credit only. The second is length against mark allocation: a page written for a three-mark question costs time needed at the end of the paper, which appears as unattempted final questions. Students trained to write everything they know are penalised by both, and both are habit repairs rather than knowledge gaps.

faqs.question: Is English A or English B the right placement for my child?
faqs.answer: It is one of the most consequential decisions of the first fortnight and it is often made quickly on limited evidence. English A assumes a different relationship with literature and with unseen analysis than most Indian board English courses build; English B is a language-acquisition course. A misplacement in either direction costs a year rather than a term. Ask the school what evidence the placement rests on, and how and when a move between the two would be reviewed.

faqs.question: How quickly do students from Indian boards adjust to the IB?
faqs.answer: Most of the marking adjustment happens inside a term once somebody has explained the system explicitly, which is why a small number of orientation sessions is usually the right purchase rather than a long programme. Internal assessment takes longer, because it is a genuinely new kind of work rather than a new way of marking a familiar kind. A mid-Diploma arrival is the exception in both cases and needs triage rather than orientation.

faqs.question: Do you offer home tuition in Abu Dhabi like we had in India?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram delivers one-to-one lessons over live video across the UAE and does not send tutors to UAE addresses; home visits are a service we run only in India. It is worth saying directly because many families have used home tuition before moving. The in-home market here is quoted at AED 180 to AED 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 by independent home tutors, and the difference from online rates is the journey rather than the teaching.

faqs.question: What should we send before the first conversation?
faqs.answer: The programme and year group each child has joined, the subject list with levels, the last marked piece or report from the previous school, and the school's internal deadlines for internal assessment and the core if you have them. For a household with more than one child, send them separately rather than as one summary. With those, the first conversation establishes which children need support and in which subjects, which is usually fewer than the family expects.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-indian-students.closingHeading: Diagnose the marking, then decide per child
abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-indian-students.closingBody: For a family arriving from CBSE or ICSE, the most useful hour costs nothing: ask each teacher whether a low mark reflects content your child has not covered or the way the answer was written. For most students from Indian boards the answer is the second, and the right purchase is then a few sessions on criteria and command terms rather than a term of teaching. Where content genuinely is short, buy one marked piece first to confirm it. Book a free trial lesson with the subject specialist, per child, and expect the conversation to end with a shorter list than it began with.

abu-dhabi/ib-tutor-for-new-expat-student.tutorsIntro: The tutors here work with students who have just arrived in the UAE: children moving into the PYP or MYP from a national curriculum, and Diploma candidates who joined part-way through a two-year course and are meeting internal assessment for the first time.

intro.heading: Not behind, mid-transition: and the two cost very different amounts
paragraphs: A family that has just landed in Abu Dhabi tends to buy tutoring in the fourth week of term, after the first report, in a mild panic. The report is usually accurate about the marks and misleading about the cause. A child who has changed country, school system, assessment culture, language of instruction and peer group inside two months will produce weak early marks for reasons that have very little to do with ability or with content. Spending on a content programme for a transition problem is how a first term gets expensive without getting better.

The distinction matters financially because the two have different price tags. A transition problem is a technique and orientation job: learning what a criterion descriptor means, learning that an explanation earns more than an answer, learning the format of an internal assessment. That is a handful of sessions. A genuine content gap, where the previous syllabus simply did not cover a topic the new one assumes, is measured in weeks per topic. Market monthly estimates in the emirate run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work, per Bestimate's Dubai rate table, so the difference between those two diagnoses across three subjects is substantial.

What changes the figure in this emirate specifically is how many subjects are in play and how late in the cycle the family arrived. A child entering the MYP in September has a full year to absorb a new assessment culture and needs very little bought help. A Diploma candidate entering the second year in October is carrying internal assessment deadlines, a prediction window and an unfamiliar examination format simultaneously, and that is the most expensive moment to arrive in the entire school system. Nobody tells relocating families this, and it is the single most useful thing on this page.

There is also a scale point worth knowing for context. Dubai's private school sector served 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering 17 different curricula, with UK curriculum at 37%, Indian at 26%, US at 14% and International Baccalaureate at 7% of the emirate's private-school enrolment. Abu Dhabi's market is smaller and differently distributed, but the pattern holds: a relocating family is choosing between systems, not just between schools, and that choice determines most of what tutoring will later be needed for.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. For a relocating family that is practically useful rather than a limitation: sessions can start before the shipping container arrives, continue from a hotel, and run from a previous time zone if the move is staged. The in-home market in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 500 an hour because the journey is priced in, and in a month when a family is still finding its way around the city, that journey is nobody's priority.
