abu-dhabi/igcse-february-march-exam-prep.programmesIntro: A transferring student is usually crossing two boundaries at once: a board boundary and a stage boundary. These are the stages in play, and what each means for a family that arrived in Abu Dhabi part-way through a cycle.

programmes.name: Lower Secondary and Checkpoint
programmes.description: The Cambridge lower secondary phase is where algebraic fluency and scientific writing are built, and Checkpoint tests in March, May and October give schools diagnostic data rather than certificates. A student arriving from an Indian board at this stage has usually covered more arithmetic content and less extended written explanation, which is a straightforward gap to close before Year 10.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools on the Cambridge pathway typically stream for IGCSE tier during Year 9, using internal and Checkpoint data. A family arriving in Year 9 should ask directly how that streaming decision will be made for a child with no Checkpoint history at the school, because the tier decision carries the grade ceiling with it.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Examined in June and November, with Core and Extended tiers in subjects such as Mathematics 0580, Physics 0625 and Chemistry 0620. The Extended tier carries the higher grade ceiling and assumes algebraic manipulation the Core papers never ask for. Tier is an entry decision made by the centre before its deadline, not a choice made in the exam hall.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the entry is made by the centre registered with the board, almost always the school itself, and each centre sets an internal cut-off that falls before the board's. A family that transferred in October should establish on day one whether the school intends to enter the child for the coming June series or hold them back a year.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Available in May/June and November, with codes such as 4MA1, 4PH1 and 4CH1. Some Pearson qualifications are modular, which gives a transferring student a route to bank one paper at a time rather than facing an entire qualification in one series. Whether that route is open depends on the qualification and the centre's entry decisions.
programmes.countryNote: Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, and the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026 with results reaching students in January. For an Abu Dhabi family, the live official timetable PDF is the only document worth planning against, because dates are revised between series.

programmes.name: AS and A Level
programmes.description: The destination for most Abu Dhabi IGCSE candidates, and the reason tier matters. A Core-tier Mathematics pass rarely supports AS Mathematics, and sixth forms in the emirate publish their own entry grades. A transferring student aiming at AS sciences needs the Extended tier, which shapes the teaching plan from the first session rather than from Year 11.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi sixth forms set entry conditions independently, and several specify both grade and tier. Where a transferring student's old board does not map cleanly onto a grade, schools fall back on internal assessment, which makes the first term's marked work unusually important for a mid-cycle arrival.

abu-dhabi/igcse-february-march-exam-prep.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects where a transferring student most often needs structured help, described from the arrival's point of view: what the IGCSE paper expects that the previous board did not, and where the first marks go missing.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Transferring students are often ahead on procedural arithmetic and behind on the unstructured multi-step questions at the end of an Extended paper. Bounds, three-dimensional trigonometry and algebraic fractions are the usual gaps, alongside the habit of showing a method line that a method-marked question requires.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: The content overlap with Indian boards is high; the assessment style is not. Extended papers ask for graph interpretation, anomalous-result identification and written explanations of relationships, and marks are lost where a candidate produces a correct number without the reasoning the mark scheme credits.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles and stoichiometry are the heaviest mark sink, and a transferring student usually has the arithmetic but not the paper's phrasing. Qualitative analysis tables reward memorised precision, and organic reaction conditions must be stated exactly rather than described in general terms.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: The subject most sensitive to command words at this level. Describe, explain and suggest each carry a different mark-scheme meaning, and a long, accurate answer written to the wrong command word earns the knowledge mark and nothing more. This is fast to fix with marked practice.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Transferring students frequently sit this rather than First Language English, and the summary task is where marks go: copying from the passage instead of compressing it. The directed-writing task is marked on register and audience, both of which are specified in the prompt and both of which are routinely ignored.

subjects.name: First Language English
subjects.description: Marked on reading as much as on writing. The directed-response task requires evidence used in service of an argument rather than a retelling of the passage, and the composition is assessed on controlled structure. Students arriving from a different examination culture often write at length and lose structure marks.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics / Further Pure
subjects.description: Often the right subject for a transferring student who was strong in an Indian board's mathematics, because the calculus and trigonometric-identity content is partly familiar. The gap is notation and presentation conventions, which are specific to the board and quick to teach.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies
subjects.description: The data-response questions carry the grade and are lost on application. A definition without application to the stimulus material scores the knowledge mark only. Transferring students who learned the subject as content rather than as analysis feel this immediately in their first marked paper.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Programming ability transfers well; written conventions do not. Trace tables, pseudocode style and the specific vocabulary of data representation and the fetch-execute cycle carry marks, and a competent coder can lose a grade band on presentation alone.

subjects.name: Arabic and UAE social studies alongside IGCSE
subjects.description: Private schools in the UAE teach Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed international curriculum, and for a child new to the country these are new subjects as well as new timetable load. A realistic plan counts those lessons as fixed rather than assuming they can be set aside during a transfer term.

abu-dhabi/igcse-february-march-exam-prep.regionsIntro: Where a newly arrived family lands in Abu Dhabi shapes which schools have places, what the school run costs in time, and therefore when lessons can realistically sit. These notes are about that, not about scenery.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Shamkha
regions.note: The usual landing zone for families relocating on a villa budget, and a catchment where mid-year places appear more often than on the island. The school run can run to forty minutes each way in term time, which pushes weekday lessons to 5pm or later.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment living with short commutes, which makes a 4pm start workable and suits a transferring student who needs frequent short sessions rather than long weekend blocks. Sibling scheduling in a shared apartment is the practical constraint here.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: A large mainland catchment with a wide spread of fee levels and one of the highest concentrations of Indian-curriculum and British-curriculum households in the emirate. Travel to island schools is long enough that online delivery changes the weekly arithmetic outright.

regions.name: Al Raha and Al Bandar
regions.note: Close to the Khalifa City school cluster, with families who often combine one weekday evening session and one weekend double. Demand for Extended-tier science support here outruns the number of specialists physically present in the emirate.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: A short list of schools and the shortest school runs in the capital, which allows earlier weekday sessions. For a transferring student that matters, because the first term's marked work is what the school will use to set tier and predicted performance.

regions.name: Baniyas and Al Wathba
regions.note: Further from the island with fewer international-curriculum options nearby, so families travel or choose locally and supplement. This is the part of the emirate where live video is the only realistic route to a Cambridge Extended-tier subject specialist.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Under the same emirate authority as the capital but an hour inland, with a smaller pool of IGCSE specialists on the ground. Transferring families here are the most likely to be told no local tutor covers their subject, which is precisely the case online delivery solves.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor
schoolClusters.note: Where most mid-year IGCSE transfers land, and the cluster that generates the heaviest demand for Extended-tier mathematics and science support in a transfer term. Entry policies for a child arriving after the June entry deadline differ sharply between these schools, so ask before enrolling.

schoolClusters.city: Island, Saadiyat and Al Bateen
schoolClusters.note: Smaller cohorts, longer waiting lists and the shortest commutes. A transferring student here is often the only new arrival in a Year 11 class, which makes the first marked paper the school's main source of information about them.

schoolClusters.city: Mainland Abu Dhabi and Al Ain
schoolClusters.note: A wide geography with a broad fee spread and fewer subject specialists present locally. Families in this cluster are the ones most often searching an exam series that does not apply to them, because their previous school's calendar was set somewhere else.

abu-dhabi/igcse-february-march-exam-prep.modesIntro: Three shapes of support, chosen by how much of the syllabus is genuinely new rather than by how thorough each sounds. A transfer term and a single-subject repair are not the same job.

modes.title: Transfer-term rebuild
modes.description: For a student who arrived mid-cycle and is meeting the board, the tier and the paper format together. Two to three subjects, taught from the live syllabus rather than from revision notes, with the first marked paper used to set the order of work. This is the highest-load option and the one where a monthly AED figure is the useful unit, because it runs for a term or more.
bullets: Syllabus mapped against what the previous board actually covered
First marked paper used to rank topics, not to assign a grade
Written summary the new school can use when it sets tier
Session count reviewed monthly rather than fixed for the year

modes.title: Single-subject June plan
modes.description: One subject, one or two sessions a week, running to the June series. Suits a student whose school work is broadly on track in everything except one paper. Costed as a monthly figure against the market bands, and the easiest option to stop or extend because nothing else depends on it.
bullets: Fixed weekly slot held for the whole plan
Marked past paper every third or fourth session
Topic list rewritten after each marked paper

modes.title: November sequencing or resit block

sections.heading: The short answer: which IGCSE series an Abu Dhabi candidate can enter
paragraphs: Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series. The additional February/March window exists, but Cambridge offers it to India only, so a candidate entered through a centre in Abu Dhabi cannot sit it. Cambridge also runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October, and those are diagnostic tests rather than certificating exams, which is one reason the March month keeps appearing on school calendars here and causing confusion.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE sits in May/June and November each year. Between the two boards, then, an Abu Dhabi family has two realistic entry windows: the main summer series and the autumn series, with results from the autumn series reaching students in January. Pearson's published record makes that concrete: November 2025 International GCSE results reached students on 22 January 2026, and the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026.

There is one further administrative detail that costs candidates real exams and is almost never mentioned on tutoring sites. Every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Ask your centre which zone it is in before planning a single revision week.
If a site has handed you February or March dates for a UAE candidate, treat everything else on it with the same scepticism. A wrong date is not a stylistic flaw; it is the one error a parent acts on.

sections.heading: Five real reasons Abu Dhabi families search for a February sitting
paragraphs: The first and largest group is families who moved from India. The February/March window is a fixture of the school calendar there, and a parent who managed one child's exams in Bengaluru or Delhi reasonably expects the same structure in the capital. There is nothing careless about the assumption; the series simply does not extend to this country.

The second group has read a tutoring site that published February key dates to a UAE audience. This happened at scale: pages quoting a February exam window and a late-November entry deadline were served to UAE parents who had no access to either. If that is how you got here, the useful correction is not just the right month but the right owner of the date, which is the centre your child is entered through.

The third group is looking for an early exit. A Year 11 student who is ready, or a family relocating again in spring, wants the earliest possible certificate. The honest answer is that the earliest available window is the June series, and that where timing is genuinely urgent the November series after it is the sequencing tool rather than a February one.

The fourth group has a child who missed the June entry and does not want to wait a full year. For them, November is the answer, and it is a better answer than most realise: a full sitting, examined to the same standard, with results in January. The fifth group is private candidates, who have the same two windows as everybody else but must arrange an external centre, which has its own cut-offs and its own published fees.

sections.heading: What the June route costs in Abu Dhabi, priced by the month
paragraphs: Hourly rates are how this market advertises and monthly totals are how families actually budget, so this page uses the month. Bestimate's Dubai rate table converts weekly one-hour sessions into monthly estimates of AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work. Monthly packages observed in the market sit at AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Those monthly bands translate from published hourly rates. EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to AED 65 an hour and Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52 at the budget end; Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; TutorChase quotes AED 270; Bestimate puts IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, and BartyED publishes AED 650 for a premium named tutor. In-home visits in the emirate are quoted at AED 180 to AED 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 by independent home tutors, with the difference being travel rather than teaching.

What pushes an Abu Dhabi transfer family towards the upper band is subject count, not ambition. A single-subject June plan is one line in a monthly budget. A transfer term covering Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry from the live syllabus is three, and it runs for two terms rather than six weeks. Setting that expectation in month one is more useful than quoting a low hourly rate and letting the total arrive by surprise in March.

IB Gram does not publish a rate card on this page. The route is a free trial lesson, on the single condition that it is one lesson, followed by a consultation where subject count, tier and the real number of weeks are established before hours are quoted. Any figure quoted before those three are known is a guess dressed as a price.

sections.heading: Moving from an Indian board mid-cycle: the gap, subject by subject
paragraphs: A student transferring from CBSE or ICSE into an Abu Dhabi Cambridge or Pearson school is rarely behind on content. The gap is in what the paper rewards. Indian board assessment leans on recall and procedural accuracy; IGCSE Extended papers lean on application, written explanation and the specific meanings of command words. A student who was comfortably strong at home can produce a weak first marked paper here and conclude, wrongly, that they have fallen behind.

In mathematics the transfer is usually favourable. Algebraic technique arrives ahead of where the Extended paper needs it, and the work is in bounds, three-dimensional trigonometry, and the unstructured final questions where no scaffolding is given. Additional Mathematics is often a realistic add-on rather than a stretch, because the calculus and identity work overlaps with what the previous board covered.

In the sciences the direction reverses. Content overlap is high, but Extended papers ask candidates to interpret graphs, identify and justify anomalous results, and explain relationships in prose. Writing a correct numerical answer with no reasoning line loses marks that were available. Chemistry adds the qualitative-analysis tables, which must be memorised precisely rather than understood generally.

In English the move is from a literature-heavy diet to a comprehension and directed-writing diet, with register and audience specified in each prompt. The CBSE to IGCSE transfer is, in practice, a six-to-twelve week technique project per subject plus whatever genuine content gaps the previous syllabus left. Naming which of those two is in play requires a marked paper, not a conversation.

sections.heading: June or November: how to choose when you have arrived late
paragraphs: The decision turns on one question: how many usable teaching weeks exist between now and each entry. Count the weeks, subtract half-term, subtract the school's own assessment weeks, and subtract the fortnight before the papers when nothing new can be learned. What remains is the real number, and it is always smaller than the nominal one. A family arriving in Abu Dhabi in October typically has a workable June plan in one or two subjects and an unrealistic one in four.

Where June is realistic, it is the better choice, because results arrive in August and the academic year closes cleanly. Where it is not, November is a genuine alternative rather than a consolation: the papers are set to the same standard, the series is open to UAE candidates, and results reach students in January. The cost of November is that an offer or a sixth-form place has to be held pending a January result, which the receiving institution needs to be told about in writing and early.

The third option, which schools raise more often than parents expect, is to repeat the year. For a student who arrived with eight months of a two-year course remaining and three Extended-tier sciences to build, that can be the honest answer, and no amount of tuition changes the arithmetic. A tutor who tells you four subjects can be rebuilt from scratch in one term is selling hours.

Whichever window is chosen, the entry belongs to the centre. The school's exams officer decides the internal cut-off, the option codes and the tier. Those three facts, in writing, are worth more at this stage than any revision plan, because a plan built against an entry that was never made is wasted work.

sections.heading: If your child has already started an Indian board syllabus this year
paragraphs: This is the hardest version of the transfer, and it deserves a straight answer rather than reassurance. A student part-way through an Indian board's Class 10 cycle who moves to an Abu Dhabi school in the second half of the year is being asked to change board, tier structure and assessment calendar at the point where the previous course was about to be examined. The content already covered is not wasted, but the route to a certificate has changed.

There are three practical paths. The student can continue with the previous board as a private candidate where an approved centre in the UAE offers it, which keeps the certificate on track but means managing registration independently. They can enter the IGCSE June series in a reduced number of subjects, which protects the strongest subjects and defers the rest. Or they can sit the November series, which buys a full extra term of teaching at the price of a January result.

The choice is usually made on subject count. A student with two strong subjects and three weak ones does better entering the two for June and the rest for November than entering five and preparing none of them properly. Schools sometimes resist split entries because they complicate internal reporting, which is a conversation to have with the exams officer rather than a rule.

Whatever is decided, the teaching plan should start with a marked paper in each subject under consideration. That single artefact tells you which subjects are technique repairs and which are content rebuilds, and the two have completely different costs. Deciding on a feeling rather than a marked paper is how a family ends up paying for a term of work in the wrong subject.

sections.heading: How lessons run, and what IB Gram does not do in the UAE
paragraphs: All teaching is one-to-one over live video, with screen sharing, a shared whiteboard and the student's own marked scripts open during the session. There is no group class. Gulf Standard Time lessons are scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school week, which means late-afternoon and evening weekday slots, longer weekend blocks for families with a long school run, and post-Iftar timing during Ramadan.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India, and no page on this site should suggest otherwise. For a family that has just moved here from an Indian city, that distinction is worth stating plainly, because the service they may have used before is not the service being described now.

The argument for online on this particular page is subject supply. A newly arrived family in Al Shamkha, Baniyas or Al Ain is choosing a tutor from whoever can reach a new address, in a city they do not yet know, during a term that has already started. Live video removes the radius and leaves the only question that matters: who can teach Cambridge Extended-tier Chemistry and mark the paper. The in-home market in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 500 an hour precisely because the journey is priced in, and that premium buys nothing that reaches a mark scheme.

Where no specialist is free for a subject at the hours a family needs, we say so and offer a different slot, a later start, or a referral. That limit is stated here because a page that never mentions one is concealing it.

sections.heading: ADEK, equivalency and the paperwork a transfer sets off
paragraphs: In Abu Dhabi, the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai's regulator is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, Sharjah's is the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. For a transferring family, the regulator matters mainly as the authority behind school licensing, inspection outcomes and fee approvals.

Alongside the school's own curriculum, there is a federal baseline: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must follow the Ministry's general regulations. In Dubai, KHDA has published the detail most clearly, requiring Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies in all private schools regardless of licensed curriculum, with separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, and combined classes for both groups strictly prohibited. A child arriving from India meets these subjects for the first time, and they are timetabled load from week one.

The other paperwork is MoE equivalency, which matters at the end rather than the beginning. For the British track, the published requirement is five subjects from the accredited list in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five, plus one subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One ranking competitor states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the published rule is five.

Equivalency is a process run by the authority, not by a tutoring service, and nothing here should be read as IB Gram performing or guaranteeing it. The IB points threshold circulating online has not been confirmed on an official source, so this page does not publish one. Verify your own case on the Ministry's own pages or with the emirate's attestation authority, and do not treat tutoring as a requirement for it.

faqs.question: Can my child in Abu Dhabi sit the Cambridge February March IGCSE series?
faqs.answer: No. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series, and the additional February/March series is offered to India only. A candidate entered through a centre in Abu Dhabi therefore sits June or November. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE follows the same pattern here, running in May/June and November. If you have seen February or March dates presented for UAE candidates, they were either Checkpoint test dates, which are diagnostic rather than certificating, or published in error.

faqs.question: Why do so many tutoring sites publish February dates for UAE readers?
faqs.answer: Because the series genuinely exists and a page that does not check its geography will repeat the dates it found. The Cambridge February/March window is real; it is offered to India only. Pages written for a general audience and then localised with a city name inherit the wrong calendar, and a parent planning around a late-autumn entry deadline for a February exam loses a term. The check is quick: read the series availability on the board's own exam administration pages, then confirm the entry with your centre.

faqs.question: We moved from an Indian school in October. Is the June series realistic?
faqs.answer: Count the usable weeks before answering. Take the weeks to the first paper, subtract half-term, the school's own assessment weeks and the fortnight before the exams when nothing new lands, and the real number is usually far smaller than it looks. One or two subjects for June is often realistic for an October arrival; four Extended-tier subjects rebuilt from scratch generally is not. The alternative is the November series, which is a full sitting examined to the same standard, with results reaching students in January.

faqs.question: What does a transfer term of tutoring cost per month in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Budget per subject and multiply. Market monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work, per Bestimate's Dubai rate table. A three-subject transfer term therefore sits well above a single-subject plan, and it runs for two terms rather than six weeks. Those are market figures rather than an IB Gram price list; our route is a free trial lesson and a consultation first.

faqs.question: Is my child behind after moving from CBSE or ICSE to IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Usually not on content. The gap is in what the paper rewards. Indian board assessment leans towards recall and procedural accuracy; IGCSE Extended papers ask for application, written reasoning and command-word discipline. A strong student can produce a weak first marked paper here for purely technical reasons. In mathematics the transfer is often favourable, with algebraic technique arriving ahead of requirement. In the sciences, the work is in writing out reasoning that the previous syllabus did not ask to be written.

faqs.question: Can my child finish the Indian board syllabus as a private candidate instead?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, where an approved centre in the UAE offers that board's exams and the family is willing to manage registration independently. It keeps a nearly finished certificate on track, which can be the right call for a student transferring late in a Class 10 cycle. The trade-off is that the school your child now attends is teaching a different syllabus, so the two run in parallel. Ask the centre directly what it offers, what it charges and what its internal deadlines are, in writing.

faqs.question: Should we enter fewer subjects for June and the rest in November?
faqs.answer: For a late arrival this is often the strongest option. Entering two well-prepared subjects for June and deferring three to November produces better grades than entering five and preparing none of them properly. Schools sometimes resist split entries because they complicate internal reporting rather than because a rule forbids it, so raise it with the exams officer as a conversation. The decision should rest on one marked paper per subject, which tells you which subjects are close and which are not.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge zone is our Abu Dhabi centre in, and does it matter?
faqs.answer: It matters enough to ask before planning a revision week. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version, and states it is essential to use the correct version for your zone, adding it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Only the centre can tell you which zone it sits in. Get it in writing, then build the plan from that timetable rather than from a version found through a general search.

faqs.question: Do my child's Arabic and Islamic studies lessons count for MoE equivalency?
faqs.answer: Not within the five-subject count on the British track. The published requirement is five subjects from the accredited list in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among those five, plus one subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One ranking competitor states six subjects are required, which is wrong. Verify your own case with the Ministry or the emirate's attestation authority rather than with a tutoring site.

faqs.question: Does my new school have to teach Arabic and social studies as well?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must follow the Ministry's general regulations. KHDA has published the clearest public detail for Dubai, requiring these subjects in all private schools regardless of licensed curriculum, with separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies. For a newly arrived child these are new subjects and fixed timetable load, which a tutoring plan has to work around rather than ignore.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help choose between Core and Extended tier for June?
faqs.answer: A tutor can give you the evidence; the centre makes the entry. The useful input is a marked Extended paper sat under timed conditions, which shows whether the candidate is two topics short or a syllabus short. Extended carries the higher grade ceiling and assumes algebraic fluency Core does not test, and most Abu Dhabi sixth forms expect it for AS sciences and mathematics. The decision has a deadline, set by the centre's internal cut-off, so it should be made on marked evidence well before then.

faqs.question: How quickly can lessons start after we arrive in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Usually within a few days for mainstream subjects, because delivery is online and no travel has to be arranged. The honest exception is Extended-tier Physics, Chemistry and Additional Mathematics in the autumn term, where specialist demand peaks and a particular time slot may not be available immediately. Where that happens we say so and offer a different slot, a later start or a referral rather than filling the hour with someone who cannot mark the paper. A free trial lesson with the actual subject tutor comes first either way.

faqs.question: Are lessons face to face anywhere in the UAE?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram delivers one-to-one lessons over live video to families across the UAE, and does not send tutors to UAE addresses; home visits are a service we offer only in India. The in-home market in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 by independent home tutors, with the difference being the journey rather than the teaching. For a family new to Abu Dhabi, the practical gain is choosing a subject specialist rather than whoever lives near a new address.

faqs.question: What should we send you when asking about a transfer plan?
faqs.answer: Four things, and the plan writes itself from them. The board and tier your new school has entered or intends to enter, the subject list, the last report or marked paper from the previous school, and the date your school's exams officer has given as its internal entry cut-off. If any of those are unknown, finding them out is the first task. We would rather spend the first conversation establishing which series your child is actually entered for than quoting hours against an entry that does not yet exist.

intro.heading: The rate is the least interesting number in an IGCSE tuition budget
paragraphs: Most Abu Dhabi families research IGCSE home tuition by collecting hourly rates. It is a reasonable instinct and it answers the wrong question. The published market in this emirate runs from roughly AED 45 an hour at the budget online end to AED 650 at the named-specialist end, and within that range the correlation between price and grade movement is weak. What correlates strongly is three things the rate does not express: how many contact hours the budget actually buys, when in the two-year IGCSE cycle those hours fall, and whether anything happens between the sessions.

Take two households in Khalifa City with the same annual figure to spend. The first buys a visiting tutor at AED 250 an hour from February of Year 11 and gets around sixteen hours, all of them in the four months when a tutor can only triage. The second buys qualified online tuition at AED 180 an hour from the autumn of Year 10 and gets around fifty-five hours, the first twenty of which are spent rebuilding algebraic manipulation so the rest of three subjects becomes teachable. Same money. The second household is buying teaching; the first is buying damage control at a premium.

So this page is organised around the budget rather than the price list. It publishes what the market charges, with each figure attributed to the provider and the date that published it, because nobody else in this search result publishes AED at all - three of the six pages we researched quote no price whatsoever, and the two that do quote US dollars, a currency UAE families do not transact in. Then it shows what a fixed AED 1,000 a month buys in each format, what a 60-minute slot really delivers once travel and settling are counted, and which contract terms quietly cost money.

On the home-tuition question, plainly: IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE. Home tuition is a service we provide only in India. For Abu Dhabi households the lesson is one-to-one over live video, with your child's marked papers on screen. The cost consequence is straightforward - the travel premium disappears, which in this emirate is between a quarter and a half of a visiting tutor's quote, and the money that premium represents converts directly into additional contact hours or into a shorter commitment.

None of the figures on this page are our price list. They are other providers' published rates, dated October 2026, presented so you can hold any quote - including ours - against the market. Where this page tells you to spend less, or to spend nothing because the school already runs the support free, that advice is worth more to you than the booking is to us. The review point described at the end exists for the same reason: a tuition budget that cannot be stopped is not a budget.

abu-dhabi/igcse-home-tuition.programmesIntro: Price varies by stage as much as by subject, and so does value. These are the four points in the sequence where Abu Dhabi families buy IGCSE tuition, with what the hour is worth at each.

programmes.name: Year 9 and the options decision
programmes.description: The cheapest intervention point in the entire sequence, and the least used. Nothing has been entered, so a weak foundation can be rebuilt without competing against a syllabus. One or two hours spent understanding the options sheet is frequently worth more than ten hours of later content teaching.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi options evenings decide First Language against Second Language English, three separate sciences against a coordinated award, and Computer Science against ICT. Each of those choices has a price attached two years later, when it turns out to be the wrong route for a sixth-form place and cannot be undone.

programmes.name: Year 10, the teaching year
programmes.description: The only stage at which paid hours can rebuild a foundation rather than patch topics. Six to eight sessions on algebraic manipulation changes the back half of Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry simultaneously, which is three subjects improved for the price of one intervention.
programmes.countryNote: Families who start in Year 10 generally spend less in total across the two years than families who start in Year 11, because the Year 11 bill is driven by subject count and urgency rather than by rate. That is arithmetic rather than a sales argument.

programmes.name: Year 11, autumn and winter
programmes.description: Mocks produce the first genuinely useful data of the cycle, and forecast grades are collected shortly after. Spending here buys both grade movement and influence over what the centre submits, which spending in the spring does not.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi centres submit forecast grades to the board well before the papers are sat. For the June series that submission lands in the spring term, weeks ahead of the first paper, and the exams officer at the school holds the exact date. Improvement that arrives after it is not reflected in the forecast, which matters for conditional sixth-form offers.

programmes.name: Year 11, final term
programmes.description: The most expensive hours in the cycle and the least productive per dirham, because the work available is technique and a short list of high-mark topics rather than teaching. Worth buying in two subjects, not five, with a stated end date set by the examination timetable.
programmes.countryNote: Demand peaks here across the emirate, which is also when availability tightens and specialist tutors are already committed. Families in Al Raha and Khalifa City who wait until March regularly find the rate they were quoted in January is no longer on offer.

programmes.name: Results, resits and the next course
programmes.description: A single-subject resit in a November series is a normal arrangement and runs through an examination centre, with the centre's own fee and deadlines on top of the board's. The transition block into Year 12 is separately the best-value purchase of the whole cycle.
programmes.countryNote: The decision window is the weeks around August results, not September. Families who deliberate for a month frequently find that both the resit entry deadline and the useful preparation time have gone, which converts a cheap decision into an expensive one.

abu-dhabi/igcse-home-tuition.subjectsIntro: Subjects do not all cost the same to fix, because the gap in each is a different size. Below are the IGCSE subjects Abu Dhabi families most often fund, with an honest estimate of how much tuition each typically needs.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: The most funded subject in the emirate and the one where spend timing matters most. An algebra rebuild in Year 10 runs six to eight sessions and pays off across three subjects. The same weakness patched in Year 11 needs more hours and delivers less.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Usually a narrow, expensive-looking problem with a cheap fix: quantitative chemistry. Four focused sessions on moles and stoichiometry move more marks than twelve sessions of general revision, so this is a subject where a small, well-diagnosed block is the right purchase.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Electricity and electromagnetism carry the losses, and the fix is a single repeatable method rather than more content, so budget three to four sessions. The practical-skills paper needs separate attention and rarely appears in anybody's budget until it is too late.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-heavy, so a genuine knowledge gap is slow and costly to close. The cheap wins are command-word discrimination and data questions - typically two or three sessions - which is why a diagnostic before booking a term matters more here than elsewhere.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Summary and directed writing are the two most teachable components in the IGCSE set, so four to six sessions commonly produce visible movement. Reading-response improvement is slower, because it rests on inference built over years rather than on technique.

subjects.name: English Language, First Language
subjects.description: Directed writing responds quickly to taught structures; reading responses do not. Families budgeting for a full-grade shift here should plan a term rather than a block, and should expect the writing half to improve first by a visible margin.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: The fastest-moving subjects per dirham in the whole set, because almost all avoidable loss is answer structure on case-study command words. Two taught structures plus marked practice is often a four-session purchase rather than a term.

subjects.name: Coordinated and Combined Science
subjects.description: Budget for a coverage audit first. Students frequently assume untaught content is out of scope, and a session spent checking the school's coverage against the published syllabus regularly finds two topics nobody has taught - which is cheaper to discover in November than in May.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Almost entirely habit-based loss: no named examples, resource unread. A four-week block that installs a read-and-annotate routine and three memorised case studies is usually the whole intervention, which makes this one of the better-value subjects to fund.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Costs diverge sharply. Computer Science tuition is exam-technique and algorithm work and prices like any other written subject. ICT carries a substantial practical workload that is administered by the school, so outside tuition can do less and should be budgeted smaller.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.levels: Cambridge 0508 First Language; 0544 Arabic Foreign Language
subjects.description: Specialist availability rather than rate drives the cost here, particularly for the first-language route. Federal regulation requires private schools to teach Arabic language, so it is a timetabled subject, and placement in the wrong syllabus is the expensive error.

subjects.name: Mathematics, additional or international
subjects.description: Taken by students heading for A Level or Higher Level mathematics, with calculus and trigonometric identities arriving earlier than expected. Front-loaded content, so Year 10 spending is markedly more efficient here than Year 11 spending.

abu-dhabi/igcse-home-tuition.regionsIntro: What changes the number across Abu Dhabi communities is mostly travel, and travel is a line item only in a visiting arrangement. These are the areas we are asked about, with the cost effect in each.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Schools within a short radius and a dense tutor market, so visiting quotes here sit at the lower end of the in-home band. The saving from removing travel is correspondingly smaller, and families choose online mainly for subject coverage instead.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah and Al Bateen
regions.note: Central island districts with the shortest journeys in the emirate, where in-home quotes are least inflated by travel. The cost question here is usually session length and whether marking is included rather than the headline rate.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Long journeys from the island push visiting quotes towards the upper half of the band, and a 60-minute slot frequently starts late. This is the corridor where converting the travel premium into extra contact hours changes the plan most.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Mid-distance from the island with heavy demand in the spring term, which tightens availability and firms up rates from February onwards. Families who book in the autumn here pay less and get a wider choice of tutor.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Among the longest drives in the emirate, so travel can be a quarter to a half of a visiting quote. Several specialist subjects are effectively unavailable in-home at any price, which is a coverage cost rather than a cash one.

regions.name: Al Reef and Al Ghadeer
regions.note: Mainland communities where in-home availability narrows to whoever is already working nearby, so quotes vary widely between providers for identical work. Worth collecting three quotes rather than two.

regions.name: Mussafah and Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Large districts where group tuition at centres is more available than elsewhere, which puts a genuine lower-cost option on the table for subjects where a group format can work at all.

regions.name: Yas Island and Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Younger year-group profile, so more Year 9 and Year 10 enquiries - which is the stage at which the same budget buys the most. Families here are structurally better placed to spend early, and often do not realise it.

schoolClusters.city: Island schools: Al Mushrif, Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
schoolClusters.note: Short journeys and a settled examination culture, which keeps in-home quotes at the lower end and makes the school's own free subject clinics unusually accessible. Ask what the school runs before funding anything; it is the only zero-cost option on the list.

schoolClusters.city: The mainland and island corridor: Khalifa City, Al Raha, Yas and Saadiyat
schoolClusters.note: Longest journeys, highest travel premiums and the sharpest spring-term demand peak in the emirate. The practical consequence is that autumn booking is cheaper and better supplied than spring booking for identical work.

abu-dhabi/igcse-home-tuition.modesIntro: Three purchasing shapes, each with a different cost profile. All are delivered one-to-one over live video, and all include marking of written work within the session rather than as an extra line.

modes.title: Weekly session, bought by the month
modes.description: One or two 50-minute sessions a week, invoiced monthly, with a stated notice period for cancellation. The lowest-risk way to buy tuition because the commitment is short and the exit is cheap, which matters when you do not yet know whether the match will work.
bullets: Monthly invoicing with a stated notice period, not a term's commitment
Marking of written work included in the session
Slot set after the first week, once the household timetable is known
Stops at a month's notice without forfeiting unused sessions

modes.title: Fixed block with a stated end date
modes.description: Six to twelve sessions aimed at one named gap, agreed and priced in advance, finishing on a date set before it starts. The right shape for a diagnosed narrow problem, such as quantitative chemistry or case-study structure, where the work genuinely has a finish line.
bullets: Named target and session count agreed in writing before payment
Baseline in the first session, same check repeated in the last
No automatic rollover into weekly sessions
Unused sessions do not expire inside the agreed window

modes.title: Diagnostic hour, bought on its own
modes.description: A single session that only identifies and prices the problem: what the repeated loss is, whether it is technique or content, how many sessions each would take, and whether the school's own free provision would cover it. Frequently the only thing a family needs to buy.

No obligation to book anything afterwards

modes.title: Transition block between Year 11 and Year 12
modes.description: Four to eight sessions across the summer aimed at the content the next course assumes on day one. Measured per dirham against grade outcomes in the following year, this is consistently the best-value block in the cycle, and almost nobody budgets for it.
bullets: Built from the actual Year 12 course the student is entering

sections.heading: What IGCSE home tuition costs in Abu Dhabi, and what AED 1,000 a month actually buys
paragraphs: The direct answer. As at October 2026, published rates in this market run as follows, each attributed to the provider that published it: EdFlik from AED 45 to AED 65 an hour; Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52; Unitors IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; TutorChase AED 270; BartyED AED 650. Bestimate's 2026 rate table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350, with home tutors advertising up to AED 500, and IB, IGCSE and A-Level specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. Monthly packages advertised include around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. None of these figures are ours.

Those bands are the easy part. The harder and more useful question is what a fixed monthly figure converts into, because that is the number a household actually plans around. A budget of AED 1,000 a month buys four hours of in-home tuition at AED 250, or around five and a half hours of qualified online tuition at AED 180, or sixteen hours at a budget online rate, or ten hours of small-group time. Those are materially different purchases, and three of them are not interchangeable with the fourth.

The reason the conversion matters is frequency. Below roughly one session a week, nothing consolidates: the gap between lessons exceeds the period over which a new method stays available, so each session begins with recovery rather than progress. Above roughly two sessions a week in one subject, returns fall sharply, because the limiting factor becomes the work the student does alone between lessons rather than the teaching. The sweet band for a single IGCSE subject is one to two sessions a week with a written task in between, and the right question about any quote is whether the budget reaches that frequency in the subjects that matter.

Above two sessions a week in one subject, the limit is independent work, not teaching
Ask what a quote converts to in sessions per month, not what it is per hour
Ask whether marking of written work is inside the rate or billed separately

sections.heading: Why the month you spend in matters more than the rate you negotiate
paragraphs: Two households with identical totals can get very different outcomes, and the variable is timing rather than price. An hour in Year 10 can teach: there is room to take a student off the current topic and rebuild a foundation, after which the rest of the syllabus becomes teachable. An hour in February of Year 11 mostly cannot. With the series weeks away, a tutor patches topic by topic in whatever order urgency dictates, and the underlying weakness keeps resurfacing because nobody can afford the eight weeks it would take to remove it.

The quantitative subjects show this most clearly. Algebraic manipulation underpins the later content in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry. Rebuilt in Year 10 across six to eight sessions, it improves performance in three subjects at once, which is the only genuine multiplier available in this market. Addressed in the final term, it is patched inside individual topics at full cost and without the multiplier. The grade still moves. It moves less, in fewer subjects, for more money.

There is a second timing effect that families discover late. Abu Dhabi centres submit forecast grades to the board well before the papers: for a June series the forecast goes in during the spring term, weeks ahead of the first paper, and for a November series it goes in during the autumn, so the window closes earlier than most parents assume. The exams officer at the school holds the exact deadline and will give it on request. Improvement arriving after that submission is invisible to the forecast, which is the figure some conditional sixth-form offers rest on. Work done in the autumn and winter of a June-series year therefore buys two things: grade movement and influence over what the school submits. Work started once the forecast has already gone in buys only the first.

sections.heading: Paying for sixty minutes and receiving forty-two
paragraphs: An hourly rate implies an hour of teaching. In practice a nominal slot contains setting-up, settling, a tutor arriving late because the drive from the island took longer than planned, a hunt for the right exercise book, and a few minutes at the end that nobody uses. The gap between nominal and actual is where a surprising amount of money goes, and it is systematically larger in visiting arrangements than in video ones, for the obvious reason that the drive is a variable and the login is not.

The honest numbers are worth having in front of you when comparing quotes. A 60-minute in-home slot in Abu Dhabi commonly delivers somewhere in the forties of minutes of teaching once arrival, settling and winding down are counted; a 50-minute video session commonly delivers the high forties, because the tutor is present at the stated minute and the student's work was photographed before the lesson started. At AED 250 an hour that difference is not trivial, and nobody puts it in a quote.

Two practical consequences. First, compare quotes on cost per teaching hour rather than per booked hour, and ask what happens when a tutor is late - whether the session runs over, whether it is credited, or whether it simply shrinks. Second, prefer the arrangement where preparation happens before the clock starts: marked work sent in advance, the topic agreed in advance, the task from last week already attempted. That is administration, it is free, and it converts to roughly ten minutes of teaching per session, which over a term is several hours you did not pay for.
bullets: Compare cost per teaching hour, not per booked hour
Ask what happens when a tutor is late: run over, credit, or shrink
Send marked work before the session, not during it
Agree the topic in advance - that alone converts to teaching minutes

sections.heading: The terms nobody reads until they cost money
paragraphs: Tuition in this market is sold informally, and the terms that matter are usually unwritten until a dispute makes them urgent. A family discovers in March that a package expires at the end of the term, or that a session cancelled with four hours' notice is chargeable, or that marking a mock paper is billed separately at an hourly rate. None of these are scandals. They are ordinary commercial terms that were never stated, and the remedy is to ask six questions before paying rather than after.

On pricing specifically, two points of hygiene. Ask whether a quoted figure includes VAT, and get the answer in writing on the invoice; we do not state the UAE VAT treatment of tuition fees on this page, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority citation rather than an opinion. And be careful with the word free: a free trial should mean a stated length, no card details and no obligation, and any provider using free with conditions attached should state those conditions on the same screen as the word.

One further term deserves attention because it involves your child rather than your money. A lead form that collects a child's school, year group, grades and sometimes a photograph is processing personal data about a minor, and the UAE has a personal data protection law - Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021. Ask what is collected, why, how long it is kept and how to have it deleted, and expect a privacy link on every page that asks for it. A provider who cannot answer that about a thirteen-year-old's grade data is telling you something useful.

sections.heading: What a free trial is for, and what it is not
paragraphs: Almost every provider in this market offers a trial, and most families use it to find out whether their child likes the tutor. That is worth knowing and it is the smaller half of the value. A trial is primarily a diagnostic instrument, and the thing to judge is whether the tutor can name the problem by the end of it. A tutor who finishes a 45-minute session with a general impression and an enthusiastic tone has told you nothing you could not have guessed. A tutor who finishes it saying the losses are concentrated in quantitative questions, that this is a stoichiometry gap rather than a Chemistry gap, and that it is four sessions of work, has given you something you can price.

Our own trial is 45 minutes, free, with no card details taken, and it works best if you send a marked paper beforehand - then the session can test a hypothesis instead of forming one. You should expect to leave with three things in writing: the named loss, whether it is technique or content, and the number of sessions each would take. You should also expect, in a reasonable minority of cases, to be told that the school's own free subject clinic would cover this, or that the problem is upstream of any subject and belongs with the learning-support team.

The word free carries an obligation to state the conditions in the same place. Ours are: one trial per student, 45 minutes, no payment details requested, no obligation to book, and the tutor who teaches the trial is the tutor you would continue with unless you ask to change. If any provider's trial requires card details to begin, that is a subscription with a delayed first payment rather than a free trial, and it should be read as such before a date is agreed.
bullets: Judge a trial on whether the tutor can name the loss, not on rapport alone
Send a marked paper first, so the session tests a hypothesis rather than forming one
Expect three things in writing: the loss, technique or content, and sessions needed
A trial requiring card details is a subscription with a delayed payment

sections.heading: The five ways an IGCSE tuition budget gets wasted
paragraphs: These are the patterns we see most often, and each one is identifiable in advance. The first is spreading the budget across five subjects, which produces fortnightly contact in each - below the frequency at which anything consolidates - so every subject feels attended to and none moves. Two subjects weekly beats five subjects fortnightly at the same cost, every time, and choosing the two is the hard part rather than the expensive part.

The second is paying a tutor to supervise homework. A session spent working through whatever the school set that week is pleasant, reassuring and almost valueless, because the agenda is set by the school's timetable rather than by the student's actual losses. The third is funding a target the entry form has already excluded: a Core or Foundation tier entry caps the awardable grade, so tuition aimed above that ceiling cannot deliver it regardless of quality. Ask for the tier in writing before funding anything.

The fourth is sessions with nothing in between. Teaching that is not followed by independent attempt does not become retention, so the loop of task set, task attempted, task checked is the mechanism rather than an optional extra - and a tutor who sets no written work is charging for the enjoyable part only. The fifth is the absence of a review point. A plan that cannot be stopped becomes an annuity, and the amount families spend on tuition that stopped working two months earlier is, in our experience of these conversations, the single largest avoidable cost in this market.
bullets: Five subjects fortnightly consolidates nothing; two subjects weekly does
A tutor supervising homework is working to the school's agenda, not the student's losses
Funding a grade above the tier ceiling cannot work - get the tier in writing
No written task between sessions means no retention
No review point turns a plan into an annuity

sections.heading: Two children, one budget
paragraphs: A large share of Abu Dhabi enquiries involve two children, and the money question is usually framed as whether a shared session halves the cost. Where the children are in different year groups it does not, in any useful sense. Two years of age difference is two years of content difference, so the shared hour becomes one student taught while the other waits, and the household has paid full price for half an hour of attention per child.

The arrangement that does save money is one tutor across consecutive slots. Thirty-five minutes for a Year 9 followed by fifty minutes for a Year 11 costs less than two separately scheduled sessions in administration and in household time, keeps the commitment to a single evening block, and gives each child their own target and record. It also produces a genuine economy the invoice does not show: one tutor who sees both children spots a shared gap - most often algebraic manipulation - and fixes it once rather than twice.

Where a shared session is genuinely the right purchase is the narrow case of two students in the same year, on the same syllabus and tier, with similar profiles. Then the sharing is pedagogically useful, because explaining to a peer consolidates better than listening does, and a per-student rate below the one-to-one figure is fair value. Outside that case, a provider recommending a shared session regardless of the year gap is optimising their calendar rather than your budget, and the difference is visible in how quickly they ask what year each child is in.
bullets: Different years: consecutive slots, not a shared screen
One evening block committed instead of two
A single tutor fixes a shared household gap once rather than twice
